remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.insight: In a sorted list, duplicates are adjacent, so unlink the next node while it has the same value.
steps: Set `cur = head`.
While `cur` and `cur.next` exist, if their values are equal, set `cur.next = cur.next.next`.
Else, move `cur` to `cur.next`.
Return `head`.
hints: In a sorted list, equal values sit next to each other, so compare each node only with its next node.

first-bad-version.insight: The versions form a good-then-bad sequence, so binary search finds the first bad version.
steps: Set `l = 1` and `r = n`.
While `l < r`, compute `mid = l + (r - l) / 2` to avoid overflow.
If `isBadVersion(mid)`, set `r = mid`; else set `l = mid + 1`.
Return `l`.
hints: Every version after a bad version is also bad, so the versions form a good-then-bad sequence with one boundary.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array-ii.insight: Two pointers: copy a number to write index `k` only if it differs from `nums[k - 2]`, so each value appears at most twice.
steps: Set `k = 0`.
For each `x` in `nums`, if `k < 2` or `x != nums[k - 2]`, set `nums[k] = x` and increase `k`.
Return `k`.
hints: After the first two, a value can stay only if it differs from the kept value two places back.

validate-binary-search-tree.insight: Recursive DFS with bounds: pass the open range `(low, high)` down the tree; each node must be strictly inside its range.
steps: Write `valid(node, low, high)` that returns true for a null node.
If `node.val <= low` or `node.val >= high`, return false.
Return `valid(node.left, low, node.val)` and `valid(node.right, node.val, high)`.
Start with infinite bounds, not integer limits, because node values can equal the integer limits.
hints: Each node limits the whole subtree below it, not only its children, so pass a lower bound and an upper bound down.

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.insight: A stack keeps the reduced prefix; a new character that equals the top cancels it.
steps: Start with an empty stack. For each character `c`, if the stack is not empty and its top equals `c`, pop it.
Else, push `c`.
Join the stack from bottom to top and return it.
hints: A removal can make two new letters adjacent, so keep the reduced text so far and compare each new letter with its last letter.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.insight: Binary search on the sorted half; when `nums[mid]` equals `nums[r]`, no half is known sorted, so shrink the range by one.
steps: Set `l = 0` and `r = n - 1`. While `l <= r`, compute `mid`, and return true if `nums[mid] == target`.
If `nums[mid] == nums[r]`, decrease `r` by 1 and continue.
If `nums[mid] < nums[r]`, the right half is sorted; search it if `nums[mid] < target <= nums[r]`, else search left.
Else, the left half is sorted; search it if `nums[l] <= target < nums[mid]`, else search right.
Return false when the range is empty.
hints: One half is always in order, and `nums[mid]` versus `nums[r]` tells which. When they are equal and `nums[mid]` is not the target, `nums[r]` is not either, so drop it.

predict-the-winner.insight: Interval DP on the score difference: the player to move on `nums[i..j]` takes one end and subtracts the best reply difference.
steps: Let `dp[i][j]` be the best score difference for the player to move on `nums[i..j]`.
Set `dp[i][i] = nums[i]`.
For longer intervals, set `dp[i][j] = max(nums[i] - dp[i+1][j], nums[j] - dp[i][j-1])`.
Fill `i` from high to low and `j` from `i + 1` up.
Return `dp[0][n-1] >= 0`, because a tie counts as a win.
hints: The player to move on `nums[i..j]` takes one end, and the opponent then plays the same game on the smaller range. Track the score difference.

find-missing-elements.insight: The smallest and largest values fix the range, so put the numbers in a hash set and scan the range between them.
steps: Find `mn` and `mx`, the minimum and maximum of `nums`, and let `R = mx - mn`.
Put all numbers in a hash set.
For each `x` from `mn + 1` to `mx - 1`, add `x` to the result if the set does not have it.
Return the result, which is already sorted.
hints: The smallest and largest values stay, so the full range is known; check which values in that range do not appear.

copy-list-with-random-pointer.insight: Interleave each copy right after its original node, so `copy.random = original.random.next`, then split the two lists.
steps: If `head` is null, return null.
For each node, insert a new node with the same value right after it.
For each original node `x` with a non-null `random`, set `x.next.random = x.random.next`.
Save `copyHead = head.next`. Walk the list again, restore the original `next` links, and link each copy to the next copy.
Return `copyHead`. As an alternative, use a hash map from original to copy, with `O(n)` extra space.
hints: Put each copy right after its original node; then, when `x.random` is not null, the copy of `x.random` is `x.random.next`.

first-unique-character-in-a-string.insight: Count every character first, then scan again and return the first index whose count is 1.
steps: Count each letter in an array of 26.
Scan `s` from the left and return the first `i` with count 1.
Return -1 if no such index exists.
hints: Uniqueness depends on the whole string, so count all characters first, then scan from the left.

sum-of-subarray-minimums.insight: Contribution technique: monotonic stacks find how many subarrays have `arr[i]` as their minimum.
steps: Find `left[i]`, the index of the previous element strictly less than `arr[i]`, or -1.
Find `right[i]`, the index of the next element less than or equal to `arr[i]`, or `n`.
Use strict on one side and non-strict on the other so equal values are counted once.
Add `arr[i] * (i - left[i]) * (right[i] - i)` to the answer.
Return the sum modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: For each element, count the subarrays where it is the minimum, from the nearest smaller values on each side. With equal values, count a tie on one side only.

single-number-ii.insight: Bit counting: count each bit position modulo 3; bits from the triples cancel, and the remaining bits form the single number.
steps: For each bit `b` from 0 to 31, sum bit `b` over all numbers.
If the sum modulo 3 is 1, set bit `b` in the answer.
In Python, subtract `2^32` from the answer if bit 31 is set.
Return the answer.
hints: Look at one bit position at a time: the triples add a multiple of 3 to each bit count.

second-highest-salary.insight: Sort the distinct salaries in descending order and skip one; wrap the query so that an empty result becomes NULL.
steps: Select `DISTINCT salary` from `Employee`, order by `salary DESC`, and use `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1`.
Wrap that query as a scalar subquery: `SELECT (...) AS SecondHighestSalary`.
Rely on the scalar subquery to return NULL when fewer than two distinct salaries exist.
hints: Skip the top distinct salary. A subquery used as a single value gives NULL when it finds no row, so wrap the query in one.

search-a-2d-matrix.insight: The rows join into one sorted array of length `m * n`, so binary search with index `k` mapped to `matrix[k / n][k % n]`.
steps: Set `l = 0` and `r = m * n - 1`.
While `l <= r`, compute `mid` and read `matrix[mid / n][mid % n]`.
Return true if the value equals `target`.
Set `l = mid + 1` if the value is smaller, else set `r = mid - 1`.
Return false when the range is empty.
hints: Read row by row, the matrix is one sorted list of `m * n` values. Find how a list index maps back to a row and a column.

subsets.insight: Backtracking: for each element, branch on skip or take; every leaf is one subset of the power set.
steps: Write `dfs(i)` with a current list `path`.
If `i == n`, add a copy of `path` to the result and return.
Else, call `dfs(i + 1)` without `nums[i]`. Then append `nums[i]`, call `dfs(i + 1)`, and pop it.
Start with an empty `path` and result, call `dfs(0)`, and return the result.
hints: Each element is either in the subset or not, so each subset is one sequence of take-or-skip choices.

symmetric-tree.insight: A tree is symmetric when its left and right subtrees are mirrors; check mirror pairs with recursive DFS.
steps: Write `mirror(a, b)` that returns true if both nodes are null.
Return false if only one node is null or the values differ.
Return `mirror(a.left, b.right)` and `mirror(a.right, b.left)`.
Call `mirror(root.left, root.right)`.
hints: A tree is symmetric when its left subtree mirrors its right subtree: the outer pair and the inner pair of children must match.

reverse-words-in-a-string.insight: Two pointers cut out each word and skip runs of spaces; then reverse the word order and join with single spaces.
steps: Use two pointers to skip spaces and cut out each word.
Add each word to a list.
Reverse the list.
Join the words with one space and return the result.
hints: Extra spaces carry no meaning, so pull out the words first, then put them back in the opposite order with one space.

maximal-square.insight: DP: the largest square side that ends at a cell is one plus the smallest side at its left, top, and top-left neighbors.
steps: Make `dp` of size `(m + 1) x (n + 1)` filled with 0, and set `s = 0`.
Visit the rows from top to bottom and the columns from left to right.
For each cell with `matrix[i][j] == '1'`, set `dp[i+1][j+1] = 1 + min(dp[i][j], dp[i][j+1], dp[i+1][j])`.
Set `s = max(s, dp[i+1][j+1])`.
Return `s * s`.
hints: A square of side `s` ends at a cell only if squares of side `s - 1` end at its left, top, and top-left neighbors.

reverse-pairs.insight: Merge sort: when both halves are sorted, count the cross pairs `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]` with two pointers before the merge.
steps: For the range `[l, r]`, return 0 if `l >= r`. Else, split at `mid` and count the pairs in each half recursively.
Set `j = mid + 1`. For each `i` from `l` to `mid`, advance `j` while `j <= r` and `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`.
Add `j - (mid + 1)` to the count; `j` never moves back because the left half is sorted.
Merge the two halves by value, and return the count.
Use 64-bit math for `2 * nums[j]` to avoid overflow.
hints: Split the array into two halves. When both halves are in order, one forward scan counts the cross pairs with `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`.

can-place-flowers.insight: Greedy: plant at every empty plot whose neighbors are empty; an early plant never blocks a better placement.
steps: Walk the `m` plots from left to right.
Treat positions outside the array as empty.
If `flowerbed[i]` and both neighbors are 0, set `flowerbed[i] = 1` and decrease `n`.
Return true if `n <= 0`.
hints: A plant as far left as possible never hurts, because it leaves the most room for the plots on the right.

maximum-average-subarray-i.insight: A fixed-size sliding window keeps the sum of `k` elements; the maximum average comes from the maximum sum.
steps: Compute the sum of the first `k` elements, and set `best` to this sum.
For each `i` from `k` to `n - 1`, add `nums[i]` and subtract `nums[i - k]`.
Set `best = max(best, sum)` after each slide.
Return `best / k`.
hints: The length `k` is fixed, so the largest average comes from the largest sum. Each next sum adds one element and removes one.

frequency-of-the-most-frequent-element.insight: Sort, then use a sliding window: the window can all become its right end value if `nums[r] * len - windowSum <= k`.
steps: Sort `nums`, and set `l = 0`, `sum = 0`, and `best = 0`.
Move `r` across the array and add `nums[r]` to `sum`.
While `nums[r] * (r - l + 1) - sum > k`, subtract `nums[l]` and move `l` right.
Set `best = max(best, r - l + 1)`.
Use 64-bit integers for the cost, and return `best`.
hints: Only increments are allowed, so the cheapest values to raise to a target are the values right below it. In ascending order, a run costs `max * len - sum`.

largest-number.insight: Sort the numbers as strings with a custom order: `a` goes before `b` when `a + b > b + a`.
steps: Convert every number to a string.
Sort with the comparator that puts `a` first if `a + b > b + a`.
Join the strings.
If the result starts with `0`, return `"0"`, because all numbers are zero.
hints: For two numbers `a` and `b`, the correct order depends only on whether the string `a + b` beats `b + a`.

odd-even-linked-list.insight: Build the odd chain and the even chain in one pass with two pointers, then link the odd tail to the even head.
steps: If `head` is null, return it.
Set `odd = head`, `even = head.next`, and save `evenHead = even`.
While `even` and `even.next` exist, set `odd.next = even.next` and move `odd` forward.
Then set `even.next = odd.next` and move `even` forward.
Set `odd.next = evenHead` and return `head`.
hints: Build two separate chains in one pass, one for odd positions and one for even positions, then link the odd tail to the even head.

article-views-i.insight: A self-view is a row where `author_id` equals `viewer_id`; filter these rows, remove duplicates, and sort.
steps: Select `DISTINCT author_id AS id` from `Views`.
Keep the rows where `author_id = viewer_id`.
Order the result by `id` in ascending order.
hints: An author views their own article when a row has `author_id` equal to `viewer_id`; one author can match many rows.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.insight: Divide and conquer: the first preorder value is the root, and its inorder index, found with a hash map, splits the two subtrees.
steps: Map each value to its index in `inorder`.
Write `build(i, j, size)`, where `i` starts the preorder range and `j` starts the inorder range.
If `size` is 0, return null.
Take `preorder[i]` as the root, find its inorder index `k`, and set `leftSize = k - j`.
Build the left child from `(i + 1, j, leftSize)` and the right child from `(i + 1 + leftSize, k + 1, size - leftSize - 1)`.
hints: The first preorder value is the root, and its position in `inorder` tells how many nodes go to the left subtree.

swim-in-rising-water.insight: Dijkstra with a min-heap on the path maximum: always expand the reachable cell with the lowest elevation until you reach the corner.
steps: Push `(grid[0][0], 0, 0)` into a min-heap and mark the start cell as seen.
Pop the entry with the smallest time `t`.
If its cell is `(n - 1, n - 1)`, return `t`.
For each unseen neighbor, mark it and push `(max(t, height), row, col)`, where `height` is its elevation.
hints: The cost of a path is its highest cell, so always grow the reachable area through the lowest cell on its border.

set-mismatch.insight: Mark each seen value `v` by a negative sign at index `v - 1`; a mark that is already negative shows the duplicate.
steps: For each value `v = |nums[i]|`, check `nums[v - 1]`.
If it is negative, record `v` as the duplicate; else, negate it.
Scan again and find the index `j` where `nums[j]` is still positive.
Return `[duplicate, j + 1]`, because `j + 1` is the missing value.
hints: Values are in `[1, n]`, so the sign of `nums[v - 1]` can record whether `v` was seen.

longest-non-decreasing-subarray-after-re.insight: Precompute non-decreasing run lengths that end and start at each index; a replacement at `i` can join the runs on both sides.
steps: Compute `left[i]`, the length of the non-decreasing run that ends at `i`.
Compute `right[i]`, the length of the non-decreasing run that starts at `i`.
For each `i`, if `nums[i - 1] <= nums[i + 1]`, take `left[i - 1] + 1 + right[i + 1]` as a candidate.
Else, take `max(left[i - 1], right[i + 1]) + 1` as a candidate.
At the two array ends, treat the missing run as length 0 and always join.
Return the largest candidate.
hints: A replaced element joins the run ending before it with the run starting after it, if the left neighbor is at most the right neighbor. Know both run lengths at every index.

partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.insight: Meet in the middle: enumerate the subsets of each half grouped by size, then pair sizes `k` and `n - k` with binary search.
steps: Split `nums` into two halves of `n` elements each.
For each half, list every subset as a signed sum: chosen elements plus, others minus, grouped by subset size.
Sort each group of the right half.
For each left value `a` of size `k`, binary search the right group of size `n - k` near `-a`.
Return the minimum of `|a + b|` over all such pairs.
hints: Each half has at most 15 elements, so list every subset sum of each half. A size-`k` subset on the left pairs with a size-`n - k` subset on the right.

range-sum-query-immutable.insight: Precompute prefix sums once, so each range sum is the difference of two prefix values.
steps: In the constructor, build `s` of length `n + 1` with `s[0] = 0` and `s[i + 1] = s[i] + nums[i]`.
For `sumRange(left, right)`, return `s[right + 1] - s[left]`.
hints: Many queries hit one fixed array, so store the running totals once; a range sum is then the difference of two totals.

smallest-subsequence-of-distinct-charact.insight: Monotonic stack: pop a larger top letter when it appears again later, so smaller letters move to the front.
steps: Record the last index of each letter.
For each index `i`, skip `s[i]` if it is already in the stack.
While the stack top is greater than `s[i]` and appears after `i`, pop it and clear its mark.
Push `s[i]` and mark it as in the stack.
Return the stack as a string.
hints: A larger letter already chosen can go when a smaller letter arrives and the larger letter appears again later.

check-divisibility-by-digit-sum-and-prod.insight: Extract the digits with modulo 10 to get their sum and product, then do one divisibility test.
steps: Set `s = 0`, `p = 1`, and `x = n`.
While `x > 0`, take `d = x % 10`, add `d` to `s`, and multiply `p` by `d`.
Set `x` to `x` divided by 10 with integer division at the end of each loop.
Return true if `n % (s + p) == 0`.
hints: Take the digits one at a time with `% 10` and `// 10`, and build the sum and the product together.

distinct-subsequences.insight: DP over prefixes: `dp[i][j]` counts the ways to form `t[:j]` from `s[:i]`; a match adds the ways that use `s[i-1]`.
steps: Make an `(m + 1) x (n + 1)` table `dp` of zeros, where `m` and `n` are the lengths of `s` and `t`.
Set `dp[i][0] = 1` for every `i`, because the empty `t` matches once.
For `i` from 1 to `m` and `j` from 1 to `n`, set `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]` to skip `s[i-1]`.
Return `dp[m][n]`.
hints: Each character of `s` is either skipped or, when it matches, used for the current character of `t`. Count the ways for each pair of prefixes.

minimum-operations-to-reduce-x-to-zero.insight: Removals from both ends leave a middle subarray with sum `total - x`; find the longest such subarray with a sliding window.
steps: Set `target = sum(nums) - x`; if `target < 0`, return -1.
Move `r` across the array and add `nums[r]` to the window sum.
While the sum is above `target`, subtract `nums[l]` and move `l` right.
If the sum equals `target`, update the longest length with `r - l + 1`.
Return `n - longest`, or -1 if no window matched.
hints: Removals from both ends leave one middle subarray, so find the longest subarray with sum `total - x`.

minimum-sum-of-squared-difference.insight: Merge `k1` and `k2` into one budget, then greedily lower the largest differences first, level by level, with a count array.
steps: Set `k = k1 + k2` and compute each `d = |nums1[i] - nums2[i]|`.
If the sum of all `d` is at most `k`, return 0.
Count the differences in `cnt` and scan each value `v` from the largest `M` down.
Move `take = min(cnt[v], k)` items from `v` to `v - 1`, and subtract `take` from `k`.
Stop when `k` is 0, then return the sum of `cnt[v] * v * v`.
hints: `k1` and `k2` act as one shared budget, and each unit does the most good on the current largest difference.

merge-k-sorted-lists.insight: Keep the current head of each list in a min-heap; pop the smallest node, append it, and push its successor.
steps: Push every non-null head of the `k` lists into a min-heap keyed by value.
Pop the smallest node and append it to the result tail.
If the node has a next node, push that node into the heap.
Repeat for all `N` nodes until the heap is empty, then return `dummy.next`.
hints: The next node of the result is always the smallest among the `k` current list heads.

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.insight: Two pointers with a gap: give a fast pointer an `n`-step lead, so the slow pointer stops at the node before the target.
steps: Make a dummy node before `head`, and start `fast` and `slow` at it.
Move `fast` forward `n` steps.
Move both pointers until `fast.next` is null.
Set `slow.next = slow.next.next` and return `dummy.next`.
Use the dummy so that removal of the head needs no special case.
hints: Give one walker an `n`-node lead; when it reaches the last node, the other is right before the target. Start both at a dummy node before `head`.

set-matrix-zeroes.insight: Use the first row and the first column as zero markers, with two flags for whether they themselves need zeros.
steps: Set two flags if the first row or the first column has a 0.
For each cell with `i >= 1` and `j >= 1` and value 0, set `matrix[i][0]` and `matrix[0][j]` to 0.
For each cell with `i >= 1` and `j >= 1`, set it to 0 if its row or column marker is 0.
Last, set the first row and the first column to 0 if their flags are set.
hints: Store each row's zero marker in its first cell and each column's marker in its top cell. Row 0 and column 0 share one corner, so track them apart.

reverse-linked-list-ii.insight: Walk to the node before `left`, then move each next node of the window to the front of the window, in one pass.
steps: Make a dummy node before `head`, and move `pre` from it `left - 1` steps.
Set `cur = pre.next`.
Repeat `right - left` times: take `nxt = cur.next` and set `cur.next = nxt.next`.
Insert `nxt` right after `pre`: set `nxt.next = pre.next` and `pre.next = nxt`.
Return `dummy.next`.
hints: Stop at the node before position `left`; then move each later node of the range to the front of the range, one at a time.

word-ladder.insight: BFS on words finds the shortest sequence; the neighbors of a word are the dictionary words that differ in one letter.
steps: Put the `N` words of `wordList` in a set; if `endWord` is not in it, return 0.
Start BFS from `beginWord` at level 1.
For each word, try each of the 26 letters at each of the `L` positions.
If a new word is in the set, remove it from the set and add it to the queue.
When you add `endWord`, return the current level plus 1. If the queue empties, return 0.
hints: Treat each word as a node, with an edge to each dictionary word one letter away. To find neighbors fast, try all 26 letters at each position.

word-break.insight: DP over prefixes: `dp[i]` is true when some `dp[j]` is true and `s[j:i]` is a dictionary word.
steps: Put the words in a hash set of total length `D`. Make `dp` of `n + 1` false values, and set `dp[0] = true`.
For each `i` from 1 to `n`, check each `j` with `i - j` at most `L`, the longest word length.
If `dp[j]` is true and `s[j:i]` is in the set, set `dp[i] = true` and stop.
Return `dp[n]`.
hints: A prefix of `s` can be split if a shorter splittable prefix plus one dictionary word forms it.

course-schedule-ii.insight: Kahn's topological sort: take courses with in-degree 0 in order; the pop order is a valid schedule if it has every course.
steps: Build edges `b -> a` for each of the `E` pairs `[a, b]` and count in-degrees.
Put every course with in-degree 0 into a queue.
Pop a course, append it to the order, and decrease the in-degree of its neighbors.
Push each neighbor whose in-degree becomes 0.
Return the order if it has all `V` courses, else return an empty array.
hints: A course is ready when all its prerequisites are done; take ready courses one by one and update the counts of the others.

russian-doll-envelopes.insight: Sort by width ascending and height descending; the answer is then the longest strictly increasing subsequence of the heights.
steps: Sort the envelopes by width ascending, and by height descending when widths tie.
Use the descending tie order so that envelopes of equal width cannot nest.
Run the binary-search LIS on the heights with a `tails` array.
For each height, replace the first tail `>= height`, or append it if none exists.
Return the length of `tails`.
hints: After you order by width, only heights matter, but equal widths cannot nest; so put equal widths in descending height order.

number-of-provinces.insight: A province is a connected component, so a DFS from each unvisited city marks one whole province.
steps: Make a `visited` array of size `n` and set the count to 0.
For each city `i` that is not visited, add one to the count and call `dfs(i)`.
In `dfs(u)`, mark `u` as visited.
Call `dfs(j)` for each city `j` that is not visited and has `isConnected[u][j] == 1`.
Return the count after the loop.
hints: A province is one connected group of cities. Count how many times you start from a city that no earlier group reached.

accounts-merge.insight: Use union-find on account indices and join two accounts when they share an email.
steps: Make a union-find over the account indices.
Keep a map from each email to the first account index that has it; `L` is the total email count.
If an email is already in the map, union the current account with the stored account.
For each email in the map, group it under the root of its stored account.
For each group, sort the emails and put the root account name first.
hints: Two accounts belong to one person when they share an email, and these links chain across accounts. Each person is one connected group of accounts.

capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.insight: A larger capacity never needs more days, so binary search on the answer finds the least capacity.
steps: Set `lo` to the maximum weight and `hi` to the total weight `S`.
For a candidate capacity, load packages in order and start a new day when the load exceeds it.
If the day count is at most `days`, the capacity is feasible.
Binary search for the smallest feasible capacity in `[lo, hi]`.
hints: If a capacity ships all packages within `days` days, every larger capacity also does. Can you test one candidate capacity in a single pass?

fizz-buzz.insight: A single pass with divisibility checks builds the answer; test divisibility by 15 first.
steps: For each `i` from 1 to `n`, check `i % 15 == 0` first and add "FizzBuzz".
Else, if `i % 3 == 0`, add "Fizz".
Else, if `i % 5 == 0`, add "Buzz".
Else, add the string form of `i`.
hints: A number divisible by both 3 and 5 is divisible by 15, so check that case before the single-divisor cases.

majority-element-ii.insight: At most two values can appear more than `n / 3` times, so Boyer-Moore voting with two candidates finds them.
steps: Keep two candidates and two counts, and set all of them to zero.
If the value equals a candidate, increment the count of that candidate.
Else, if a count is zero, make the value that candidate with count 1.
Else, decrement both counts.
In a second pass, count each distinct candidate, and keep it only if it appears more than `n / 3` times.
hints: At most two values can appear more than `n / 3` times. If you cancel three different values together, these frequent values survive.

combinations.insight: Backtracking picks numbers in increasing order, so each combination appears once.
steps: Write `dfs(start)` that holds the current path.
If the path has `k` numbers, add a copy to the answer and return.
For each `j` from `start` to `n`, push `j`, call `dfs(j + 1)`, then pop `j`.
Stop the loop early when too few numbers remain to reach length `k`.
hints: Build each combination in increasing order of numbers, so every set appears only once. Stop early when too few numbers remain to reach `k`.

kth-missing-positive-number.insight: The count of missing numbers before index `i` is `arr[i] - i - 1`, which increases, so binary search applies.
steps: Binary search for the first index `i` where `arr[i] - i - 1 >= k`.
Let `left` be that index; it can be `n` if no index qualifies.
Return `left + k`, because `left` array values are below the answer.
hints: Before index `i`, exactly `arr[i] - i - 1` positive numbers are missing, and this count never decreases as `i` grows.

count-and-say.insight: Start from "1" and build each term from the previous term with run-length encoding. `m` is the length of the longest term.
steps: Set `s` to "1".
Repeat `n - 1` times.
Scan `s` with two pointers to find each run of equal characters.
For each run, append the run length and then the character to a new string.
Replace `s` with the new string.
hints: A group of equal digits ends where the digit changes or where the string ends. Handle the last group the same way as the others.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.insight: In a BST, the LCA is the first node on the root path whose value lies between `p` and `q`. `h` is the tree height.
steps: Start at the root.
If both `p.val` and `q.val` are smaller than the node value, go to the left child.
If both are larger, go to the right child.
Else, return the current node.
hints: If `p` and `q` are both smaller than a node, the answer is in its left subtree. Where do the paths to `p` and `q` split?

valid-parenthesis-string.insight: A greedy scan keeps the minimum and maximum possible count of open parentheses.
steps: Set `lo` and `hi` to 0.
For '(', increment both; for ')', decrement both; for '*', decrement `lo` and increment `hi`.
If `hi` becomes negative, return false.
Set `lo` to `max(lo, 0)` after each character.
At the end, return `lo == 0`.
hints: A `*` makes the count of open parentheses uncertain. Track the smallest and the largest count that are possible at each position.

find-the-highest-altitude.insight: Each altitude is a prefix sum of `gain`, so the answer is the maximum prefix sum, with the start altitude 0 included.
steps: Set `alt` and `best` to 0.
For each value in `gain`, add it to `alt`.
Update `best` with `max(best, alt)`.
Return `best`.
hints: Each altitude is the running total of `gain` up to that point, and the start altitude 0 also counts.

number-of-recent-calls.insight: Ping times only increase, so a queue drops old requests from the front and its size is the answer.
steps: Keep a queue of ping times.
On `ping(t)`, push `t` to the back.
Pop from the front while the front time is less than `t - 3000`.
Return the queue size; `W` is the count of pings in the 3000 ms window.
hints: Ping times only increase, so a request that falls out of the 3000 ms range never returns. Drop old requests from the oldest end.

path-with-minimum-effort.insight: Dijkstra with a min-heap works when the path cost is the maximum edge, not the sum of edges.
steps: Set `dist` of every cell to infinity and `dist[0][0]` to 0. `m` and `n` are the row and column counts.
Push `(0, 0, 0)` as `(effort, row, col)` into a min-heap.
Pop the cell with the smallest effort; if it is the target, return the effort.
For each neighbor, compute `max(effort, abs(height difference))`.
If that value is less than the neighbor `dist`, update it and push the neighbor.
hints: The effort of a path is its largest single step, not a total. Always extend the reachable cell with the lowest effort found so far.

maximum-good-subarray-sum.insight: A subarray sum is a difference of prefix sums, so a hash map stores the smallest prefix sum before each value.
steps: Set `s = 0` and the answer to negative infinity.
Keep a map from value `v` to the smallest prefix sum before an index that holds `v`.
For each index `i`, first store `nums[i]` with the prefix sum before `i`, and keep the smaller sum.
Add `nums[i]` to `s`. Check the keys `nums[i] - k` and `nums[i] + k` separately.
For each key in the map, update the answer with `s` minus its stored sum.
Return 0 if the answer is still negative infinity, else the answer.
hints: A subarray sum is the running total at its end minus the running total before its start. For each value, remember the smallest total before an index that holds it.

search-in-a-binary-search-tree.insight: The BST order tells which single subtree can hold the value, so each comparison drops one side. `h` is the tree height.
steps: Start at the root.
If the node is null or its value equals `val`, return the node.
If `val` is less than the node value, go left.
Else, go right.
hints: The value order of the tree tells you which single subtree can hold `val`, so each comparison removes one side.

power-of-three.insight: Divide by 3 while the number is divisible; a power of three reduces to exactly 1.
steps: If `n <= 0`, return false.
While `n % 3 == 0`, divide `n` by 3.
Return `n == 1`.
Without loops, return `n > 0 and 1162261467 % n == 0`, because `3^19` is the largest power in range.
hints: A power of three has no prime factor other than 3. Remove factors of 3 and check what remains.

find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.insight: Count the digits of each number and test the parity of that count.
steps: For each number, find its digit count with repeated division by 10; `M` is the largest value.
If the count is even, add one to the answer.
Return the answer.
hints: Each integer division by 10 removes one decimal digit.

find-the-safest-path-in-a-grid.insight: Multi-source BFS from all thieves gives each cell its safeness; then a max-heap Dijkstra maximizes the minimum safeness on the path.
steps: Run BFS from all thief cells together to get `dist` for every cell.
Push `(dist[0][0], 0, 0)` into a max-heap and mark the start as seen.
Pop the cell with the largest value; if it is `(n - 1, n - 1)`, return that value.
For each unseen neighbor, mark it and push `min(value, dist of neighbor)`.
hints: First compute the distance from every cell to its nearest thief, with all thieves as starts at the same time. A path then scores its smallest cell distance.

stone-game-iii.insight: Use DP on suffixes: `dp[i]` is the best score difference the current player can get from index `i`.
steps: Set `dp[n]` to 0.
For `i` from `n - 1` down to 0, take 1, 2, or 3 stones, but not more than `n - i`.
For each choice, the value is the sum taken minus `dp[j + 1]`, where `j` is the last stone taken.
Set `dp[i]` to the maximum value.
Return "Alice" if `dp[0] > 0`, "Bob" if `dp[0] < 0`, else "Tie".
hints: Both players face the same game on the remaining stones. Track the best score difference that the current player can get from index `i`.

richest-customer-wealth.insight: The wealth of a customer is a row sum, so the answer is the maximum row sum.
steps: For each row of `accounts`, compute the sum.
Keep the largest sum.
Return the largest sum.
hints: The wealth of a customer is the sum of one row, so compare the row sums.

dungeon-game.insight: Run DP from the princess back to the start, because the health need at a cell depends only on later cells.
steps: Let `dp[i][j]` be the minimum health needed on entry to cell `(i, j)`.
Set `dp[m][n - 1]` and `dp[m - 1][n]` to 1, and all other border cells to infinity.
For `i` and `j` in reverse order, set `need` to `min(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j + 1]) - dungeon[i][j]`.
Set `dp[i][j]` to `max(1, need)`, because health must stay at least 1.
Return `dp[0][0]`.
hints: The health that you need at a cell depends only on the cells after it. Work backward from the princess, and keep health at least 1.

subsets-ii.insight: Sort the array, then backtrack and skip a value equal to the previous one at the same tree level.
steps: Sort `nums`.
Write `dfs(start)` that first adds a copy of the current path to the answer.
For each `j` from `start` to `n - 1`, skip `j` if `j > start` and `nums[j] == nums[j - 1]`.
Else, push `nums[j]`, call `dfs(j + 1)`, then pop.
hints: Duplicate subsets come from equal values in different positions. Put equal values next to each other, and at each choice point use a repeated value only once.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.insight: A post-order DFS returns the best downward path from each node and updates a global answer with the path that bends there. `h` is the tree height.
steps: Write `dfs(node)` that returns 0 for a null node.
Set `left` and `right` to the larger of 0 and the child result, to drop negative branches.
Update the answer with `node.val + left + right`.
Return `node.val + max(left, right)` to the parent.
Start the answer at negative infinity, because all values can be negative.
hints: A best path bends at one highest node and uses at most one downward branch on each side. Drop a branch when its sum is negative.

implement-stack-using-queues.insight: Keep the queue in stack order: after each push, rotate the older items behind the new item.
steps: On `push(x)`, add `x` to the back of the queue.
Then move the front item to the back `size - 1` times, so `x` is at the front. `n` is the stack size.
On `pop`, remove and return the front item.
On `top`, return the front item; on `empty`, return whether the queue is empty.
hints: The allowed removal takes the front item, but a stack must return the newest item. Moving a front item to the back changes which item is at the front.

pacific-atlantic-water-flow.insight: Search in reverse from each ocean border and move only to cells of equal or greater height.
steps: Run BFS or DFS from all top row and left column cells to mark the cells that reach the Pacific.
Run a second search from all bottom row and right column cells to mark the cells that reach the Atlantic.
In each search, enter an unmarked neighbor only if its height is at least the current height.
Return the cells that both searches mark.
hints: Do not search from every cell. Start from the cells on each ocean border and move uphill, to cells of equal or greater height.

big-countries.insight: One table scan with an OR filter selects the countries that meet either size condition.
steps: Select `name`, `population`, and `area` from `World`; `n` is its row count.
Keep rows where `area >= 3000000` OR `population >= 25000000`.
hints: A country that meets only one size limit still belongs in the result.

valid-sudoku.insight: Use one set of seen digits for each row, each column, and each 3 x 3 box, and stop on a repeat.
steps: Make 9 sets for rows, 9 for columns, and 9 for boxes.
For each filled cell `(i, j)`, compute the box index `(i // 3) * 3 + j // 3`.
If the digit is already in its row, column, or box set, return false.
Else, add the digit to all three sets.
Return true after the scan.
hints: Each filled digit belongs to one row, one column, and one 3 x 3 box. The box of cell `(i, j)` is `(i // 3) * 3 + j // 3`.

sudoku-solver.insight: Backtracking fills empty cells one at a time, with row, column, and box sets to reject conflicts in constant time.
steps: Record the used digits for each row, column, and box, and list the `E` empty cells.
Write `dfs(k)` that fills the `k`-th empty cell and returns true when all cells are filled.
Try each digit that is not in the row, column, or box of the cell.
Place the digit, mark it used, and call `dfs(k + 1)`. If it returns true, return true.
Else, remove the digit and unmark it before the next digit.
Return false when all digits fail. Start with `dfs(0)`.
hints: A digit that fits one cell now can leave a later cell with no valid digit. Keep each choice reversible, and record the used digits per row, column, and box.

insert-interval.insight: The intervals are sorted and disjoint, so one linear pass splits them into left, overlap, and right parts.
steps: Add every interval that ends before `newInterval` starts to the answer.
Merge every interval that starts at or before the end of `newInterval` into it with min and max.
Add the merged `newInterval`.
Add the remaining intervals.
hints: The intervals are already sorted and do not overlap. They split into three parts: fully left of `newInterval`, overlapping it, and fully right of it.

edit-distance.insight: Use 2D DP: `dp[i][j]` is the edit distance between the first `i` characters of `word1` and the first `j` of `word2`. `m` and `n` are the two lengths.
steps: Set `dp[i][0] = i` and `dp[0][j] = j`.
If `word1[i - 1] == word2[j - 1]`, set `dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1]`.
Else, set `dp[i][j]` to 1 plus the minimum of `dp[i - 1][j]`, `dp[i][j - 1]`, and `dp[i - 1][j - 1]`.
Return `dp[m][n]`.
hints: The best cost for the full strings depends on the best costs for shorter prefixes. Compare the last characters of the two prefixes.

minimum-window-substring.insight: A sliding window grows on the right until it covers `t`, then shrinks on the left while it still covers `t`.
steps: Count the characters of `t` in `need`, and set `missing` to the length of `t`; `C` is the alphabet size.
Move `right`; if `need` of the character is positive, decrement `missing`; always decrement `need`.
While `missing == 0`, record the window if it is the shortest so far.
Then increment `need` of the left character, and if it becomes positive, increment `missing`.
Move `left` forward, and return the shortest window or an empty string.
hints: If a range covers `t`, every larger range covers it too. Extra copies of a required character can leave the range while enough copies remain.

remove-k-digits.insight: A monotonic increasing stack removes a digit when a smaller digit follows it, which makes the number smallest.
steps: For each digit, pop the stack while `k > 0` and the top is greater than the digit.
Decrement `k` for each pop, then push the digit.
If `k > 0` after the scan, remove `k` digits from the end.
Strip leading zeros, and return "0" if the result is empty.
hints: A digit that is larger than the digit after it makes the number bigger. Remove such digits from the left first.

coin-change-ii.insight: Use complete knapsack DP with coins in the outer loop, so each combination counts once regardless of order.
steps: Set `dp[0] = 1` and all other `dp` values to 0.
For each coin `c`, loop `x` from `c` up to `amount`. `n` is the number of coins.
Add `dp[x - c]` to `dp[x]`.
Return `dp[amount]`.
hints: Order does not matter, so `1 + 2` and `2 + 1` are one way. Add coin types one at a time, and update the way count for every amount.

random-pick-with-weight.insight: Prefix sums of the weights split the total into segments, and binary search finds the segment of a random number.
steps: Build the prefix sum array `pre` of `w` once in O(n) time; `n` is the length of `w`.
On `pickIndex`, draw a random integer `x` in `[1, pre[-1]]`.
Binary search for the first index `i` with `pre[i] >= x`.
Return `i`.
hints: Lay the weights end to end on a number line of length `sum(w)`. A random point lands in the segment of index `i` with the correct probability.

find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.insight: Use the array itself as a marker set: negate the value at index `x - 1` for each value `x`.
steps: For each value `x`, let `i = abs(x) - 1`.
If `nums[i]` is positive, negate it.
After the pass, each index `i` with a positive value means `i + 1` is missing.
Return all such `i + 1`.
hints: Each value `x` points to index `x - 1`. Mark that index inside the array itself, without losing the value that it holds.

sum-of-two-integers.insight: XOR gives the sum without carry and AND shifted left gives the carry; repeat until the carry is zero.
steps: Loop while `b` is not zero.
Set `carry` to `(a & b) << 1`.
Set `a` to `a ^ b` and `b` to `carry`.
In Python, mask each value with `0xFFFFFFFF`, and convert a final value above `0x7FFFFFFF` to a negative number.
Return `a`.
hints: Split addition into two parts: the sum without carry, and the carry bits. Which bit operations produce each part?

candy.insight: Two greedy passes handle the left neighbor rule and the right neighbor rule; each child takes the larger result.
steps: Set `left[i] = 1` for all `i`.
For `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, if `ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]`, set `left[i] = left[i - 1] + 1`.
Set `right = 1` and the total to `left[n - 1]`.
For `i` from `n - 2` down to 0, set `right` to `right + 1` if `ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]`, else to 1.
Add `max(left[i], right)` to the total, and return the total after the loop.
hints: Without the right-neighbor rule, the minimum count of a child is the length of the rising run that ends at it. The right-neighbor rule is the mirror image.

implement-queue-using-stacks.insight: Use an input stack and an output stack; move items to the output stack only when it is empty.
steps: On `push(x)`, push `x` onto the input stack.
On `pop` or `peek`, if the output stack is empty, move all items from the input stack to it.
Then pop or read the top of the output stack.
On `empty`, return true only if both stacks are empty. `n` is the item count.
hints: Moving all items from one stack to another reverses their order, so the oldest item comes to the top. Moved items can stay there until you remove them.

online-stock-span.insight: A monotonic decreasing stack of `(price, span)` pairs merges the spans of all lower or equal earlier prices.
steps: On `next(price)`, set `span` to 1.
While the stack top price is at most `price`, pop it and add its span to `span`.
Push `(price, span)` onto the stack.
Return `span`. `n` is the number of calls to `next`.
hints: An earlier day with a price at most today's price can never end a later span. Only the days that can still end a span need to stay.

assign-cookies.insight: Sort both arrays and give each child the smallest cookie that satisfies it, with two pointers.
steps: Sort `g` of length `m` and `s` of length `n`.
Set pointer `i` on children and `j` on cookies to 0.
If `s[j] >= g[i]`, increment `i`.
Always increment `j`, and stop when either array ends.
Return `i`.
assign-cookies.time: O(m log m + n log n)
hints: The child with the smallest need is the easiest to satisfy. Match small needs with small cookies first, and do not waste a large cookie.

path-sum-iii.insight: Prefix sums along the root path, stored in a hash map of counts, find downward paths with sum `targetSum`.
steps: Keep a map `cnt` from prefix sum to count, with `cnt[0] = 1`.
In a DFS, add the node value to the running sum `s`.
Add `cnt[s - targetSum]` to the answer, then increment `cnt[s]`.
Recurse into both children.
Before return, decrement `cnt[s]`, so other branches do not see this path.
hints: A downward path sum is the difference of two root-to-node totals on one path. Include a total of zero for the point above the root.

car-pooling.insight: A difference array over locations adds passengers at each pickup and removes them at each drop-off.
steps: Make a difference array `d` that covers all locations up to the largest location `M`.
For each trip, add `numPassengers` at `from` and subtract it at `to`.
Scan `d` and keep the running sum of passengers.
If the running sum exceeds `capacity` at any location, return false.
Return true after the scan.
hints: The passenger count changes only at pickup and drop-off locations. A passenger who leaves at a location does not use a seat there.

range-sum-query-2d-immutable.insight: A 2D prefix sum array answers each rectangle sum in constant time with inclusion-exclusion.
steps: Build `s` of size `(m + 1) x (n + 1)`, where `m` and `n` are the row and column counts of `matrix`.
Let `s[i][j]` be the sum of the top-left `i x j` block.
For a query, return `s[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - s[r1][c2 + 1] - s[r2 + 1][c1] + s[r1][c1]`.
hints: Precompute the sum of every rectangle that starts at the top-left corner. Any rectangle sum is then a combination of four such sums.

subarray-sums-divisible-by-k.insight: Two prefix sums with the same remainder modulo `k` bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by `k`.
steps: Keep a count map of remainders, with `cnt[0] = 1`.
Add each value to the running sum `s`, and compute `r = ((s % k) + k) % k`.
Add `cnt[r]` to the answer, then increment `cnt[r]`.
Keep the extra `+ k`, because negative values give negative remainders in some languages.
hints: A subarray sum is divisible by `k` when the running totals at its two ends have the same remainder modulo `k`. Make negative remainders positive.

move-pieces-to-obtain-a-string.insight: Pieces cannot pass each other, so the piece sequences must match, and each piece can move only in its own direction.
steps: List the non-blank characters with their indices for `start` and for `target`.
If the lists have different lengths, return false.
Compare the pairs in order; if the letters differ, return false.
For an 'L', return false if its `start` index is less than its `target` index.
For an 'R', return false if its `start` index is greater than its `target` index.
Else, return true.
hints: Pieces cannot pass each other, so the letter sequences without blanks must be equal. An `L` moves only left, and an `R` moves only right.

convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.insight: Build the tree in in-order sequence, so the list pointer moves forward once and each middle node becomes a root.
steps: Count the list length `n`.
Write `build(l, r)` that returns null if `l > r`.
Let `mid = (l + r) // 2`, and build the left subtree with `build(l, mid - 1)`.
Make a node from the current list node, then move the list pointer to the next node.
Build the right subtree with `build(mid + 1, r)` and return the node.
hints: Once you know each subtree's size, you can decide its shape before you consume its values from the list.

implement-trie-prefix-tree.insight: Each trie node holds child links for each letter and an end flag, so operations walk one node per character.
steps: Make a node with 26 child links and an `isEnd` flag; `L` is the word length.
On `insert`, walk the characters, make missing children, and set `isEnd` on the last node.
Write a helper that walks a string and returns the last node or null.
On `search`, return true if the helper node exists and has `isEnd` set.
On `startsWith`, return true if the helper node exists; `T` is the total inserted characters.
hints: After inserting `apple`, a search for `app` must fail while a start check for `app` succeeds. What extra fact distinguishes these results?

binary-tree-right-side-view.insight: A level-order BFS sees each level in order, and the last node of each level is visible from the right.
steps: Push the root into a queue if it is not null.
For each level, pop exactly the current queue size of nodes.
Push the left and right children of each popped node.
Add the value of the last popped node of the level to the answer.
hints: From the right side, you see one node per depth: the last node at that depth in left-to-right order.

find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.insight: Store every number prefix of `arr1` in a hash set, then remove digits from each `arr2` value until a prefix matches.
steps: For each `x` in `arr1`, while `x > 0`, add `x` to a set and set `x` to `x // 10`.
For each `y` in `arr2`, set `y` to `y // 10` until `y` is in the set or is 0.
If `y` is in the set, update the answer with the digit count of `y`.
Return the answer, or 0 if no prefix matches. `m` and `n` are the lengths of `arr1` and `arr2`, and `M` is the largest value.
hints: Integer division by 10 removes the last digit and leaves a shorter prefix. Each positive input has only a few such prefixes.

maximum-score-from-grid-operations.insight: Column DP on black heights: the score of a column depends only on its own height and the heights of its two neighbors.
steps: Let `k[j]` in `0..n` be the black height of column `j`, and `s[j][h]` the sum of its top `h` cells.
Column `j` scores `max(0, s[j][max(k[j - 1], k[j + 1])] - s[j][k[j]])`, with height 0 outside the grid.
Let `f[cur][prev]` be the best score before column `j`, with `k[j] = cur` and `k[j - 1] = prev`. For column 0, set `f[cur][0] = 0` and other states to negative infinity.
For next height `nxt`, case `prev <= nxt`: take the prefix maximum of `f[cur][prev]` and add `max(0, s[j][nxt] - s[j][cur])`.
Case `prev > nxt`: take the suffix maximum of `f[cur][prev] + max(0, s[j][prev] - s[j][cur])`. Set the new `f[nxt][cur]` to the larger case.
After the last column, add its score with right height 0, and return the largest value.
hints: The score of a column depends only on its own black height and the heights of its two neighbors. Process columns left to right and keep the last two heights.

customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-an.insight: A LEFT JOIN with a NULL filter finds visits that have no transaction, and GROUP BY counts them per customer.
steps: LEFT JOIN `Visits` (`n` rows) to `Transactions` (`m` rows) on `visit_id`.
Keep rows where `transaction_id` IS NULL.
GROUP BY `customer_id` and return `COUNT(*)` as `count_no_trans`.
hints: A visit without a transaction has no matching row in `Transactions`. One customer can have both kinds of visits, so check each visit.

find-the-prefix-common-array-of-two-arra.insight: Count how many times each value has appeared in both prefixes; a value becomes common when its count reaches 2.
steps: Make a count array `cnt` of size `n + 1` and set `common` to 0.
At index `i`, increment `cnt[A[i]]`, and if it becomes 2, increment `common`.
Do the same for `B[i]`.
Set `C[i] = common`.
hints: Only the two values read at index `i` can change the common count. Each value appears exactly once in each array.

angle-between-hands-of-a-clock.insight: Compute each hand angle from 12 o'clock with direct math, then take the smaller of the two angles between them.
steps: Set the minute angle to `6 * minutes`.
Set the hour angle to `30 * (hour % 12) + 0.5 * minutes`.
Let `d` be the absolute difference of the two angles.
Return `min(d, 360 - d)`.
hints: The hour hand also moves with the minutes, at 0.5 degrees per minute. The answer is the smaller of the angle and `360` minus it.

subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.insight: With `n` at most 100, fix each left end, extend the right end, and keep a set of distinct values.
steps: For each left end `i`, make an empty set.
For each right end `j` from `i` to `n - 1`, add `nums[j]` to the set.
Add the square of the set size to the answer.
Return the answer.
hints: `n` is at most 100, so every subarray is affordable. Extending a subarray by one element raises its distinct count only when that value is new.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.insight: DP over the last value with `up` and `down` counts, and prefix sums make each length step linear in the value range.
steps: Map values to `0..m - 1`, where `m = r - l + 1`, and set `up[v] = down[v] = 1`.
Let `up[v]` count arrays that end at `v` with a rise, and `down[v]` with a fall.
Repeat `n - 1` times: new `up[v]` is the sum of `down[u]` for all `u < v`.
New `down[v]` is the sum of `up[u]` for all `u > v`.
Compute both sums with prefix and suffix sums modulo `10^9 + 7`.
Return the sum of all `up` and `down` values modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: The next value depends only on the last value and the direction of the last step. After a rise, the next value must be smaller.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-i.insight: Because `nums` is sorted, each connected component is a contiguous run of indices, split where the adjacent gap exceeds `maxDiff`.
steps: Set `group[0] = 0`.
For each `i` from 1, increment the group id if `nums[i] - nums[i - 1] > maxDiff`.
Set `group[i]` to the current group id.
For each query `(u, v)`, return `group[u] == group[v]`.
hints: `nums` is sorted, so each connected group is a run of adjacent indices. A group ends where the gap between neighbors exceeds `maxDiff`.

sequential-digits.insight: Only 36 numbers have sequential digits, so generate each from a start digit and keep those in `[low, high]`.
steps: For each start digit `d` from 1 to 9, set `x = d`.
Append the next digit with `x = x * 10 + next` while the next digit is at most 9.
After each append, keep `x` if it is in `[low, high]`.
Sort the kept numbers and return them.
hints: Only 36 numbers have sequential digits. Each one is fixed by its first digit and its length.

minimum-height-trees.insight: Topological trimming removes leaves layer by layer; the last one or two nodes are the centers of the tree.
steps: If `n == 1`, return `[0]`.
Build the adjacency list and the degree of each node.
Put all nodes with degree 1 in a queue.
Remove leaves level by level; decrement neighbor degrees and queue each new leaf.
Return the nodes of the last level that you remove.
hints: For a tree with more than two nodes, a leaf is never a best root: its neighbor has a smaller greatest distance.

minimum-number-of-pushes-to-type-word-i.insight: All letters are distinct, so a greedy plan fills the 8 keys evenly: 8 letters cost 1 push, the next 8 cost 2.
steps: Let `n` be the word length.
For the letter at 0-based position `i`, the cost is `i // 8 + 1`.
Return the sum of the costs for all positions.
hints: All letters are distinct, so only the number of letters on each key matters. The first letter on a key costs 1 push.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-i.insight: A number with a 0 digit appears within 10 steps and has product 0, so a short linear scan from `n` is enough.
steps: For each `x` from `n` upward, compute the product of its digits.
If the product is divisible by `t`, return `x`.
hints: Within 10 numbers from `n`, some number has a digit 0. Its digit product is 0, and every `t` divides 0.

meeting-rooms-iii.insight: Two min-heaps simulate the schedule: one holds free room numbers, and one holds busy rooms by end time and number.
steps: Sort the `m` meetings by start time and put all room numbers in the `idle` heap.
For each meeting, move every busy room with end time at most the start to `idle`.
If `idle` is not empty, pop the lowest room and push `(end, room)` to `busy`.
Else, pop the busy room with the earliest end `t` and push `(t + duration, room)`.
Count the meetings per room, and return the lowest room with the highest count.
Use 64-bit end times, because delays can grow large.
meeting-rooms-iii.time: O(m log m + m log n)
hints: At each meeting start, you need two fast answers: the lowest free room, and the busy room that becomes free first.

find-the-lexicographically-smallest-vali.insight: Greedy two pointers take each index as early as possible, and a suffix match array tells when the one change is safe.
steps: Let `n` and `m` be the lengths of `word1` and `word2`. Set `suf[n] = m`.
Scan `word1` from right to left; `suf[i]` is the smallest `j` such that `word2[j:]` is a subsequence of `word1[i:]`.
Scan `word1` from left to right with pointer `j` in `word2` and a `changed` flag, and stop when `j == m`.
If `word1[i] == word2[j]`, take index `i` and increment `j`.
Else, if not `changed` and `suf[i + 1] <= j + 1`, take `i`, set `changed`, and increment `j`.
Return the taken indices if `j == m`, else an empty array.
hints: Take each index as early as possible. Before you use your one allowed change, check that the rest of `word2` still fits in the rest of `word1`.

smallest-missing-integer-greater-than-se.insight: Sum the longest sequential prefix, then count up from that sum until you find a value that is not in a hash set of `nums`.
steps: Set `s = nums[0]`.
Add `nums[i]` to `s` while `nums[i] == nums[i - 1] + 1`, and stop at the first break.
Put all values of `nums` in a set.
While `s` is in the set, increment `s`.
Return `s`.
hints: The sum of the sequential prefix is a lower limit for the answer. Values anywhere in `nums`, not only in the prefix, can rule out a candidate.

distinct-subsequences-ii.insight: DP by last character: `f[c]` counts distinct subsequences that end with `c`, and a new `c` replaces that whole count.
steps: Make an array `f` of 26 zeros.
For each character `c`, set `f[c]` to the sum of all `f` values plus 1.
Take all sums modulo `10^9 + 7`.
Return the sum of `f`.
hints: Group distinct subsequences by their last character. When `c` appears again, the new count for `c` replaces the old one, because it includes all of them.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.insight: A dummy head and pointer rewiring swap each adjacent pair in one pass.
steps: Make a dummy node before `head` and set `prev` to the dummy.
While `prev.next` and `prev.next.next` exist, let `a` and `b` be those two nodes.
Set `prev.next = b`, `a.next = b.next`, and `b.next = a`.
Move `prev` to `a`.
Return `dummy.next`.
hints: Put a dummy node before the head, so every pair has a previous node. Each swap changes three `next` pointers.

word-search.insight: Backtracking DFS from each cell matches the word one character at a time and marks the cells on the current path.
steps: Write `dfs(i, j, k)` that returns true when `k` equals the word length `L`.
Return false if the cell is out of the grid or `board[i][j]` differs from `word[k]`.
Mark the cell as used, and call `dfs` on the four neighbors with `k + 1`.
Restore the cell before you return.
Return true if `dfs(i, j, 0)` is true for any start cell.
hints: A cell cannot repeat inside one path, but a failed path must not block that cell for a different path.

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.insight: A stack holds operands; each operator pops two values and pushes the result.
steps: For each token, if it is a number, push it.
Else, pop `b` and then `a`.
Push `a op b`, and use division that truncates toward zero.
Return the only value on the stack.
hints: Each operator applies to the two most recent values that are not yet used. Its result becomes a new value in their place.

basic-calculator.insight: A stack saves the result and sign before each parenthesis, so the expression is evaluated in one pass.
steps: Keep `result`, `sign = 1`, and a stack.
Read a full number and add `sign * number` to `result`.
On '+' or '-', set `sign` to 1 or -1.
On '(', push `result` and `sign`, then reset `result = 0` and `sign = 1`.
On ')', pop `s` and `r`, and set `result = r + s * result`.
Return `result`.
hints: Only `+` and `-` occur, so each number gets a final sign. Before a `(`, save the current result and the sign in front of the parentheses.

add-digits.insight: The digital root follows a math rule modulo 9: it is `1 + (num - 1) % 9` for a positive number.
steps: If `num == 0`, return 0.
Else, return `1 + (num - 1) % 9`.
hints: A number and its digit sum have the same remainder modulo 9. What does that tell you about the final single digit?

flood-fill.insight: A DFS from the start pixel recolors every connected pixel that has the original color.
steps: Let `orig` be the color of the start pixel.
If `orig == color`, return the image unchanged to prevent an infinite loop.
Run DFS from the start pixel and set each visited pixel to `color`.
Visit only the four neighbors that are inside the image and have `orig`.
hints: Changing a pixel's color can also record that you visited it. Check what happens when the old and new colors match.

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.insight: Bellman-Ford limited to `k + 1` rounds finds the cheapest price with at most `k + 1` edges.
steps: Set `dist[src] = 0` and all other `dist` values to infinity.
Repeat `k + 1` times.
Copy `dist` to `prev`, so one round uses at most one more edge.
For each flight `(u, v, w)`, set `dist[v] = min(dist[v], prev[u] + w)`. `E` is the number of flights.
Return `dist[dst]`, or -1 if it is still infinity.
hints: At most `k` stops means at most `k + 1` flights. Track the cheapest price to each city for a limited number of flights, not the cheapest price overall.

the-earliest-moment-when-everyone-become.insight: Sort the logs by time and join people with union-find; the answer is the time when one component remains.
steps: Sort the `m` logs by timestamp.
Make a union-find over `n` people and set `components = n`.
For each log, if the two people have different roots, union them and decrement `components`.
When `components` becomes 1, return the current timestamp.
Return -1 after the loop.
hints: Friend groups only grow over time, so the logs matter in time order. A log lowers the group count only when it joins two different groups.

shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.insight: BFS on an unweighted grid with 8 directions finds the shortest clear path in cells.
steps: If `grid[0][0]` or the target cell is 1, return -1.
Push `(0, 0)` with length 1 and mark it as visited.
Pop a cell; if it is the target, return its length.
Check the 8 neighbors. Mark each one inside the grid, equal to 0, and not visited, then push it with length plus 1.
Return -1 when the queue is empty.
hints: Every move costs 1, so explore cells in order of distance from the start, with 8 directions from each cell.

replace-employee-id-with-the-unique-iden.insight: A LEFT JOIN keeps every employee and gives NULL when no unique ID matches.
steps: Select `unique_id` and `name`.
LEFT JOIN `Employees` (`n` rows) to `EmployeeUNI` (`m` rows) on `id`.
hints: Every employee must appear, even without a unique ID. Which join keeps the rows that have no match?

minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.insight: More days never reduce the count of bouquets, so binary search on the answer finds the first feasible day.
steps: If `m * k > n`, return -1.
For a candidate day `d`, scan the flowers and count runs of bloomed flowers.
Add one bouquet for every `k` adjacent bloomed flowers, and reset the run at an unbloomed flower.
Binary search `d` between 1 and `M`, the maximum of `bloomDay`.
Return the smallest `d` that makes at least `m` bouquets.
hints: Waiting more days never decreases the number of bouquets. Can you check one candidate day in a single pass?

average-time-of-process-per-machine.insight: A self-join pairs each start row with its end row, and GROUP BY machine averages the durations.
steps: Join `Activity` as `a` with `Activity` as `b` on `machine_id` and `process_id`; `n` is the row count.
Keep rows where `a` is 'start' and `b` is 'end'.
GROUP BY `machine_id` and compute `AVG(b.timestamp - a.timestamp)`.
Round the average to 3 decimal places as `processing_time`.
hints: Each process has a 'start' row and an 'end' row in the same table. Match these two rows on `machine_id` and `process_id`.

count-good-numbers.insight: Even indices have 5 choices and odd indices have 4, so the answer is a product of two powers from fast exponentiation.
steps: Let `even = (n + 1) // 2` and `odd = n // 2`.
Compute `5^even` and `4^odd` modulo `10^9 + 7` with fast exponentiation.
Return their product modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Each index has a fixed number of allowed digits, independent of the other indices. `n` can be `10^15`, so you need a fast way to compute large powers.

search-a-2d-matrix-ii.insight: Start at the top-right corner: each comparison removes one row or one column.
steps: Set `i = 0` and `j = n - 1`.
If `matrix[i][j] == target`, return true.
If `matrix[i][j] > target`, decrement `j`.
Else, increment `i`.
Return false when `i` or `j` leaves the matrix.
hints: Look for a corner where horizontal and vertical moves change values in opposite directions.

peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.insight: Binary search on the slope: if `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, the peak is to the right.
steps: Set `left = 0` and `right = n - 1`.
While `left < right`, set `mid = (left + right) // 2`.
If `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, set `left = mid + 1`.
Else, set `right = mid`.
Return `left`.
hints: Away from the peak, the direction of a neighboring change tells you which side contains the peak.

counter.insight: A closure keeps the current value in a captured variable, and each call returns it and then increments it.
steps: In `createCounter(n)`, store `n` in a local variable `i`.
Return a function that returns `i++`.
hints: The returned function keeps access to the variables of `createCounter`, so a local variable keeps the count between calls.

combination-sum-ii.insight: Sort the candidates, then backtrack and skip equal values at the same tree level to avoid duplicate combinations.
steps: Sort `candidates`.
Write `dfs(start, remain)` that adds a copy of the path when `remain == 0`.
For each `j` from `start`, stop the loop if `candidates[j] > remain`.
Skip `j` if `j > start` and `candidates[j] == candidates[j - 1]`.
Else, push `candidates[j]`, call `dfs(j + 1, remain - candidates[j])`, then pop.
Start with an empty path, call `dfs(0, target)`, and return the list of combinations.
hints: Equal values can appear together in one combination. But for the same next position, choosing either of two equal values gives the same result.

binary-subarrays-with-sum.insight: Count prefix sums in a hash map; each earlier prefix equal to `s - goal` ends a subarray with sum `goal`.
steps: Keep a count map with `cnt[0] = 1` and a running sum `s`.
For each value, add it to `s`.
Add `cnt[s - goal]` to the answer.
Increment `cnt[s]`.
Return the answer.
hints: A subarray sum is the difference of two running totals from the array's start. For each end, which earlier totals give exactly `goal`?

number-of-1-bits.insight: The operation `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit.
steps: Set `count` to 0.
While `n` is not 0, set `n = n & (n - 1)` and increment `count`.
Return `count`.
hints: Subtracting one flips the lowest `1` bit and every bit to its right. Compare the changed positions with the original number.

monthly-transactions-i.insight: GROUP BY year-month and country, with conditional SUM to count and total only the approved rows.
steps: Make the month key with `DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m')`; `n` is the row count of `Transactions`.
GROUP BY the month key and `country`.
Compute `COUNT(*)` and `SUM(amount)` for all rows.
Compute `SUM(state = 'approved')` and `SUM(IF(state = 'approved', amount, 0))` for approved rows.
hints: The full totals and the approved-only totals come from the same month-and-country groups. A filter on `state` before grouping loses rows the full totals need.

array-prototype-last.insight: Add a method to `Array.prototype` so every array can return its last element, or -1 when empty.
steps: Assign a function to `Array.prototype.last`.
In the function, return -1 if `this.length` is 0.
Else, return `this[this.length - 1]`.
hints: A method on `Array.prototype` is available on every array, and `this` refers to that array.

employee-bonus.insight: A LEFT JOIN keeps employees without a bonus row, and the filter treats a NULL bonus as below 1000.
steps: LEFT JOIN `Employee` (`n` rows) to `Bonus` (`m` rows) on `empId`.
Keep rows where `bonus < 1000` OR `bonus IS NULL`.
Select `name` and `bonus`.
hints: A comparison with `NULL` does not evaluate to true. Account for this when a matching bonus row is absent.

binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.insight: A level-order BFS collects each level, and a direction flag reverses every second level.
steps: Push the root into a queue if it is not null, and set `leftToRight` to true.
For each level, pop the current queue size of nodes and collect their values.
Push the non-null children of each popped node, left child before right child.
If `leftToRight` is false, reverse the level list.
Add the list to the answer and flip `leftToRight`.
hints: The order in which you visit children does not have to match the order in which you present a level.

employee-free-time.insight: Merge all work intervals of all employees; each gap between merged intervals is common free time.
steps: Put the `N` intervals of all employees in one list and sort it by start.
Set `end` to the end of the first interval.
For each later interval, if its start is greater than `end`, add `[end, start]` to the answer.
Set `end` to the maximum of `end` and the interval end.
hints: If any employee works during an interval, that interval cannot be common free time. Employee identity does not affect this exclusion.

apply-substitutions.insight: Recursion with memoization expands each key once, because values can contain nested placeholders and there is no cycle.
steps: Put the replacements in a map from key to value; `L` is the length of the result.
Write `expand(s)` that finds the first '%' and the next '%' after it.
If no placeholder exists, return `s`.
Replace the placeholder with the expanded value of its key, and cache that value per key.
Return the left part, the expanded value, and `expand` of the rest, joined.
hints: A value can contain other placeholders, but no cycle exists. Expand each key once, store its final text, and reuse it.

number-of-good-pairs.insight: Each new value forms a good pair with every earlier equal value, so a count map gives the total in one pass.
steps: Keep a map from value to count.
For each value `x`, add `cnt[x]` to the answer.
Increment `cnt[x]`.
Return the answer.
hints: Each new value forms a pair with every earlier equal value. Keep a count for each value as you scan.

customers-who-never-order.insight: A LEFT JOIN with a NULL filter (an anti-join) finds customers that have no order row.
steps: LEFT JOIN `Customers` (`n` rows) to `Orders` (`m` rows) on `Customers.id = Orders.customerId`.
Keep rows where `Orders.id` IS NULL.
Select the customer `name` AS `Customers`.
hints: A customer who never orders has no row in `Orders` whose `customerId` matches their `id`.

rank-scores.insight: The window function `DENSE_RANK()` gives equal scores the same rank and leaves no gaps.
steps: Select `score` from `Scores`; `n` is the row count.
Compute `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)` AS `rank`.
Order the result by `score` descending.
hints: SQL has a ranking function that gives equal scores the same rank and leaves no gaps in the rank numbers.

delete-duplicate-emails.insight: Keep the smallest `id` for each email, and delete every row whose `id` is not one of these survivors.
steps: Group `Person` by `email` and select `MIN(id)` for each group; `n` is the row count.
Wrap that query in a derived table, so MySQL can read the table that it deletes from.
DELETE each row of `Person` whose `id` is not in the derived table.
hints: Find the smallest `id` for each email before you delete. MySQL does not let a delete read `Person` in a plain subquery.

maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.insight: Sort jobs by end time, then DP with binary search finds the last job that ends at or before each start.
steps: Sort the jobs by end time.
Let `dp[i]` be the best profit with the first `i` jobs, and set `dp[0] = 0`.
For job `i`, binary search the count `k` of jobs whose end is at most its start.
Set `dp[i]` to `max(dp[i - 1], dp[k] + profit)`.
Return `dp[n]`.
hints: Taking a job makes only schedules that finish by its start time relevant. Find a way to reuse their best profit.

clone-graph.insight: A DFS with a hash map from original node to clone copies each node once and handles cycles.
steps: If the node is null, return null.
If the node is in the map, return its clone.
Make a clone and put it in the map before you visit the neighbors.
Append the DFS result of each neighbor to the neighbor list of the clone.
Return the clone. `V` and `E` are the node and edge counts.
hints: The graph can have cycles, so remember the clone of each original node. Create the clone before you visit its neighbors.

bus-routes.insight: BFS over bus routes, not stops, with a map from each stop to its routes; the BFS level is the bus count.
steps: If `source == target`, return 0.
Map each stop to its routes; `S` is the total count of stops in all routes.
Put all routes at `source` in a queue with count 1, and mark them and `source` as used.
Pop a route and visit each unused stop on it. Mark the stop, and return the count if it is `target`.
Push each unused route at that stop with count plus 1, and mark the route as used.
Return -1 when the queue is empty.
hints: The answer counts buses, not stops. Treat each route as one node, and move one level of routes per bus.

factorial-trailing-zeroes.insight: Each trailing zero needs a factor 5, so count the factors of 5 in `n!` with repeated division.
steps: Set `count` to 0.
While `n > 0`, set `n = n // 5` and add `n` to `count`.
Return `count`.
hints: A trailing zero needs a factor of ten. In `n!`, factors of two are more plentiful than factors of five.

minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.insight: A greedy scan counts open parentheses that wait for a match and close parentheses that have no match.
steps: Set `open` and `add` to 0.
On '(', increment `open`.
On ')', decrement `open` if it is positive, else increment `add`.
Return `add + open`.
hints: An unmatched closing parenthesis cannot match a later opening parenthesis. Their order matters as much as their counts.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list-ii.insight: A dummy head and a `prev` pointer let you skip each whole run of duplicate values.
steps: Make a dummy node before `head` and set `prev` to the dummy.
Let `cur = prev.next`, and move `cur` forward while the next node has the same value.
If `prev.next == cur`, the value is unique, so move `prev` to `cur`.
Else, set `prev.next = cur.next` to remove the whole run.
Repeat while `prev.next` exists, and return `dummy.next`.
hints: Duplicate values sit next to each other, and you remove the whole run. A dummy node before the head handles a run at the start.

construct-uniform-parity-array-i.insight: A parity argument shows the answer is always true: odd minus even and even minus odd are both odd.
steps: If all values have the same parity, `nums1` itself is a valid uniform array.
Else, each odd value stays, and each even value minus an odd value is odd.
Both cases give a valid array, so return true without inspecting `nums1`.
hints: Subtracting an odd value changes parity. Subtracting an even value preserves parity.

minimum-path-sum.insight: Grid dynamic programming: the best sum at a cell is its value plus the smaller best sum of the top or left cell.
steps: Make `dp`, a row array of length `n`.
Fill the first row with running sums, because the path can only come from the left.
For each later row, set `dp[0]` to `dp[0] + grid[i][0]`.
For `j >= 1`, set `dp[j]` to `grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j - 1])`.
Return `dp[n - 1]`.
hints: You reach each cell only from the cell above it or the cell to its left, so which of those two gives the cheaper path?

minimum-falling-path-sum.insight: Row-by-row dynamic programming: the best sum at a cell is its value plus the smallest of three cells above it.
steps: Copy the first row into `dp`.
For each next row `i`, make a new array `cur`.
Set `cur[j]` to `matrix[i][j]` plus the minimum of `dp[j - 1]`, `dp[j]`, and `dp[j + 1]`.
Ignore the neighbors that are outside the columns.
Replace `dp` with `cur`, and at the end return the minimum of `dp`.
hints: The cheapest path that ends at a cell comes from one of the three cells directly above it.

triangle-judgement.insight: Three lengths form a triangle only when each pair of lengths has a sum greater than the third length.
steps: Select all columns from `Triangle`.
Add a column `triangle` with a `CASE` or `IF` expression.
Return `Yes` when `x + y > z`, `x + z > y`, and `y + z > x` are all true.
Else, return `No`.
hints: A side as long as the other two together gives a flat line, not a triangle. Any of the three sides can be that long side.

find-target-indices-after-sorting-array.insight: Counting replaces sorting: the target indices start after all smaller values and continue for the number of equal values.
steps: Count `less`, the number of values smaller than `target`.
Count `equal`, the number of values equal to `target`.
Return the indices from `less` to `less + equal - 1`.
hints: You do not need the full order: the first target index equals the number of values smaller than `target`.

block-placement-queries.insight: Process queries offline in reverse so obstacles are only removed; a binary indexed tree keeps prefix maximums of gaps.
steps: Put all obstacles and the sentinels `0` and `m + 1` in an ordered set, where `m` is the largest coordinate.
For each obstacle `x2` with predecessor `x1`, store the gap `x2 - x1` at index `x2` in a prefix-maximum tree.
Go through the queries from last to first, and reverse the collected answers at the end.
For a type-2 query, find the last obstacle `pre <= x` in the set.
The answer is true if the tree maximum up to `pre` or `x - pre` is at least `sz`.
For a type-1 query, find the predecessor `pre` and successor `nxt` of `x`. Remove `x`, then store `nxt - pre` at `nxt`.
