hints: Read the queries from last to first, so obstacles only disappear and gaps only join. Also count the free part between the last obstacle and `x`.

earliest-finish-time-for-land-and-water-.insight: Greedy: for a fixed order, only the earliest finish time of the first category matters, so one scan of the second category is enough.
steps: For the order land then water, find `minEnd`, the minimum of `landStartTime[i] + landDuration[i]`.
For each water ride, compute `max(minEnd, waterStartTime[j]) + waterDuration[j]` and keep the minimum.
Do the same calculation for the order water then land.
Return the smaller result of the two orders.
hints: For a fixed order of the two categories, only the earliest finish time in the first category matters for each ride in the second category.

students-and-examinations.insight: A cross join of students and subjects gives every pair; a left join to the exams keeps the pairs with zero attempts.
steps: Cross join `Students` with `Subjects` to get each student and subject pair.
Left join `Examinations` on both `student_id` and `subject_name`.
Group by `student_id` and `subject_name`.
Use `COUNT(e.student_id)` so that a pair with no exam row gives zero.
Order the result by `student_id` and `subject_name`. Let `S`, `T`, and `E` be the row counts of the three tables.
hints: Each student needs a row for each subject, even with zero attempts, so first build all student and subject pairs.

maximum-sum-circular-subarray.insight: Kadane's algorithm twice: a wrapping subarray equals the total sum minus a minimum subarray in the middle.
steps: Run Kadane's algorithm to get `maxSum`, the largest subarray sum.
In the same pass, run it for `minSum`, the smallest subarray sum, and compute `total`.
If `maxSum < 0`, all values are negative, so return `maxSum`.
Else, return the larger of `maxSum` and `total - minSum`.
hints: A subarray that wraps around the end equals the total sum minus a subarray in the middle. Which middle part do you remove?

queries-quality-and-percentage.insight: One GROUP BY per query name computes both metrics as averages: the ratio average and the average of a boolean condition.
steps: Ignore rows where `query_name` is null.
Group the rows by `query_name`.
Compute `quality` as `ROUND(AVG(rating / position), 2)`.
Compute `poor_query_percentage` as `ROUND(AVG(rating < 3) * 100, 2)`.
hints: The poor query percentage is the average of a true or false condition, times 100, within each `query_name` group.

boats-to-save-people.insight: Sort and use two pointers: the heaviest person goes in each boat, with the lightest person if the pair fits.
steps: Sort `people` in ascending order.
Set `i` to the lightest person and `j` to the heaviest person.
While `i <= j`, check if `people[i] + people[j] <= limit`.
If the pair fits, put `people[i]` in the boat and increase `i`.
In all cases, put `people[j]` in the boat, decrease `j`, and add one boat.
hints: The heaviest person always needs a boat; the only question is whether the lightest remaining person fits in the same boat.

consecutive-numbers.insight: Window functions LAG and LEAD compare each row with its two neighbors in id order to find three equal values in a row.
steps: Over the rows ordered by `id`, compute `LAG(num)` and `LEAD(num)` for each row.
Keep the rows where `num` equals both the previous and the next value.
Select `DISTINCT num` as `ConsecutiveNums`.
As an alternative, self-join `Logs` three times on `id`, `id + 1`, and `id + 2` with equal `num`.
hints: In `id` order, a value occurs three times in a row when a row has the same `num` as its previous and next rows.

count-complete-tree-nodes.insight: In a complete tree, compare the heights of the two subtrees: one of them is always a perfect tree with a known size.
steps: If the root is null, return 0.
Compute `l`, the height of the left subtree, by following left children only.
Compute `r`, the height of the right subtree, in the same way.
If `l == r`, the left subtree is perfect, so return `2^l` plus the count of the right subtree.
Else, the right subtree is perfect, so return `2^r` plus the count of the left subtree.
hints: Follow left children to get the height of each subtree. When the two heights are equal, the left subtree is perfect, so you know its size.

count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.insight: Map `target` to +1 and other values to -1; a subarray is valid when its prefix balance increases strictly.
steps: Keep `cur`, the running balance, and a count map of earlier balances, starting with balance 0 once.
Keep `less`, the number of earlier balances that are strictly less than `cur`.
If `nums[j]` equals `target`, add the count of `cur` to `less`, then increase `cur`.
Else, decrease `cur`, then subtract the count of the new `cur` from `less`.
Add `less` to the answer, then add one to the count of `cur`.
hints: Change `target` to +1 and other values to -1. A subarray is valid when its sum is positive, so compare each running total with earlier running totals.

flatten-binary-tree-to-linked-list.insight: Morris-style rewiring: put the right subtree after the rightmost node of the left subtree, then move the left subtree to the right.
steps: Set `cur` to the root.
If `cur` has a left child, find `pre`, the rightmost node of the left subtree.
Set `pre.right` to `cur.right`.
Set `cur.right` to `cur.left`, and set `cur.left` to null.
Move `cur` to `cur.right` and repeat until `cur` is null.
hints: The original right subtree must follow every node of the left subtree. The rightmost node of the left subtree has an empty right link to hold it.

continuous-subarray-sum.insight: Prefix sums modulo `k`: two equal remainders at least two indices apart mark a subarray with a sum that is a multiple of `k`.
steps: Make a map from remainder to first index, with remainder 0 at index -1.
Keep a running sum `s` of `nums[i]` modulo `k`.
If the map has `s` at index `j` and `i - j >= 2`, return true.
If the map does not have `s`, store `s` with index `i`.
Return false after the loop.
hints: Two running totals with the same remainder modulo `k` enclose a subarray whose sum is a multiple of `k`. Its length must be at least 2.

sorted-gcd-pair-queries.insight: Count pairs with each exact GCD by inclusion-exclusion over multiples, then answer each query by binary search on prefix sums.
steps: Count how many times each value occurs, up to `M`, the largest value.
For `i` from `M` down to 1, let `v` be the number of values that are multiples of `i`.
Set `cntG[i]` to `v * (v - 1) / 2` minus `cntG[j]` for each multiple `j = 2i, 3i, ...`.
Build prefix sums of `cntG`.
For each of the `q` queries, binary search the first index whose prefix sum is greater than the query value.
hints: Pairs of two multiples of `g` have a GCD that is a multiple of `g`. Remove the pairs whose exact GCD is `2g`, `3g`, and so on.

kth-ancestor-of-a-tree-node.insight: Binary lifting: store each node's ancestor at every power of two, then jump by the set bits of `k`.
steps: Set `up[0][v]` to `parent[v]` for every node.
For `j` from 1 to `L - 1`, where `L = floor(log2(n)) + 1`, set `up[j][v]` to `up[j - 1][up[j - 1][v]]`.
If the middle node is -1, set `up[j][v]` to -1. This setup takes O(n log n) time.
To answer a query, go through the set bits `j` of `k`, and move `node` to `up[j][node]` for each one.
If `node` becomes -1, return -1; else return `node` at the end.
hints: Write `k` as a sum of powers of two. If you know the ancestor of each node at each power-of-two distance, how many jumps do you need?

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i.insight: Counting sort: the first half decides the palindrome, so put half of each letter in alphabetical order, then mirror it.
steps: Count each letter in `s`.
For each letter from `a` to `z`, add half of its count to the first half `t`.
Start with an empty middle. If a letter has an odd count, use it as the middle letter.
Return `t`, then the middle letter, then the reverse of `t`.
hints: The first half of the palindrome decides the full string, so put half of the copies of each letter in alphabetical order.

kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies.insight: A kid can have the most candies when their count plus all extra candies reaches the current maximum.
steps: Find `mx`, the maximum value in `candies`.
For each kid `i`, the result is true if `candies[i] + extraCandies >= mx`.
hints: Every kid is compared with the same value, which you can find once. A tie for the greatest count also counts.

stone-game-ii.insight: Minimax memoized search on state (`i`, `M`) with suffix sums: a player gets the remaining stones minus the best result of the opponent.
steps: Compute `suffix[i]`, the sum of `piles[i:]`.
Define `dfs(i, M)` as the most stones the current player can get from index `i`.
If `i + 2M >= n`, return `suffix[i]`, because the player takes all remaining piles.
Else, try each `x` from 1 to `2M` and take the maximum of `suffix[i] - dfs(i + x, max(M, x))`.
Return `dfs(0, 1)`.
hints: The stones you get from index `i` equal all remaining stones minus the best total your opponent gets after your move. The state is `i` and `M`.

last-day-where-you-can-still-cross.insight: Reverse time with union-find: turn cells back into land from the last day and stop when the top and bottom connect.
steps: Start with every cell as water. Make a union-find with one node for each cell, plus virtual `top` and `bottom` nodes.
Go through `cells` from the last index `i` down to 0, and mark `cells[i]` as land.
Union the cell with each land neighbor in four directions.
Union a cell in the first row with `top`, and a cell in the last row with `bottom`.
When `top` and `bottom` connect, return `i`, because that grid is the state after day `i`.
hints: Go backward in time: start with all water and turn cells back into land. The first moment that the top row connects to the bottom row gives the answer.

making-a-large-island.insight: Label each island with an ID and its size, then try each water cell and add the sizes of distinct neighboring islands.
steps: Use DFS or union-find to give each island an ID and record its size.
Set the answer to the largest island size, or 0 if there is no island.
For each water cell, collect the distinct island IDs of its four neighbors.
Update the answer with 1 plus the sizes of those distinct islands.
If the grid has no water, the answer is `n * n`.
hints: A flipped cell joins only the islands next to it, so you can know their sizes in advance. Two of those neighbors can be in one island.

unique-3-digit-even-numbers.insight: Enumerate the candidate numbers instead of digit choices: test each even three-digit number against the digit counts.
steps: Count how many times each digit occurs in `digits`.
For each even number from 100 to 998, count its three digits.
Add one to the answer if no digit needs more copies than the input has.
Return the answer.
hints: There are only 450 even three-digit numbers, however many digits `digits` has.

invalid-tweets.insight: A filter on the character length of the content finds the tweets with more than 15 characters.
steps: Select `tweet_id` from `Tweets`.
Keep the rows where `CHAR_LENGTH(content) > 15`.
Use `CHAR_LENGTH`, not `LENGTH`, because `LENGTH` counts bytes.
hints: A tweet is invalid when the number of characters in `content` is greater than 15; count characters, not bytes.

image-overlap.insight: Count translation vectors: each pair of 1-cells from the two images votes for the shift that puts one on the other.
steps: Collect the positions of all 1-cells in `img1` and in `img2`.
For each pair `(a, b)` with `a` from `img1` and `b` from `img2`, compute the shift `b - a`.
Count each shift in a hash map.
Return the largest count, or 0 if the map is empty.
hints: Each pair of 1-cells, one from each image, votes for the one shift that puts them on top of each other. Which shift gets the most votes?

reverse-degree-of-a-string.insight: One scan adds, for each letter, its reversed alphabet rank times its 1-based position.
steps: For each position `i` from 1 to `n`, let `c` be the letter at that position.
Compute the reversed rank as `26 - (c - 'a')`.
Add the rank times `i` to the answer.
hints: The reversed rank of a letter is 26 minus its zero-based alphabet index; multiply it by the 1-based position of the letter.

score-of-parentheses.insight: Only each innermost `()` pair adds score, and it adds `2^depth`, where `depth` is the number of pairs around it.
steps: Keep `depth`, the number of open parentheses, starting at 0.
For `(`, increase `depth`.
For `)`, decrease `depth`.
If that `)` comes directly after a `(`, add `1 << depth` to the answer.
hints: Only each innermost `()` adds score, and it adds `2^depth`, where `depth` is the number of pairs around it.

surrounded-regions.insight: Search from the border: an `O` region survives only if it connects to an `O` on the edge.
steps: Start a DFS or BFS from each `O` cell on the border.
Mark each reached `O` cell with a temporary mark, such as `#`.
Scan the full board after the searches.
Change each remaining `O` to `X`, and change each `#` back to `O`.
hints: An `O` region stays only if it touches the border, so start from the border `O` cells instead of from each region.

delete-node-in-a-linked-list.insight: Without access to the previous node, copy the next node into the given node, then remove the next node.
steps: Set `node.val` to `node.next.val`.
Set `node.next` to `node.next.next`.
hints: Only the value must disappear from the list, not the given node object. The given node always has a next node.

wildcard-matching.insight: Two-dimensional dynamic programming on prefixes: a `*` either matches nothing or takes one more character of `s`.
steps: Let `dp[i][j]` be true when the first `i` characters of `s` match the first `j` characters of `p`.
Fill the table with false. Set `dp[0][0]` true, and set `dp[0][j]` true only while `p[0..j-1]` has only `*` characters.
For `i` from 1 to `m` and `j` from 1 to `n`: if `p[j - 1]` is `*`, set `dp[i][j]` to `dp[i][j - 1] or dp[i - 1][j]`.
If `p[j - 1]` is `?` or equals `s[i - 1]`, set `dp[i][j]` to `dp[i - 1][j - 1]`.
Return `dp[m][n]`, where `m` and `n` are the lengths of `s` and `p`. Mismatched cells stay false.
hints: Compare prefixes of `s` and `p`: a `*` either matches nothing or takes one more character of `s`.

permutation-sequence.insight: Factorial number system: each position skips whole blocks of `(n - 1 - i)!` permutations to select its digit.
steps: Make a list of the unused digits 1 to `n`, and set `k` to `k - 1`.
For each position `i`, compute `f = (n - 1 - i)!`.
Take the unused digit at index `k / f`, with integer division, and remove it from the list.
Set `k` to `k % f`.
Join the selected digits.
hints: Permutations with the same first digit form a block of `(n - 1)!` items. After you fix a digit, the rest splits into smaller blocks the same way.

maximal-rectangle.insight: Treat each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive `1` heights, then solve largest rectangle in histogram with a monotonic stack.
steps: Keep `heights[j]`, the number of consecutive `1` cells that end at the current row in column `j`.
For each row, set `heights[j]` to `heights[j] + 1` for a `1`, else to 0.
Run a monotonic increasing stack of column indices over `heights`, with an extra height 0 at the end.
Before you push a shorter bar at index `j`, pop each taller bar.
The area of a popped bar is its height times `j - top - 1`, where `top` is the new stack top or -1.
Keep the largest area over all rows.
hints: Treat each row as the floor of a histogram. Each bar height counts the consecutive `1` cells upward, including the cell in that row.

linked-list-cycle-ii.insight: Floyd's cycle detection: after the fast and slow pointers meet, a pointer from the head meets the slow pointer at the cycle start.
steps: Set `slow` and `fast` to the head. While `fast` and `fast.next` are not null, move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps.
If the loop ends without a meeting, return null because there is no cycle.
When `slow` and `fast` meet, set a pointer `p` to the head.
Move `p` and `slow` one step at a time until they meet.
Return the node where they meet.
hints: A walker that moves two steps and a walker that moves one step meet inside the cycle. The head is as far from the cycle start as that meeting point, plus whole loops.

invert-binary-tree.insight: Recursion: swap the left and right children of each node, then invert both subtrees.
steps: If the node is null, return null.
Invert the left subtree and the right subtree recursively.
Swap the two inverted subtrees, and return the node; the recursion depth is the tree height `h`.
hints: The root keeps its value, and its original left subtree moves to the right side. Is that subtree the same as before, or also mirrored?

permutation-in-string.insight: A fixed-size sliding window over `s2` with letter counts finds a window that has the same counts as `s1`.
steps: Count the letters of `s1` in `need`, and let `m` and `n` be the lengths of `s1` and `s2`.
Move a window of length `m` over `s2` and keep its letter counts in `window`.
Add the new right letter, and remove the letter that leaves on the left.
If `window` equals `need`, return true.
Return false after the scan.
hints: A rearrangement changes letter order but keeps each letter's count and the length. How much changes between two neighboring candidates in `s2`?

range-module.insight: Keep the tracked numbers as disjoint half-open intervals in a sorted map, and merge or split intervals on each update.
steps: Store the intervals in a sorted map from start to end, and let `n` be the number of stored intervals.
For `addRange`, remove all intervals that overlap or touch `[left, right)`, then insert their union.
For `removeRange`, remove all overlapping intervals, then put back the parts outside `[left, right)`.
For `queryRange`, find the last interval with start `<= left`.
Return true only if that interval has end `>= right`.
hints: Store the tracked numbers as disjoint half-open intervals in start order. An update merges or splits only the intervals that touch `[left, right)`.

shortest-palindrome.insight: The KMP prefix function finds the longest palindromic prefix of `s`; add the reverse of the rest in front.
steps: Build `t = s + '#' + reverse(s)`.
Compute the KMP prefix function of `t`.
Let `L` be the last prefix value, which is the length of the longest palindromic prefix of `s`.
Return the reverse of `s[L:]` followed by `s`.
hints: Find the longest prefix of `s` that is a palindrome. That prefix is also a suffix of `reverse(s)`, so compare `s` with its reverse.

summary-ranges.insight: Two pointers group each run of consecutive numbers into one range.
steps: Set `i` to 0, and repeat while `i < n`, where `n` is the length of `nums`.
Set `j = i`. Move `j` forward while `j + 1 < n` and `nums[j + 1] == nums[j] + 1`.
If `i == j`, add the single number; else add `nums[i]->nums[j]`.
Set `i` to `j + 1`. Return the ranges; an empty `nums` gives an empty list.
hints: A range ends where the next number is not the current number plus one.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.insight: A preorder traversal with null markers encodes the tree, and the same preorder rebuilds it.
steps: To serialize, write each node value in preorder, and write `#` for each null child.
Join the tokens with commas.
To deserialize, split the string into tokens and read them in order.
For each token, return null for `#`; else make a node, then build its left and right subtrees recursively.
hints: If you also write a marker for each missing child, one preorder list of values fixes the shape of the tree exactly.

find-the-difference.insight: Bitwise XOR of all characters in both strings cancels the pairs and leaves the added character.
steps: Set `x` to 0.
XOR `x` with the code of each character in `s` and in `t`.
Return the character with code `x`.
hints: Each character of `s` has a matching copy in `t`, except the added one. Combine all character codes with an operation that cancels equal pairs.

add-strings.insight: Grade-school addition: add digits from the right end of both strings and keep a carry.
steps: Set `i` and `j` to the last indices of `num1` and `num2`, of lengths `m` and `n`.
Set `carry` to 0, and loop while `i >= 0`, `j >= 0`, or `carry > 0`.
Add the available digits and `carry`. Append the sum modulo 10, and set `carry` to the integer quotient of the sum by 10.
Decrease `i` and `j`.
Reverse the appended digits and return them as a string.
hints: A digit sum can change the position to its left, but never a position to its right.

longest-common-subsequence.insight: Two-dimensional dynamic programming on prefixes: equal last characters extend the answer, else drop one character from either string.
steps: Let `dp[i][j]` be the LCS length of the first `i` characters of `text1` and `j` characters of `text2`.
Fill row 0 and column 0 with 0. Fill the other cells for `i` and `j` in increasing order.
If `text1[i - 1] == text2[j - 1]`, set `dp[i][j]` to `dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1`.
Else, set `dp[i][j]` to `max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])`.
Return `dp[m][n]`, where `m` and `n` are the lengths of `text1` and `text2`.
hints: Compare the last characters of two prefixes: if they match, they extend the answer; else drop the last character of one string.

is-subsequence.insight: Two pointers: move through `t` and advance in `s` each time the characters match.
steps: Set `i` to 0 for `s` and `j` to 0 for `t`.
While both pointers are inside their strings, increase `i` if `s[i] == t[j]`.
Increase `j` in each loop.
Return true if `i` equals the length of `s`; the loop is linear in `n`, the length of `t`.
hints: Match each character of `s` to its earliest possible position in `t`; an early match never blocks a later match.

non-overlapping-intervals.insight: Greedy interval scheduling: sort by end and keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end.
steps: Sort the intervals by end.
Set `end` to the end of the first interval, and count it as kept.
For each next interval, if its start is `>= end`, keep it and set `end` to its end.
Return the total number of intervals minus the kept count.
hints: Count the most intervals you can keep. The interval that ends first leaves the most room for the others.

product-price-at-a-given-date.insight: For each product, the price is the last change on or before 2019-08-16, else the default price 10.
steps: In a subquery, find `MAX(change_date)` per product, with `change_date <= '2019-08-16'`.
Join it back to `Products` to get the `new_price` of that change.
Left join the distinct `product_id` list to this result.
Use `IFNULL(price, 10)` for products with no change before the date.
hints: The price of each product is its last change on or before `2019-08-16`; a product with no such change keeps the price 10.

find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.insight: Use the array as its own hash set: make `nums[x - 1]` negative to mark that `x` was seen.
steps: For each value, let `x = abs(nums[i])`.
If `nums[x - 1]` is already negative, add `x` to the answer.
Else, make `nums[x - 1]` negative.
Return the answer.
hints: Each value `x` is in `1..n`, so index `x - 1` can hold a seen mark, such as a negative sign.

find-missing-and-repeated-values.insight: A count array over the values 1 to `n^2` shows the value that occurs twice and the value that does not occur.
steps: Make a count array of length `n * n + 1`.
Count each value in the grid.
The value with count 2 is the repeated value `a`.
The value with count 0 is the missing value `b`.
Return `[a, b]`.
hints: The values are in `1..n^2`, a small range, so you can reserve one slot for every possible value.

time-based-key-value-store.insight: Hash map of sorted lists: timestamps arrive in increasing order, so binary search finds the latest value at or before a time.
steps: Map each key to a list of `(timestamp, value)` pairs, and let `n` be the number of `set` calls.
For `set`, append the pair, which keeps the list sorted.
For `get`, binary search the last pair with a timestamp `<= timestamp`.
Return its value, or an empty string if no such pair exists.
hints: The `set` calls for a key arrive with increasing timestamps, so the list for each key is already in time order.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.insight: Post-order recursion: the first node whose two subtrees each contain one target is the lowest common ancestor.
steps: If the node is null, `p`, or `q`, return the node.
Search the left subtree and the right subtree recursively.
If both results are not null, return the current node.
Else, return the result that is not null; the recursion depth is the tree height `h`.
hints: If `p` and `q` are in different child subtrees, the current node is the answer. A target node can also be the ancestor of the other target.

simplify-path.insight: A stack of directory names: `..` removes the top name, and empty parts and `.` do nothing.
steps: Split `path` on `/`.
Skip empty parts and `.`.
For `..`, pop the stack if it is not empty.
Push all other parts, including names such as `...`.
Return `/` followed by the stack items joined with `/`.
hints: A `..` cancels the most recent directory name that is still kept, even after earlier cancellations.

number-of-substrings-containing-all-thre.insight: For each right end, all start positions up to the smallest last position of `a`, `b`, and `c` give valid substrings.
steps: Keep `last`, the last index of each of `a`, `b`, and `c`, starting at -1.
For each index `i`, update `last` for `s[i]`.
Add `min(last) + 1` to the answer, which is the count of valid start positions.
Return the answer.
hints: For a fixed right end, each start position at or before the smallest last index of `a`, `b`, and `c` gives a valid substring.

rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.insight: Two write pointers place positives at even indices and negatives at odd indices, which keeps the original order of each sign.
steps: Make an answer array of length `n`, and set `i = 0` and `j = 1`.
For each `x` in `nums`, if `x > 0`, write it at `ans[i]` and add 2 to `i`.
Else, write `x` at `ans[j]` and add 2 to `j`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Each sign always fills indices of one parity, and the order within each sign stays the same.

convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.insight: Divide and conquer: the middle element becomes the root, so the two halves give balanced subtrees.
steps: Define `build(l, r)` for the subarray from `l` to `r`.
If `l > r`, return null.
Make a node from `nums[mid]`, where `mid = floor((l + r) / 2)`.
Set its left child to `build(l, mid - 1)` and its right child to `build(mid + 1, r)`. Return the node.
Return `build(0, n - 1)`.
hints: A root near an end leaves unequal numbers of values on its two sides. Which position splits those values most evenly?

remove-outermost-parentheses.insight: A depth counter shows the outermost parentheses: they open at depth 0 and close back to depth 0.
steps: Keep `depth`, starting at 0.
For `(`, append it if `depth > 0`, then increase `depth`.
For `)`, decrease `depth`, then append it if `depth > 0`.
Return the appended characters.
hints: Track the depth: an outermost `(` opens at depth 0, and an outermost `)` brings the depth back to 0.

lfu-cache.insight: Hash maps plus one doubly linked list per frequency, with a tracked minimum frequency, give constant time for each operation.
steps: Map keys to list nodes with value and frequency, map each frequency to a doubly linked list, and keep `minFreq`.
To touch a key, unlink its node from list `f` and append it to list `f + 1`.
Delete an empty list. If list `minFreq` was deleted after a touch, increase `minFreq` by one.
For `get`, return -1 for a missing key; else touch the key and return its value.
For `put` on an existing key, update its value and touch the key.
For a new key, remove the oldest key of list `minFreq` if full, then insert with frequency 1 and `minFreq = 1`.
hints: Group the keys by use count, and keep each group in recent-use order. The key to remove is the oldest key in the group with the smallest count.

duplicate-emails.insight: GROUP BY email with a HAVING filter finds each email that occurs more than once.
steps: Group the `Person` rows by `email`.
Keep the groups where `COUNT(*) > 1`.
Select `email` as `Email`.
hints: The `id` values are unique, but several rows can share one `email`. Treat those rows as one unit when you test repetition.

third-maximum-number.insight: One pass keeps the three largest distinct values in three variables, and skips duplicates of them.
steps: Set `first`, `second`, and `third` to minus infinity, below every input value.
For each `x`, skip it if it equals one of the three.
If `x > first`, shift the values down and set `first = x`.
Else, if `x > second`, shift `second` to `third` and set `second = x`; else, if `x > third`, set `third = x`.
Return `third` if it is not minus infinity; else return `first`.
hints: You need only the three largest distinct values, so keep three variables and ignore each value that equals one of them.

min-cost-to-connect-all-points.insight: Minimum spanning tree on a complete graph: dense Prim's algorithm with a distance array runs in quadratic time.
steps: Set `dist[0] = 0` and all other distances to infinity.
Repeat `n` times: pick the unvisited point `u` with the smallest `dist`.
Mark `u` as visited and add `dist[u]` to the answer.
For each unvisited point `v`, set `dist[v]` to the minimum of `dist[v]` and the Manhattan distance from `u` to `v`.
Return the answer.
hints: Every pair of points is a possible edge, so there are about `n^2 / 2` edges. The cheapest edge that leaves a connected group is always safe.

backspace-string-compare.insight: Two pointers from the end of each string, with a skip counter for `#`, compare the final characters without extra memory.
steps: Set `i` and `j` to the last indices of `s` and `t`, which have lengths `m` and `n`.
For each string, move its pointer left past `#` characters and past the characters that they erase.
Use a counter that increases on `#` and decreases on each skipped character.
Compare `s[i]` and `t[j]`; return false if they differ or only one string has a character left.
Decrease both pointers and repeat; return true when both strings are done.
hints: Read both strings from the end: each `#` tells you to skip one more earlier character, so you do not need to rebuild the strings.

water-bottles.insight: Simulation: exchange all possible empty bottles in batches and carry the leftover empty bottles forward.
steps: Set `ans` and `empty` to `numBottles`.
While `empty >= numExchange`, compute `full = empty / numExchange` with integer division.
Add `full` to `ans`.
Set `empty` to `empty % numExchange + full`.
Return `ans`.
hints: After each exchange, the new full bottles also become empty bottles, so keep the leftover empty bottles for the next exchange.

partition-list.insight: Build two separate lists with dummy heads, one for small values and one for the other values, then join them.
steps: Make two dummy heads, `small` and `large`.
Append each node to `small` if its value is less than `x`; else append it to `large`.
Set the next pointer of the last `large` node to null to stop a cycle.
Link the last `small` node to the first real `large` node.
Return the node after the `small` dummy.
hints: Nodes on the same side of `x` keep their original order. Keep a separate growing tail for each side.

kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.insight: A min-heap that holds the `k` largest values has the `k`th largest value at its top.
steps: Start with an empty min-heap. Push each initial value into it, one at a time.
After each push, pop the smallest value if the heap size is more than `k`.
For `add(val)`, push `val` and pop once if the size is more than `k`.
Return the top of the heap.
hints: You need to keep only the `k` largest values seen so far. The answer is the smallest of those `k` values.

two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst.insight: A traversal with a hash set finds a pair because each node checks whether its complement was seen before.
steps: Traverse the tree with DFS and keep a set of seen values.
At each node, return true if `k - node.val` is in the set.
Else, add `node.val` to the set and continue to the children.
Return false if the traversal ends.
hints: For each node, the partner value is `k - node.val`, so ask whether you saw that partner at an earlier node.

permutations-ii.insight: Backtracking on the sorted array: use a duplicate value only after its previous equal copy is used, so each permutation occurs once.
steps: Sort `nums` and make a `used` array.
At each depth, try each index `i` that is not used.
Skip `i` if `i > 0`, `nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`, and `used[i - 1]` is false.
Mark `i` as used, add `nums[i]`, recurse, then undo both.
When the path has length `n`, add a copy to the answer.
hints: Equal values are interchangeable. Put equal values next to each other, and use a copy only when the equal copy before it is already in use.

insert-into-a-binary-search-tree.insight: Follow the binary search tree order down to an empty child position, and attach the new node there.
steps: If the root is null, return a new node with `val`.
Start at the root, and go left if `val` is smaller, else go right.
When the next child is null, attach the new node there; this takes at most `h` steps, the tree height.
Return the root.
hints: You never need to move existing nodes. Each comparison with `val` rules out one subtree, until no subtree is left.

maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.insight: A fixed-size sliding window with a count map and a running sum: the window is valid when the map has `k` keys.
steps: Keep a count map and the sum of the current window of length `k`.
Add `nums[i]` to the window and remove `nums[i - k]` when `i >= k`.
Delete a key from the map when its count becomes 0.
When the window has length `k` and the map has `k` keys, update the answer with the sum.
Return the answer, which is 0 if no window is valid.
hints: Two neighboring subarrays of length `k` share `k - 1` elements. What must you update for the sum and for the repeated-value test?

valid-perfect-square.insight: Binary search on the root: find whether some integer `x` in `[1, num]` has `x * x == num`.
steps: Set `lo = 1` and `hi = num`.
While `lo <= hi`, compute `mid` and `sq = mid * mid` with 64-bit integers.
If `sq == num`, return true.
If `sq < num`, set `lo = mid + 1`; else set `hi = mid - 1`.
Return false after the loop.
hints: The value `x * x` increases as `x` increases, so each test of a candidate root removes half of the remaining candidates.

shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k.insight: Prefix sums with a monotonic deque: negative values break sliding windows, so keep prefix indices with increasing prefix sums.
steps: Compute prefix sums `P` with `P[0] = 0`. Start with an empty deque and an answer of infinity.
For `j` from 0 to `n`, while a front exists and `P[j] - P[front] >= k`, set the answer to `min(answer, j - front)` and pop it.
While the deque is not empty and `P[back] >= P[j]`, pop the back, because `j` is a better start.
Push `j` at the back.
Return the answer, or -1 if it is still infinity.
hints: With negative values, a later start index whose running total is not greater than an earlier one is always a better start. Keep only increasing running totals.

delete-nodes-and-return-forest.insight: Post-order DFS: a deleted node sends its remaining children to the result as new roots and returns null to its parent.
steps: Put `to_delete` in a hash set.
Define `dfs(node)`. If `node` is null, return null. Else set `node.left` and `node.right` to the recursive results.
If `node.val` is in the set, add each child that is not null to the result, and return null.
Else, return `node`.
Call `dfs(root)` and add the root to the result if the call does not return null.
hints: When you delete a node, each remaining child becomes a new root. Process the children first, so each parent knows whether a child is deleted.

game-play-analysis-i.insight: GROUP BY player with the MIN aggregate on the event date gives the first login of each player.
steps: Group the `Activity` rows by `player_id`.
Select `player_id` and `MIN(event_date)` as `first_login` for each group.
hints: The first login of a player is the earliest `event_date` among the rows of that player.

decode-ways.insight: Linear dynamic programming: the last one digit or the last two digits form the final letter of each decoding.
steps: Let `dp[i]` be the number of decodings of the first `i` characters, with `dp[0] = 1`.
For `i` from 1 to `n`, start `dp[i]` at 0. If `s[i - 1]` is not `0`, add `dp[i - 1]`.
If `i >= 2` and `s[i - 2..i - 1]` is a number from 10 to 26, add `dp[i - 2]` to `dp[i]`.
Keep only the last two values to save memory.
Return `dp[n]`.
hints: The last letter of a decoding uses the last one digit or the last two digits. Which of those two choices are valid at each position?

01-matrix.insight: Multi-source BFS: start from all zero cells at the same time, so each cell gets its distance when first reached.
steps: Put each `0` cell in the queue with distance 0, and mark each `1` cell as unvisited.
Pop a cell and look at its four neighbors.
For each unvisited neighbor, set its distance to the current distance plus 1.
Push that neighbor into the queue.
Return the distance matrix when the queue is empty.
hints: Start from all `0` cells at the same time instead of from each `1` cell, and go outward one step per round.

maximum-path-score-in-a-grid.insight: Grid dynamic programming with cost as an extra state: track the best score for each cell and each total cost used.
steps: Let `dp[i][j][c]` be the best score at cell `(i, j)` with total cost `c`, or minus infinity.
Fill all states with minus infinity, then set `dp[0][0][0] = 0`, because `grid[0][0]` is 0.
For each cell, let its cost be 1 if its value is not 0, else 0.
Visit the other cells in row-major order. For each `c >= cost`, take the best top or left state at `c - cost`.
Add the cell value if that best is not minus infinity. Skip a top or left cell outside the grid.
Return the maximum of `dp[m - 1][n - 1][c]` for `c <= k`, or -1 if none is reachable.
hints: Score alone does not decide which path is better, because cost also limits the path. Track the best score at each cell for each total cost.

last-stone-weight-ii.insight: The final weight is the difference of two subset sums, so a 0/1 knapsack finds the subset sum nearest to half the total.
steps: Compute `s`, the total weight, and let `half = s / 2` with integer division.
Make a boolean array `dp` of size `half + 1` with `dp[0]` true.
For each stone `w`, for `j` from `half` down to `w`, set `dp[j]` to `dp[j] or dp[j - w]`.
Find the largest `j` with `dp[j]` true.
Return `s - 2 * j`.
hints: Each stone ends with a plus or minus sign, so the stones split into two groups. Make the sum of one group as close to half the total as possible.

cherry-pickup.insight: Replace the round trip with two walkers that move from the start at the same time, with dynamic programming on step and rows.
steps: Let `dp[t][i1][i2]` be the most cherries when both walkers made `t` steps and are in rows `i1` and `i2`.
Fill all states with minus infinity, and set `dp[0][0][0] = grid[0][0]`. The columns are `j1 = t - i1` and `j2 = t - i2`.
For `t` from 1 to `2n - 2`, skip states with a thorn or outside the grid; these stay minus infinity.
Take the best of the four previous move pairs, where each walker came from above or from the left.
If that best is not minus infinity, add `grid[i1][j1]`, and add `grid[i2][j2]` only if the two cells differ.
Return `max(0, dp[2n - 2][n - 1][n - 1])`; minus infinity means that no path exists.
hints: Replace the round trip with two walkers that start together and move one step at a time. When both are on the same cell, count its cherries once.

create-a-dataframe-from-list.insight: The pandas DataFrame constructor turns a list of rows into a table directly when you give it the column names.
steps: Call `pd.DataFrame(student_data, columns=['student_id', 'age'])`.
Return the result, which keeps the row order of the list.
hints: The outer list already gives the row order; the missing information is the name of each column.

minimum-cost-for-tickets.insight: Dynamic programming over calendar days: on a travel day, the cheapest cost ends with a 1-day, 7-day, or 30-day pass.
steps: Let `dp[d]` be the minimum cost to cover all travel days up to day `d`, with `dp[0] = 0`.
If `d` is not a travel day, set `dp[d] = dp[d - 1]`.
Else, take the minimum of `dp[d - 1] + costs[0]`, `dp[d - 7] + costs[1]`, and `dp[d - 30] + costs[2]`.
Use 0 for a negative day index.
Return `dp[D]`, where `D` is the last travel day.
hints: The cheapest plan up to a travel day ends with a 1-day, 7-day, or 30-day pass that covers it. Which earlier days does that pass leave uncovered?

corporate-flight-bookings.insight: A difference array makes each range booking two point updates, and one prefix sum gives the totals.
steps: Make an array `diff` of length `n + 1` with zeros.
For each of the `m` bookings, add `seats` at index `first - 1` and subtract `seats` at index `last`.
Compute the prefix sums of `diff`.
Return the first `n` prefix sums.
hints: A booking changes the difference between neighboring flights only at its two ends, however many flights it covers.

h-index.insight: Counting sort with buckets: citation counts above `n` act like `n`, so scan the buckets from `n` down.
steps: Make `cnt` of length `n + 1`, and add one at `min(c, n)` for each citation count `c`.
Scan `h` from `n` down to 0, and add `cnt[h]` to a running total `s`.
Return the first `h` with `s >= h`.
hints: A citation count above `n` acts the same as `n`, so count the papers for each citation value from 0 to `n`. Then scan from `n` down.

longest-palindromic-subsequence.insight: Interval dynamic programming: equal end characters add two to the inner answer, else drop one end.
steps: Fill an `n` by `n` table with 0. Let `dp[i][j]` be the answer for `s[i..j]`, with `dp[i][i] = 1`.
Fill `i` from `n - 1` down to 0, and `j` from `i + 1` up to `n - 1`.
If `s[i] == s[j]`, set `dp[i][j]` to `dp[i + 1][j - 1] + 2`.
Else, set `dp[i][j]` to `max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])`.
Return `dp[0][n - 1]`.
hints: Look at the two ends of a substring: equal ends add 2 to the answer for the inside; else drop one end.

count-the-number-of-special-characters-i.insight: A letter is special when its last lowercase index comes before its first uppercase index, so record both in one scan.
steps: Scan `word` once and record `last[c]` for each lowercase letter.
In the same scan, record `first[C]` for each uppercase letter.
Count each letter where both records exist and `last[c] < first[C]`.
hints: A letter is special when its last lowercase position comes before its first uppercase position.

palindrome-partitioning-ii.insight: Precompute a palindrome table, then use dynamic programming on prefixes, where the last part is a palindrome `s[j..i]`.
steps: Fill `pal[j][i]` for `j` from `n - 1` down to 0 and `i >= j`. Set it true when `s[j] == s[i]` and the inside is a palindrome or empty.
Let `f[i]` be the fewest cuts for `s[0..i]`, and compute it for `i` from 0 to `n - 1`.
If `pal[0][i]` is true, set `f[i] = 0`.
Else, set `f[i]` to the minimum of `f[j - 1] + 1` for each `j >= 1` with `pal[j][i]` true.
Return `f[n - 1]`.
hints: The last part of each partition of `s[0..i]` is a palindrome `s[j..i]`. Find out first which substrings are palindromes.

find-words-containing-character.insight: A linear scan with a membership test per word finds every index whose word contains `x`. Let `L` be the total length of all words.
steps: For each index `i`, check whether `x` occurs in `words[i]`.
If it occurs, add `i` to the answer.
Return the answer.
hints: Once you find `x` in a word, later matches in that word add no new index.

left-and-right-sum-differences.insight: Running sums: start with the total as the right sum, and move each value from the right sum to the left sum.
steps: Set `l = 0` and `r` to the sum of `nums`.
For each `x`, subtract `x` from `r`.
Append `abs(l - r)` to the answer.
Add `x` to `l`.
hints: The right sum equals the total minus the left sum minus the current value, so one running left sum is enough.

average-selling-price.insight: A left join on product and date range attaches each sale to its price, then a weighted average per product follows.
steps: Start from `Prices`, and left join `UnitsSold` on `product_id` and `purchase_date BETWEEN start_date AND end_date`.
Group by the `product_id` of `Prices`, so that a product with no sales stays in the result.
Compute `ROUND(SUM(price * units) / SUM(units), 2)`.
Wrap it in `IFNULL(..., 0)` for products with no sales.
hints: A sale matches the price row whose date range contains `purchase_date`. The average price is total revenue divided by total units, for each product.

number-of-ways-to-assign-edge-weights-ii.insight: A path of `d` edges has `2^(d - 1)` odd-cost assignments; binary lifting LCA gives `d` for each query.
steps: Run BFS from node 1 to get the depth and parent of each node.
Build a binary lifting table for the lowest common ancestor.
For each of the `q` queries, find `a`, the LCA of `u` and `v`.
Set `d = depth[u] + depth[v] - 2 * depth[a]`.
The answer is 0 if `d == 0`; else it is `2^(d - 1)` modulo `10^9 + 7`, from a precomputed table.
hints: Only the number of edges on the path matters: for `d >= 1` edges, exactly half of the `2^d` weight choices give an odd cost.

minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.insight: Greedy interval piercing: sort by end, and shoot each arrow at the end of the first balloon that it must burst.
steps: Sort the balloons by their end coordinate.
Set `arrow` to minus infinity and the count to 0.
For each balloon `[a, b]`, if `a > arrow`, add one arrow and set `arrow = b`.
A balloon with `a <= arrow` is already burst, because touching counts.
Return the count.
hints: Look at the balloon that ends first: an arrow at its end bursts it and each balloon that starts at or before that point.

minimum-area-rectangle-ii.insight: Enumerate a corner and two neighbors with a right angle; a hash set confirms the fourth corner, found by vector addition.
steps: Put all points in a hash set.
For each point `p1` and each pair `p2`, `p3` of other points, require `(p2 - p1) · (p3 - p1) == 0`.
Compute the fourth corner `p4 = p2 + p3 - p1`.
If `p4` is in the set, the area is `|p2 - p1| * |p3 - p1|`.
Return the minimum area, or 0 if no rectangle exists.
hints: Three rectangle corners determine the fourth. A valid corner joins two perpendicular sides, even when the rectangle is tilted.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.insight: The transition between (value, direction) states does not depend on position, so matrix exponentiation handles `n` up to `10^9`.
steps: Let `m = r - l + 1`, and make `2m` states: a value plus the direction of the next step.
From an up state at value `y`, allow a move to each value `x > y`, which enters a down state.
From a down state at value `y`, allow a move to each value `x < y`, which enters an up state.
Raise this `2m` by `2m` transition matrix to the power `n - 1` with fast exponentiation.
Multiply by a vector of ones, sum the entries modulo `10^9 + 7`, and return the sum.
hints: The rule for the next value depends only on the current value and the direction of the next step, never on the position. How do you repeat that step `n - 1` times quickly?

all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.insight: Add parent links to turn the tree into an undirected graph, then run BFS from the target for `k` levels.
steps: Run DFS to record the parent of each node in a map.
Start BFS at `target`, with a visited set.
From each node, visit its left child, right child, and parent.
Expand exactly `k` levels. If the frontier becomes empty first, return an empty list.
Return the values of the nodes at distance exactly `k`.
hints: From a node you can also move up to its parent. Record each parent, and the tree becomes an undirected graph around `target`.

domino-and-tromino-tiling.insight: Linear dynamic programming: the tiling counts follow the recurrence `dp[n] = 2 * dp[n - 1] + dp[n - 3]`.
steps: For `i` from 3 to `n`, set `dp[i] = 2 * dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 3]` modulo `10^9 + 7`.
Keep only the last three values to save memory.
Return `dp[n]`.
hints: Classify tilings by their last block that you cannot cut: a vertical domino, two flat dominoes, or two trominoes with flat dominoes between them. Each such block of width 3 or more has two mirror forms.

maximum-element-after-decreasing-and-rea.insight: Greedy after sorting: set the first value to 1, and cap each next value at the previous value plus one.
steps: Sort `arr` in ascending order.
Set `arr[0] = 1`.
For each `i >= 1`, set `arr[i]` to `min(arr[i], arr[i - 1] + 1)`.
Return the last element.
hints: The first value must become 1, and each next value can be at most one larger. A small value cannot grow, so where does it hurt least?

last-stone-weight.insight: A max-heap gives the two heaviest stones in logarithmic time, so the game is a direct simulation.
steps: Put all stones in a max-heap.
While the heap has more than one stone, pop the two largest, `y` and `x`.
If `y != x`, push `y - x` back.
Return the last stone, or 0 if the heap is empty.
hints: Each turn needs the two heaviest stones, and the result goes back into the pile. Which structure gives you the largest value fast after each change?

find-original-array-from-doubled-array.insight: Greedy on sorted values: the smallest unmatched value must be an original value, so it must pair with its double.
steps: If the length is odd, return an empty array.
Count each value, and go through every element of the sorted array, duplicates included.
Skip a value `x` whose count is 0; else decrease the count of `x`.
If the count of `2x` is 0, return an empty array; else decrease it and add `x` to the answer.
Return the answer after the loop. Each 0 pairs with another 0, so 0 needs no special case.
hints: The smallest remaining value cannot be the double of a smaller value, so it is an original value. Pair it with its double.

reconstruct-itinerary.insight: Hierholzer's algorithm for an Eulerian path: visit the smallest destination first and add each airport after its tickets are used.
steps: Build an adjacency list from the `E` tickets, with each list sorted so that the smallest destination comes out first.
Run DFS from `JFK`.
At each airport, remove and visit the smallest destination until the list is empty.
After the loop, append the airport to the route.
Return the route in reverse order.
hints: Taking the smallest destination first can reach a dead end before all tickets are used. An airport where you get stuck belongs at the route's end.

find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid.insight: 0-1 BFS: an unsafe cell costs 1 and a safe cell costs 0, so a deque finds the least health loss.
steps: Set `dist` to infinity, then set `dist[0][0] = grid[0][0]` and put `(0, 0)` in a deque.
While the deque is not empty, pop a cell from the front and try its four neighbors.
If `dist` plus the neighbor value is smaller, update the neighbor.
Only after an update, push the neighbor to the front if its value is 0, else to the back.
Return true if `dist[m - 1][n - 1] < health`.
hints: A step onto an unsafe cell costs 1 health, and a step onto a safe cell costs 0. Find the least total loss to the last cell.

flipping-an-image.insight: Two pointers per row reverse and invert in one pass: swap the two ends and flip both bits.
steps: For each row, set `i` to the first index and `j` to the last index.
While `i < j`, swap `row[i]` and `row[j]`, then invert both with XOR 1.
Move `i` right and `j` left.
If `i == j`, invert the middle value once.
hints: Reversing a row pairs positions at equal distances from its ends. Inverting values does not change those pairs.

remove-covered-intervals.insight: Sort by start ascending and end descending; an interval is covered if its end is at most the largest end seen.
steps: Sort the intervals by start, and by end in descending order for equal starts.
Set `maxEnd`, the largest end seen, to minus infinity, and set the count of remaining intervals to 0.
For each interval, if its end is `<= maxEnd`, it is covered.
Else, add one to the count and set `maxEnd` to its end.
Return the count.
hints: If you visit intervals by increasing start, only earlier intervals can cover the current one. Equal starts need care: the larger end covers the other.

bulls-and-cows.insight: Count bulls by position, then count cows as the sum of minimum digit counts among the unmatched positions.
steps: For each index, if `secret[i] == guess[i]`, add one to `bulls`.
Else, count `secret[i]` in `cnt1` and `guess[i]` in `cnt2`.
Set `cows` to the sum of `min(cnt1[d], cnt2[d])` for each digit `d`.
Return the string `xAyB` with `x = bulls` and `y = cows`.
hints: A bull uses up a digit in both strings, so leave it out of the cow count. For the rest, how many pairs can one digit form?

keys-and-rooms.insight: Graph reachability: run DFS or BFS from room 0 through the keys and check that all rooms are visited. Let `k` be the total key count.
steps: Start DFS from room 0 and mark it as visited.
For each key in the current room, visit that room if it is not visited.
Return true if the visited count equals `n`.
hints: Rooms are nodes and keys are edges. The question is whether each room is reachable from room 0.

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.insight: The round in which a node falls off equals its height above the leaves, so a postorder DFS groups nodes by height.
steps: Run a postorder DFS that returns the height of each node, with height `-1` for a null child.
Set the height of a node to `1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)`, so a leaf gets height `0`.
Add a new empty list to `ans` when `height` equals `len(ans)`.
Append the node value to `ans[height]`.
Return `ans` after the DFS visits the root.
hints: A node falls off in round `h`, where `h` is its height: the edge count of the longest downward path to a leaf.

rank-transform-of-an-array.insight: Sort the distinct values; the rank of each value is its 1-based position in that sorted list.
steps: Put the distinct values of `arr` in a sorted list.
Make a map from each value to its index plus one.
Replace each `arr[i]` with its rank from the map.
hints: The rank of a value is one plus the number of distinct values smaller than it.

single-threaded-cpu.insight: Sort tasks by enqueue time and keep the available tasks in a min-heap keyed by processing time, then by index.
steps: Sort the task indices by `enqueueTime`, keep a pointer `p` into that order, and set the current time `t = 0`.
Push each task with `enqueueTime <= t` into the heap as `(processingTime, index)`.
If the heap is empty, move `t` to the enqueue time of the next task.
Else, pop the top task, append its index to the answer, and add its processing time to `t`.
Repeat until the answer holds all `n` tasks.
hints: Tasks enter the candidate pool in arrival order and leave it shortest first. When the pool is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival.

gcd-of-odd-and-even-sums.insight: The odd sum is `n^2` and the even sum is `n(n + 1)`; because `n` and `n + 1` are coprime, the GCD is `n`.
steps: Note that the first `n` odd numbers add up to `n * n`.
Note that the first `n` even numbers add up to `n * (n + 1)`.
Return `n`, because `gcd(n, n + 1)` is 1.
hints: The first `n` odd numbers add up to `n * n`, and the first `n` even numbers add up to `n * (n + 1)`.

maximum-nesting-depth-of-the-parentheses.insight: The depth at a position is the count of open parentheses not yet closed, so one counter gives the answer.
steps: Set `depth` and `ans` to 0.
For each `(`, increment `depth` and set `ans` to `max(ans, depth)`.
For each `)`, decrement `depth`.
Ignore all other characters, and return `ans`.
hints: The depth at each character equals the count of `(` seen so far minus the count of `)` seen so far.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-i.insight: A trade joins two adjacent zero blocks around one block of ones, so the answer is all ones plus the largest adjacent zero-block pair.
steps: Count the ones in `s` as `ones`, and set `best = 0`.
Scan `s` one maximal block of equal characters at a time, and store no blocks.
For each zero block of length `cur`, set `best = max(best, pre + cur)`.
Then set `pre = cur`, with `pre` at negative infinity before the first zero block.
Return `ones + best`.
hints: The trade turns a block of ones and the two zero blocks beside it into ones. Thus the gain is the sum of two neighboring zero blocks.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.insight: Each answer is all ones in `s` plus a gain: the largest sum of two adjacent zero runs in the query, with end runs cut.
steps: Count the ones in `s` as `ones`, and list the zero runs with `start`, `end`, and `len`.
Let `idx[i]` be the last run with `start <= i`, or -1. Build a sparse table over `len[t] + len[t + 1]`.
For each of the `q` queries `[l, r]`, set `b = idx[r]`. Set `a = idx[l]`, plus 1 if `s[l]` is `1`.
If `a >= b`, append `ones` and go to the next query. Else, let `la` and `lb` be runs `a` and `b` cut to `[l, r]`.
If `b == a + 1`, the gain is `la + lb`. Else, take the max of `la + len[a + 1]` and `len[b - 1] + lb`.
If `a + 1 <= b - 2`, also compare the table max over pairs `a + 1` to `b - 2`. Append `ones + gain`.
hints: Each answer is the count of ones in `s` plus the best sum of two neighboring zero runs in `[l, r]`. Only the two end runs change per query.

number-of-unique-xor-triplets-i.insight: Repeated indices allow any three values from 1 to `n`, so for `n >= 3` the XORs fill all values below the next power of two.
steps: Let `n` be the length of `nums`.
Note that `a ^ a ^ b = b`, so each value from 1 to `n` is a result.
If `n <= 2`, return `n`.
Else, return `1 << bitLength(n)`, the smallest power of two greater than `n`.
hints: Indices can repeat, so `a ^ a ^ b = b` gives every value from 1 to `n`. What range do XORs of values up to `n` fill?

battleships-in-a-board.insight: Each ship has exactly one top-left cell, so count the `X` cells with no `X` above and no `X` to the left.
steps: Scan each cell `(i, j)` of the board.
Skip the cell if it is not `X`.
Skip the cell if `i > 0` and the cell above is `X`. Also skip it if `j > 0` and the left cell is `X`.
Else, add 1 to the count, because this cell starts a new ship.
hints: Each ship has exactly one first cell in reading order. Which neighbors of an `X` tell you that it is that first cell?

confirmation-rate.insight: Left join `Confirmations` to `Signups` so users without requests stay, then average a confirmed flag for each user.
steps: LEFT JOIN `Confirmations` (`m` rows) to `Signups` (`n` rows) on `user_id`.
GROUP BY `user_id`.
Compute `AVG(action = 'confirmed')`, and use `IFNULL` to give 0 to users with no requests.
ROUND the rate to two decimal places.
hints: Users with no confirmation requests still need a row, with a rate of 0. Which table must the join keep in full?

cinema-seat-allocation.insight: Only rows with reservations need checks; store a seat bitmask for each such row and test the three four-seat blocks.
steps: Group the `m` reserved seats by row in a map from row to a 10-bit mask.
Start the answer at `2 * (n - number of reserved rows)`.
For each reserved row, add 2 if seats 2-5 and seats 6-9 are both free.
Else, add 1 if seats 2-5, seats 4-7, or seats 6-9 are free.
Return the answer.
hints: Only rows with a reservation need a check, because each free row holds two families. A family fits in seats 2-5, 4-7, or 6-9.

longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.insight: A sliding window with two monotonic deques gives the window maximum and minimum in amortized constant time.
steps: Keep a decreasing deque `maxQ` and an increasing deque `minQ` of indices, and set `left = 0`.
For each index `r`, pop from the back of `maxQ` the indices with smaller values, then push `r`.
Pop from the back of `minQ` each index with a value greater than `nums[r]`, then push `r`.
While `nums[maxQ[0]] - nums[minQ[0]] > limit`, increment `left`.
After each increment, pop any front index that is less than `left`.
Set `ans` to `max(ans, r - left + 1)`.
hints: A range is valid when its max minus its min is at most `limit`. As the right end moves forward, the left end never moves back.

minimum-moves-to-clean-the-classroom.insight: Run a BFS over states of cell, remaining energy, and a bitmask of uncollected litter; the first state with an empty mask gives the answer.
steps: Give each litter cell an index from 0 to `L - 1`, with `L` at most 10.
Start the BFS at the `S` cell with full `energy` and all mask bits set.
From a state with energy above 0, move to each adjacent cell that is not `X`.
Set the new energy to `energy` on an `R` cell, else to the current energy minus 1.
Clear the bit of a litter cell when you enter it, and skip states that you already visited.
Return the BFS level when the mask is 0, or -1 when the queue is empty.
hints: A cell alone is not a full state. Track the cell, the remaining energy, and which litter cells are still uncollected.

construct-uniform-parity-array-ii.insight: The smallest odd value cannot change parity, so a mixed array works only when every even value can subtract a smaller odd value.
steps: If all values have the same parity, return true.
Else, find the smallest odd value `mn`.
Note that the target parity must be odd, because `mn` cannot become even.
Return true if every even value is greater than `mn`, else return false.
hints: The smallest odd value can never become even, so a mixed array must end all odd. Which even values can then become odd?

immediate-food-delivery-ii.insight: Find the first order of each customer with a grouped subquery, then average an immediate flag over those rows.
steps: In a subquery over the `n` rows of `Delivery`, GROUP BY `customer_id` and select `MIN(order_date)`.
Keep the rows of `Delivery` whose `(customer_id, order_date)` pair is in the subquery.
Compute `AVG(order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date) * 100`.
ROUND the result to two decimal places.
hints: Only the first order of each customer counts, so find the minimum `order_date` for each `customer_id` first.

matrix-diagonal-sum.insight: Each row adds its primary and secondary diagonal cells, and the center cell of an odd-size matrix counts once.
steps: For each row `i`, add `mat[i][i]` to the total.
If `i != n - 1 - i`, also add `mat[i][n - 1 - i]`.
Return the total.
hints: Each row holds one cell of each diagonal. In an odd-size matrix, the two diagonals share the center cell.

maximum-score-of-non-overlapping-interva.insight: Use weighted interval scheduling DP with at most four picks, and keep the sorted index list of each state for lexicographic ties.
steps: Sort the intervals by start, and keep each original index.
For each `i`, binary search `nxt[i]`, the first interval with start greater than the end of `i`.
Let `f[i][k]` be the best weight from interval `i` on with at most `k` picks, and `g[i][k]` its index list.
Set `f[n][k] = 0`, `f[i][0] = 0`, and their lists empty. Fill `i` from `n - 1` down to 0 and `k` from 1 to 4.
Compare a skip, `f[i + 1][k]`, with a take, `w[i] + f[nxt[i]][k - 1]`. For a take, insert the original index into a copy of `g[nxt[i]][k - 1]` in sorted order.
Keep the larger weight, or the lexicographically smaller list on a tie, and return `g[0][4]`.
hints: Each interval is either skipped or taken, and a take jumps to the first interval that starts after it ends. You take at most four.

rectangle-overlap.insight: Two rectangles overlap with positive area when their projections overlap with positive length on both the x-axis and the y-axis.
steps: Let `rec1 = [x1, y1, x2, y2]` and `rec2 = [x3, y3, x4, y4]`.
Check that `max(x1, x3) < min(x2, x4)` for the x-axis.
Check that `max(y1, y3) < min(y2, y4)` for the y-axis.
Return true only if both checks pass.
hints: Two rectangles overlap when their x ranges overlap and their y ranges overlap, each with a positive length.

find-pivot-index.insight: With the total sum known, the right sum at index `i` is the total minus the left sum minus `nums[i]`.
steps: Compute the total sum `total`, and set `left` to 0.
For each index `i`, return `i` if `left == total - left - nums[i]`.
Else, add `nums[i]` to `left`.
Return -1 after the loop.
hints: When you know the total sum and the sum to the left of `i`, the sum to the right of `i` follows.

reverse-substrings-between-each-pair-of-.insight: Precompute each matching parenthesis pair, then walk the string and jump to the partner with a reversed direction at each parenthesis.
steps: Use a stack to find the matching index `pair[i]` for each parenthesis.
Start at `i = 0` with direction `d = 1`.
If `s[i]` is a parenthesis, set `i = pair[i]` and set `d = -d`.
Else, append `s[i]` to the result.
Move `i` by `d`, and stop when `i` leaves the string.
hints: Each enclosing pair flips the read direction of a letter once. At a parenthesis, where must the reader go next to read the inside backward?

target-sum.insight: If the numbers with a minus sign add up to `neg`, then `neg = (total - target) / 2`, so count subsets with that sum as a 0/1 knapsack.
steps: Compute `total`, the sum of `nums`.
If `total - target` is negative or odd, return 0.
Set `neg = (total - target) / 2`. Make an array `dp` of `neg + 1` zeros, and set `dp[0] = 1`.
For each `x`, for `j` from `neg` down to `x`, add `dp[j - x]` to `dp[j]`.
Return `dp[neg]`.
hints: If the numbers with a minus sign add up to `neg`, then `total - 2 * neg = target`. Count the subsets with that sum.

text-justification.insight: Pack words into each line greedily, then spread the extra spaces evenly with leftover spaces to the left gaps; the last line is left-justified.
steps: From index `i`, add words while their letters plus one space per gap fit in `maxWidth`.
If the line is the last line or has one word, join with single spaces and pad the right.
Else, let `gaps` be the word count minus one, and let `spaces` be `maxWidth` minus the line letters.
Give each gap `floor(spaces / gaps)` spaces, and give one extra space to each of the first `spaces % gaps` gaps.
Move `i` to the first word of the next line and repeat.
hints: For a line that is not the last and has two or more words, divide its spare spaces by its gap count. The remainder is the count of left gaps with one extra space.

gas-station.insight: If total gas covers total cost, a start exists, and it is the station after the last point where the running tank went negative.
steps: If `sum(gas) < sum(cost)`, return -1.
Set `start = 0` and `tank = 0`.
For each station `i`, add `gas[i] - cost[i]` to `tank`.
If `tank < 0`, set `start = i + 1` and set `tank` to 0.
Return `start`.
hints: If the tank goes negative at station `i`, no start from the current start up to `i` works. So the next candidate start is `i + 1`.

longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix.insight: Strictly increasing moves form a DAG, so a DFS with memoization computes the longest path from each cell once.
steps: Let `dfs(i, j)` return the longest increasing path that starts at cell `(i, j)`.
Set `dfs(i, j)` to 1 plus the max `dfs` over neighbors with a larger value, or 1 if none exist.
Store each result in a memo table, so each cell is computed once.
Return the max of `dfs(i, j)` over all cells.
hints: A strictly increasing path never revisits a cell, and the best path from a cell does not depend on how you arrived there.

find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.insight: Slide a window of length `len(p)` over `s` and compare its letter counts with the letter counts of `p`.
steps: Let `m` be the length of `s` and `n` the length of `p`. Count the letters of `p` in a 26-slot array `need`.
For each index `r` of `s`, add `s[r]` to the window counts `have`.
When `r >= len(p)`, remove `s[r - len(p)]` from `have`.
If `have` equals `need`, add the window start `r - len(p) + 1` to the answer.
hints: Each candidate is a substring of length `len(p)`. A move of one step changes only two letter counts.

managers-with-at-least-5-direct-reports.insight: Count direct reports for each `managerId` with GROUP BY and HAVING, then join back to `Employee` to get the names.
steps: GROUP BY `managerId` over the `n` rows of `Employee`, and keep groups with `COUNT(*) >= 5`.
JOIN the result to `Employee` on `id = managerId`.
Select the `name` column.
hints: A manager's `id` appears as the `managerId` of each direct report. So the report count of a manager is a count of rows.

unique-number-of-occurrences.insight: Count each value in a hash map, then check that no two values share the same count with a set.
steps: Count the occurrences of each value in a hash map.
Put all counts in a set.
Return true if the set size equals the number of distinct values.
hints: Count each value first. Then the question is whether any two values share the same count.

design-hit-counter.insight: Timestamps arrive in order, so a queue of hit times can drop hits older than 300 seconds from its front.
steps: In `hit(timestamp)`, push `timestamp` to the back of a queue.
In `getHits(timestamp)`, pop from the front while the front is at most `timestamp - 300`.
Return the queue size from `getHits`; let `n` be the number of hits in the queue.
For many hits per second, store `(timestamp, count)` pairs, keep a running total, and subtract the count of each popped pair.
hints: Timestamps arrive in increasing order, so the oldest hits always sit at the front and expire first.

swap-adjacent-in-lr-string.insight: `L` moves only left and `R` moves only right, and they never cross, so the sequences without `X` must match with valid shifts.
steps: Use pointer `i` in `start` and pointer `j` in `result`, and skip `X` characters in both.
If one pointer reaches the end, return true only if the other pointer also does.
If `start[i] != result[j]`, return false.
If the letter is `L` and `i < j`, or the letter is `R` and `i > j`, return false.
Advance both pointers and repeat.
hints: `L` and `R` never pass each other, so the letters without `X` keep their order. Which way can each letter move?

excel-sheet-column-title.insight: This is base 26 with digits 1 to 26, so subtract 1 before each modulo step to map `Z` correctly.
steps: While `columnNumber > 0`, subtract 1 from it.
Append the letter `'A' + columnNumber % 26`.
Set `columnNumber` to `columnNumber / 26` with integer division.
Reverse the letters and return them.
hints: This is base 26, but the digits run from 1 to 26 with no zero. Subtract 1 before each remainder step.

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.insight: All words share length `k`, so run `k` sliding windows that move one word at a time and keep word counts in a hash map.
steps: Count the words in a map `need`; let `n` be the word count and `k` the word length.
For each offset from 0 to `k - 1`, slide a window over `s`, of length `m`, in steps of `k`.
Read the next word; if it is not in `need`, clear the window and move `left` past the word.
Else, add the word, and remove words from the left while its count exceeds its count in `need`.
When the window holds `n` words, record `left` as a start index.
hints: All words have length `k`, so only `k` start offsets exist. At each offset, read `s` one word at a time.

exclusive-time-of-functions.insight: A stack holds the active call chain; at each log event, give the elapsed time to the function on top.
steps: Let `L` be the number of logs. Set `ans` to `n` zeros and `prev = 0`, and keep an empty stack of ids.
On `start` at time `t`, add `t - prev` to `ans` of the top function if the stack is not empty.
Then push the new id and set `prev = t`.
On `end` at time `t`, add `t - prev + 1` to `ans` of the top function and pop it.
Then set `prev = t + 1`, because an end log covers the whole time unit. Return `ans`.
hints: Only the most recent unfinished call runs at any time. An end log covers its whole time unit, so add 1.

basic-calculator-ii.insight: With no parentheses, apply `*` and `/` at once to the last term, and add each finished term to a running sum.
steps: Set `result = 0`, the last term `last = 0`, the current number `num = 0`, and the previous operator `op = '+'`.
Read digits into `num`, and skip spaces.
At an operator or at the string end, apply `op` to `last` and `num`.
For `+` or `-`, add `last` to `result`, and set `last` to `num` or `-num`.
For `*` or `/`, set `last` to `last * num` or `last / num`, with truncation toward zero.
Set `op` to the new operator, reset `num`, and return `result + last` at the end.
hints: A later `*` or `/` can still change the most recent term, so do not add that term to the total yet.

delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.insight: A fast pointer moves two steps for each step of a slow pointer that starts at a dummy node, so slow stops before the middle.
steps: Make a dummy node before `head`, and set `slow = dummy` and `fast = head`.
While `fast` and `fast.next` exist, move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps.
Set `slow.next = slow.next.next`.
Return `dummy.next`.
hints: A walker that moves two nodes per step reaches the end when a walker that moves one node per step reaches the middle.

maximum-width-of-binary-tree.insight: Give nodes heap-style positions, with children at `2p` and `2p + 1`, and at each BFS level take last minus first position plus one.
steps: Push `(root, 0)` into a queue.
For each level, record the position `first` of the first node in the level.
Set the level width to the last position minus `first` plus 1, and keep the maximum.
Push children with positions `2 * (p - first)` and `2 * (p - first) + 1` to keep the numbers small.
hints: Index each node as if the tree were complete and stored in an array. Then a level width depends only on the indices of its two end nodes.

nth-digit.insight: Skip whole blocks of numbers with the same digit count, then compute the exact number and digit inside the last block.
steps: Set `len = 1`, `count = 9`, and `start = 1`.
While `n > len * count`, subtract `len * count` from `n`, then increment `len` and multiply `count` and `start` by 10; use 64-bit integers here.
Set the number to `start + (n - 1) / len` with integer division.
Return the digit at index `(n - 1) % len` of that number.
hints: Group the numbers by digit count: 9 one-digit numbers, 90 two-digit numbers, 900 three-digit numbers. Skip whole groups first.

interleaving-string.insight: `dp[i][j]` is true when the first `i` characters of `s1` and the first `j` of `s2` interleave to the first `i + j` of `s3`.
steps: Let `m` and `n` be the lengths of `s1` and `s2`; if `m + n != len(s3)`, return false.
Keep one row `dp` of `n + 1` values, and visit `i` from 0 to `m` and `j` from 0 to `n`.
At `i = 0` and `j = 0`, set `dp[0] = true`. At every other cell, assign a new value to `dp[j]`.
From above: `i > 0`, the old `dp[j]` is true, and `s1[i - 1] == s3[i + j - 1]`.
From the left: `j > 0`, the new `dp[j - 1]` is true, and `s2[j - 1] == s3[i + j - 1]`.
Set `dp[j]` true if either case holds, else false. Return `dp[n]` at the end.
hints: Each character of `s3` comes from the next unused character of `s1` or of `s2`. The state is the count used from each string.

sort-characters-by-frequency.insight: Count each character, then bucket sort by frequency to output characters from the highest count down.
steps: Count each character in a hash map.
Put each character `c` in bucket `cnt[c]`, with buckets from 1 to `n`.
Walk the buckets from `n` down to 1.
Append each character in bucket `f` to the result `f` times.
hints: No character occurs more than `len(s)` times, so each count is an integer from 1 to `len(s)`.

min-cost-climbing-stairs.insight: The minimum cost to reach step `i` is the cheaper of the two ways in, from step `i - 1` or from step `i - 2`.
steps: Let `dp[i]` be the minimum cost to stand on step `i`, with `dp[0] = dp[1] = 0`.
Set `dp[i] = min(dp[i - 1] + cost[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + cost[i - 2])`.
Return `dp[n]`, where step `n` is the top.
Keep only the last two values to use constant space.
hints: You reach step `i` only from step `i - 1` or step `i - 2`, so its best cost depends only on those two.

word-ladder-ii.insight: A level-by-level BFS records the parents of each word on shortest paths, then a backtracking DFS from the end word builds all shortest sequences.
steps: Put the `N` words of length `L` in a set, and return an empty list if `endWord` is absent.
Run BFS level by level, and keep each next level as a set, so each word expands once.
Remove the words of the current level from the word set before you expand the level.
For each word, change each position to each letter, and link each new word in the set to its parent.
Stop after the level that reaches `endWord`, and return an empty list if BFS never reaches it.
Run DFS from `endWord` over the parent links to `beginWord`, and reverse each path; `P` is the output size.
hints: A word can have several predecessors at the same shortest distance, and each one leads to other paths. Keep every such link.

rectangle-area.insight: The union area is the sum of both areas minus the overlap area, with each overlap side length clamped at 0.
steps: Compute both rectangle areas.
Set `w = min(ax2, bx2) - max(ax1, bx1)` and `h = min(ay2, by2) - max(ay1, by1)`.
Return the sum of the areas minus `max(w, 0) * max(h, 0)`.
hints: The union area is both areas minus the overlap. The overlap width and height are each 0 when the ranges do not meet.

user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i.insight: Filter rows to the 30 days that end on 2019-07-27, then group by day and count distinct users.
steps: Keep the rows of `Activity` (`n` rows) with `activity_date` from `2019-06-28` to `2019-07-27` inclusive.
GROUP BY `activity_date`.
Select the date as `day` and `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` as `active_users`.
hints: The 30-day period ends on `2019-07-27`, so it starts on `2019-06-28`. Count each user once per day.

number-of-digit-one.insight: Count the ones at each decimal position separately, from the digits above, at, and below that position.
steps: Set `ans = 0`, and loop over place values `p = 1, 10, 100, ...` while `p <= n`.
Let `high = n / (10 * p)`, `cur = (n / p) % 10`, and `low = n % p`, with integer division.
If `cur == 0`, add `high * p`.
If `cur == 1`, add `high * p + low + 1`.
If `cur >= 2`, add `(high + 1) * p`, and return `ans` after the loop.
hints: Count the ones at each decimal position separately. The digits above, at, and below that position give the count.

bulb-switcher.insight: Bulb `i` toggles once per divisor of `i`, so only perfect squares, which have an odd divisor count, stay on.
steps: Note that the divisors of `i` form pairs, except the square root of a perfect square.
Return `floor(sqrt(n))`, the count of perfect squares from 1 to `n`.
hints: Bulb `i` toggles once for each divisor of `i`. Which numbers have an odd count of divisors?

most-stones-removed-with-same-row-or-col.insight: Each connected component of stones can shrink to one stone, so the answer is `n` minus the number of components, found with union-find.
steps: Treat each row and each column as a union-find node, and offset column ids to keep them apart.
For each stone `(r, c)`, union the row node `r` with the column node `c`.
Count the distinct roots among the nodes that some stone uses.
Return `n` minus that count.
hints: Stones that share a row or column link into groups, and each group can shrink to one stone. Count the groups.

n-th-tribonacci-number.insight: Keep only the last three terms and roll them forward, because each new term is their sum.
steps: Repeat `n` times: set `a, b, c = b, c, a + b + c`.
Return `a`.
