hints: Each term needs only the three terms before it. So how many values must you keep at once?

longest-palindrome.insight: Every pair of equal characters can sit on both sides of the palindrome, and one leftover character can sit at the center.
steps: Count each character.
For each count `v`, add `v - v % 2` to the answer.
If the answer is less than `len(s)`, add 1 for a center character.
Return the answer.
hints: Each pair of equal characters can sit on both sides, and one extra character can sit at the center.

perfect-number.insight: Divisors come in pairs `i` and `num / i`, so a loop up to `sqrt(num)` finds all proper divisors.
steps: If `num == 1`, return false.
Set `sum = 1`, and loop `i` from 2 while `i * i <= num`.
If `i` divides `num`, add `i`, and add `num / i` when it differs from `i`.
Return true if `sum == num`.
hints: Divisors come in pairs `i` and `num / i`, so you need to check `i` only up to `sqrt(num)`.

subtree-of-another-tree.insight: At each node of `root`, test if the tree there is identical to `subRoot` with a recursive equality check.
steps: Write `same(a, b)`: return true if both are null, and false if only one is null.
Else, `same` returns true only if the values match and both child pairs are the same.
Run a DFS over the `m` nodes of `root`, and return true if `same(node, subRoot)` holds anywhere; `subRoot` has `n` nodes.
For linear time, compare serialized trees with null markers by KMP instead.
hints: The match can start at any node of `root`. A failed match at one node does not rule out a match deeper down.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-tra.insight: Track two states per day, the best profit with no stock and with one stock, and pay the fee on each sale.
steps: Set `cash = 0` and `hold = -prices[0]`.
For each later price `p`, set `cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee)`.
Then set `hold = max(hold, cash - p)`.
Return `cash`.
hints: Each day ends with one share or with no share. Track the best profit for both states, and pay the fee on each sale.

count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.insight: Scan from the right and keep a Fenwick tree over compressed value ranks to count the smaller values already seen.
steps: Map each value to its rank among the sorted distinct values, with ranks from 1.
Scan `nums` from right to left.
For a value with rank `r`, set its answer to the Fenwick prefix sum up to `r - 1`.
Then add 1 at rank `r` in the Fenwick tree.
hints: Scan from the right, so the values already seen are exactly the values after the current index. Count the seen values smaller than it.

make-sum-divisible-by-p.insight: If the total has remainder `k`, remove the shortest subarray whose sum has remainder `k`, found with prefix remainders in a hash map.
steps: Compute `k = sum(nums) % p`, and return 0 if `k == 0`.
Set `last[0] = -1` in a hash map `last` from prefix remainder to index, set `cur = 0`, and set `ans = n`.
For each index `i`, update the prefix remainder `cur = (cur + nums[i]) % p`.
If `t = (cur - k) mod p` is in the map, set `ans = min(ans, i - last[t])`.
Then store `last[cur] = i`.
Return -1 if `ans == n`, because you cannot remove the whole array, else return `ans`.
hints: If the total has remainder `k` mod `p`, remove the shortest subarray whose sum has remainder `k`. A subarray sum is a difference of two running sums.

reverse-bits.insight: Move each of the 32 bits from position `i` to position `31 - i` with shifts and masks.
steps: Set `res = 0`.
Repeat 32 times: shift `res` left by 1 and add the lowest bit of `n`.
In each round, also shift `n` right by 1.
Return `res`.
hints: Bit `i` of the input goes to bit `31 - i` of the output.

car-fleet.insight: Sort cars by position from the target back; a car that needs more time than the fleet ahead starts a new fleet.
steps: Sort the cars by position in descending order.
Set `lead = 0` and `fleets = 0`.
For each car, compute `time = (target - position) / speed` as a real number.
If `time > lead`, add 1 to `fleets` and set `lead = time`.
Else, let the car join the fleet ahead.
Return `fleets`.
hints: Process the cars from the one closest to the target. A car that needs more time than the fleet ahead of it never catches up.

island-perimeter.insight: Each land cell adds 4 edges, and each pair of adjacent land cells hides 2 edges.
steps: For each land cell, add 4.
If the cell below is land, subtract 2.
If the cell to the right is land, subtract 2.
Return the total.
hints: Each land cell has 4 edges, and each edge shared by two land cells removes 2 from the perimeter.

unique-paths-ii.insight: The path count of a free cell is the sum of the counts from above and from the left, and an obstacle cell gets 0.
steps: Make a row array `dp` of `n` zeros, and set `dp[0] = 1`.
Visit each cell `(i, j)` in row-major order.
If the cell is an obstacle, set `dp[j] = 0`.
Else, if `j > 0`, add `dp[j - 1]` to `dp[j]`.
Return `dp[n - 1]`.
hints: A free cell is reached only from above or from the left, and an obstacle cell has 0 paths.

number-of-unique-subjects-taught-by-each.insight: Group rows by teacher and count distinct subjects, because one subject can repeat across departments.
steps: GROUP BY `teacher_id` over the `n` rows of `Teacher`.
Select `teacher_id` and `COUNT(DISTINCT subject_id)` as `cnt`.
hints: One subject can appear in more than one department for a teacher, so count each subject once per teacher.

lemonade-change.insight: Greedy change works: for a 20 bill, give a 10 and a 5 first, because 5 bills fit more cases.
steps: Keep counts `five` and `ten`.
For a 5 bill, increment `five`.
For a 10 bill, decrement `five` and increment `ten`.
For a 20 bill, use one `ten` and one `five` if `ten > 0`, else use three `five`.
Return false if `five` or `ten` goes below 0, else return true at the end.
hints: A 5 bill gives change in more cases than a 10 bill. So for a 20 bill, give a 10 and a 5 when you can.

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.insight: For each index, track the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends there and how many such subsequences exist.
steps: Set `len[i] = 1` and `cnt[i] = 1` for each `i`.
For each pair `j < i` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`, compare `len[j] + 1` with `len[i]`.
If it is greater, set `len[i] = len[j] + 1` and `cnt[i] = cnt[j]`.
Else, if it is equal, add `cnt[j]` to `cnt[i]`.
Return the sum of `cnt[i]` over all `i` where `len[i]` equals the max length.
hints: For each end index, track the best length of an increasing subsequence and the count of subsequences with that length.

rotate-function.insight: Each rotation changes `F` by a closed form, `F(k) = F(k - 1) + sum - n * nums[n - k]`, so each value takes constant time.
steps: Compute `s = sum(nums)` and `F(0) = sum(i * nums[i])`.
For `k` from 1 to `n - 1`, compute `F(k)` from `F(k - 1)` with the formula.
Return the max value of `F`.
hints: One rotation adds `sum(nums)` to `F` and subtracts `n` times the element that moves to index 0.

rotated-digits.insight: A number is good when every digit rotates to a digit and at least one digit is 2, 5, 6, or 9.
steps: For each `x` from 1 to `n`, check its digits.
Reject `x` if it has a 3, 4, or 7.
Count `x` if it has at least one 2, 5, 6, or 9.
Return the count.
hints: A number is good when no digit is 3, 4, or 7, and at least one digit is 2, 5, 6, or 9.

minimum-jumps-to-reach-end-via-prime-tel.insight: Run BFS over indices, and group indices by prime factor so each prime teleport list is used once and then cleared.
steps: Sieve the smallest prime factor of each value up to `M`, the max of `nums`.
For each index `i`, add `i` to `g[p]` for each distinct prime `p` that divides `nums[i]`.
Run BFS from index 0, with neighbors `i - 1` and `i + 1`.
If `nums[i]` is a prime `p`, also visit all indices in `g[p]`, then clear `g[p]`.
Return the BFS level when you reach index `n - 1`.
minimum-jumps-to-reach-end-via-prime-tel.time: O(M log log M + n log M)
hints: All jumps cost 1. After you teleport from prime `p` once, a later teleport from `p` reaches no new index sooner.

scramble-string.insight: Use interval DP: `dp[k][i][j]` tells if `s1[i:i+k]` scrambles to `s2[j:j+k]`, with each split tested with and without a swap.
steps: Set all states to false, then set `dp[1][i][j]` true when `s1[i] == s2[j]`.
For each length `k` from 2 to `n`, visit each `i` and `j` from 0 to `n - k`.
Try each split `h` from 1 to `k - 1`. For no swap, check `dp[h][i][j]` and `dp[k - h][i + h][j + h]`.
For a swap, check `dp[h][i][j + k - h]` and `dp[k - h][i + h][j]`.
Set `dp[k][i][j]` true if both states of either pair are true for some `h`, and return `dp[n][0][0]`.
hints: A scramble splits a string at some index and keeps or swaps the two parts. So the state is a pair of equal-length substrings.

minimum-initial-energy-to-finish-tasks.insight: Do the tasks with the largest gap `minimum - actual` first; this greedy order needs the least start energy.
steps: Sort the tasks by `minimum - actual` in descending order.
Set `ans = 0` and the current energy `cur = 0`.
For each task, if `cur < minimum`, add `minimum - cur` to `ans` and set `cur = minimum`.
Then subtract `actual` from `cur`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Compare the start energy that two tasks need in each order. How does `minimum - actual` decide which order is better?

minimum-moves-to-make-array-complementar.insight: Each pair costs 0, 1, or 2 moves on ranges of target sums, so a difference array over sums finds the minimum.
steps: Make a difference array `d` over target sums 2 to `2 * limit`.
For each pair, let `a` and `b` be the min and max of `nums[i]` and `nums[n - 1 - i]`.
Add 2 to all sums, because two moves always work.
Subtract 1 on the range `[a + 1, b + limit]`, where one move is enough.
Subtract 1 more at the single sum `a + b`, where no move is needed.
Take prefix sums of `d`, and return the minimum over sums 2 to `2 * limit`.
hints: For one pair, the target sums that need at most one move form one range. Zero moves work only for the current pair sum.

check-if-array-is-good.insight: With `n = len(nums) - 1`, the array is good when `n` appears twice and each value from 1 to `n - 1` appears.
steps: Set `n = len(nums) - 1`, and count each value.
Return false if `cnt[n] != 2`.
Return false if any value from 1 to `n - 1` has count 0.
Else, return true, because the length forces each of those values to appear once.
hints: With `n = len(nums) - 1`, a good array has `n` twice and each value from 1 to `n - 1` once.

minimum-common-value.insight: Both arrays are sorted, so two pointers find the first common value in one pass.
steps: Let `m` and `n` be the lengths of `nums1` and `nums2`, and set `i = 0` and `j = 0`.
While both pointers are in range, return `nums1[i]` if `nums1[i] == nums2[j]`.
Else, advance the pointer at the smaller value.
Return -1 when a pointer reaches the end.
hints: Both arrays are in ascending order. If the current values differ, the smaller one has no match left in the other array.

k-diff-pairs-in-an-array.insight: Count values in a hash map; for `k > 0` count keys `x` with `x + k` present, and for `k == 0` count repeated keys.
steps: Count each value in a hash map `cnt`.
If `k == 0`, count the keys with `cnt[x] >= 2`.
Else, count the keys `x` for which `x + k` is also a key.
Return the count.
hints: For `k > 0`, a pair is a distinct value `x` with `x + k` also present. For `k == 0`, a pair is a value that repeats.

solving-questions-with-brainpower.insight: Use DP from the back: the best score from question `i` is the max of a skip and a solve that jumps ahead.
steps: Let `dp[i]` be the best score from question `i` to the end, with `dp[i] = 0` for `i >= n`.
Set `dp[i] = max(dp[i + 1], points[i] + dp[i + brainpower[i] + 1])`.
Fill `dp` from `i = n - 1` down to 0, and return `dp[0]`.
hints: Look at the choices from the back: question `i` is skipped or solved, and a solve jumps to `i + brainpower[i] + 1`.

reshape-the-matrix.insight: Both matrices share one row-major order, so flat index `k` maps to `(k / n, k % n)` and to `(k / c, k % c)`.
steps: If `m * n != r * c`, return the original matrix.
For each flat index `k` from 0 to `m * n - 1`, copy `mat[k / n][k % n]` to `ans[k / c][k % c]`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Both matrices read in row order give the same flat list, so flat index `k` maps to one cell in each shape.

max-area-of-island.insight: Flood fill each island with DFS, mark its cells as visited, and keep the largest cell count.
steps: Set `best = 0`, and for each land cell, run a DFS that returns the island area.
In the DFS, return 0 if the cell is out of the grid or is 0.
Else, set the cell to 0, then return 1 plus the areas from the four neighbors.
Set `best` to the max of `best` and each area, and return `best`.
hints: Each island is a connected group of land cells. Count the cells of each group once, and mark them so you skip them later.

find-words-that-can-be-formed-by-charact.insight: Count the letters in `chars` once; a word is good when no letter count in it exceeds that supply.
steps: Count the letters of `chars`, of length `C`, in a 26-slot array.
For each word, count its letters; all words have total length `L`.
If every letter count is at most the count in `chars`, add the word length to the answer.
Return the answer.
hints: A word is good when each of its letters appears in it no more times than in `chars`.

minimum-element-after-replacement-with-d.insight: Compute the digit sum of each number and keep the running minimum.
steps: For each `x`, set `sum = 0`. Until `x` is 0, add `x % 10` to `sum` and set `x = floor(x / 10)`.
Note that each digit sum takes `O(log M)` steps, where `M` is the max value.
Keep the minimum digit sum, and return it.
hints: The remainder after division by 10 gives the last digit. Integer division by 10 removes that digit.

earliest-finish-time-for-land-and-water-.insight: For each order, only the first-category ride that ends earliest matters; then try each ride of the second category.
steps: Let `n` and `m` be the land and water ride counts. For land first, compute `minEnd`, the min of `landStartTime[i] + landDuration[i]`.
For each water ride `j`, compute `max(minEnd, waterStartTime[j]) + waterDuration[j]`, and keep the min.
Repeat with water rides first and land rides second.
Return the smaller of the two results.
hints: For a fixed order, an earlier finish of the first ride never delays the second ride. So which first ride matters?

find-common-elements-between-two-arrays.insight: Put each array in a set, then count the elements of each array that are in the other set.
steps: Make set `s1` from `nums1` and set `s2` from `nums2`.
Count the indices `i` with `nums1[i]` in `s2`.
Count the indices `j` with `nums2[j]` in `s1`.
Return both counts.
hints: An element counts when its value exists anywhere in the other array, so store the values of each array for fast lookup.

word-pattern.insight: The pattern must be a bijection, so keep two hash maps, letter to word and word to letter, and reject any conflict.
steps: Let `n` be `len(pattern)` and `m` be `len(s)`. Split `s` into words, and return false if the word count is not `n`.
For each pair of letter `c` and word `w`, check both maps.
Return false if `c` maps to another word or `w` maps to another letter.
Else, store both mappings, and return true at the end.
hints: The mapping must work in both directions: one letter to one word, and one word to one letter.

design-twitter.insight: Stamp each tweet with a global time, and merge the recent tweets of the user and followees with a max-heap to get the top 10.
steps: Keep a counter `time`, and for each of the `U` users a tweet list and a followee set.
In `postTweet`, append `(time, tweetId)` to the user list and increment `time`; `T` is the tweet count.
In `follow` and `unfollow`, add or remove the followee in the set; `E` counts follow pairs.
In `getNewsFeed`, push the newest tweet of the user and of each of the `F` followees into a max-heap.
Pop the top tweet up to 10 times, and after each pop push the next older tweet of that author.
hints: The tweets of each user are already in time order, so a feed merges a few ordered lists and stops after 10 tweets.

maximum-gap.insight: By the pigeonhole principle the max gap is at least `(max - min) / (n - 1)`, so buckets of that width only need their min and max.
steps: If `n < 2`, return 0.
Set the bucket width `w = max(1, floor((max - min) / (n - 1)))`, and make `floor((max - min) / w) + 1` buckets.
Put each `x` in bucket `floor((x - min) / w)`, and keep only the min and max of each bucket.
Scan the non-empty buckets in order, and compute each bucket min minus the previous bucket max.
Return the largest of those gaps, or 0 if only one bucket is non-empty.
hints: When `max > min`, the largest gap is at least the average gap `(max - min) / (n - 1)`. Two values closer than that never form the largest gap.

minimum-genetic-mutation.insight: This is an unweighted shortest path, so BFS from `startGene` over bank genes that differ in one character gives the answer.
steps: Put the `B` bank genes in a set `bank`.
Run BFS from `startGene` with step count 0.
For each gene, change each of the `L = 8` positions to each of `A`, `C`, `G`, and `T`.
Enqueue each new string that is in `bank`, and remove it from `bank`.
Return the step count when you dequeue `endGene`, or -1 when the queue is empty.
hints: Each mutation is one step to a bank gene that differs in one character. You need the fewest steps from `startGene`.

unique-binary-search-trees.insight: Pick each value as the root; the tree count is the product of the left and right subtree counts, which gives the Catalan numbers.
steps: Make an array `f` of `n + 1` zeros, and set `f[0] = 1`, the count for an empty tree.
For each size `i` from 1 to `n`, add `f[j - 1] * f[i - j]` to `f[i]` for each root `j` from 1 to `i`.
Return `f[n]`.
hints: The tree count depends only on the node count. Pick each root, and multiply the counts for the left and right sizes.

frog-jump.insight: Store, for each stone, the set of jump sizes that can land on it, and extend each size `k` by `k - 1`, `k`, and `k + 1`.
steps: Map each stone position to an empty set of jump sizes.
Put 0 in the set of the first stone, so the first jump has size 1.
For each stone in order, and each size `k` in its set, try jumps of `k - 1`, `k`, and `k + 1`.
If a jump is positive and lands on a stone, add that jump size to the set of that stone.
Return true if the set of the last stone is not empty.
hints: The next jump depends on the last jump size. So for each stone, keep the set of jump sizes that can land there.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-v.insight: Extend the k-transaction stock DP with three states per transaction count: flat, holding a long position, and holding a short position.
steps: Let `f[j][s]` be the best profit with at most `j` transactions in state `s`: flat, long, or short.
Set every flat value to 0. On day 0, set long to `-prices[0]` and short to `prices[0]` for each `j >= 1`.
Compute each day only from the previous day, and update only `j` from 1 to `k`.
For price `p`, set flat to the max of flat, `long + p`, and `short - p` at the same `j`.
Set long to the max of long and `flat[j - 1] - p`, and short to the max of short and `flat[j - 1] + p`.
Return the flat value for `j = k` after the last day.
hints: Each day ends flat, holding a long position, or holding a short position. Track the best profit for each state and transaction count.

number-of-strings-that-appear-as-substri.insight: Test each pattern for substring membership in `word` and count the matches.
steps: Let `n` be the pattern count, `m` the length of `word`, and `L` the max pattern length.
For each pattern, run a substring search in `word`.
Count the patterns that occur, and return the count.
hints: Each pattern is independent, so test whether `word` contains it and count the hits.

letter-case-permutation.insight: Backtracking branches at each letter into its lowercase and uppercase forms, while each digit has one branch.
steps: Convert `s` to a character array, and run DFS from index 0.
At the end of the array, add the current string to the answer.
At a digit, recurse to the next index.
At a letter, recurse once, then flip its case with `c ^ 32` and recurse again.
hints: Each letter has two choices, lowercase or uppercase, and each digit has one choice. The output has `2^L` strings for `L` letters.

rearrange-products-table.insight: Unpivot the three store columns with a `UNION ALL` of three SELECT queries, and drop rows with a null price.
steps: SELECT `product_id`, `'store1' AS store`, and `store1 AS price` FROM `Products` WHERE `store1 IS NOT NULL`.
Write the same query for `store2` and for `store3`.
Combine the three results with `UNION ALL`; `n` is the row count of `Products`.
hints: A single product row gives up to three output rows. Treat each store column as a separate source of prices.

number-of-good-paths.insight: Add edges in order of their larger endpoint value with union-find; equal max values in two merged components form new good paths.
steps: Start the answer at `n`, for the single-node paths.
Sort the edges by `max(vals[a], vals[b])`.
Give each union-find root the max value of its component and the count of nodes with that value.
For each edge, find roots `ra` and `rb`; if their max values are equal, add `cnt[ra] * cnt[rb]`.
Then merge: on equal max values add the counts, else attach the root with the smaller max.
hints: A good path stays among nodes with values at most its end value. So add edges from small values to large values, and count equal maxima when groups join.

count-palindromic-subsequences.insight: A length-5 palindrome has the form `abcba`, so for each center multiply the left count of pairs `ab` by the right count of `ba`.
steps: Scan `s` from left to right with `cnt[a]`, the count of digit `a` so far.
Let `pre[i][a][b]` be the count of subsequence pairs `(a, b)` in `s[0..i-1]`.
At digit `d = s[i]`, copy `pre[i]` to `pre[i + 1]`, add `cnt[a]` to `pre[i + 1][a][d]` for each `a`, then increment `cnt[d]`.
Reset `cnt` and a running pair table `R`. From right to left, first copy `R` to `suf[i]`, the pair counts in `s[i+1..n-1]`. Then add `cnt[y]` to `R[s[i]][y]` for each `y`, and increment `cnt[s[i]]`.
For each center `i`, add `pre[i][a][b] * suf[i][b][a]` over all 100 digit pairs.
Return the sum modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: A length-5 palindrome has the form `abcba`. For each center, count the pairs `ab` on the left and `ba` on the right.

number-of-paths-with-max-score.insight: A DP from `S` to `E` keeps the best score and its path count per cell; a better predecessor replaces the count, a tie adds.
steps: Let `f[i][j]` be the best score from `S` to `(i, j)`, and `g[i][j]` its path count.
Set `f` to -1 everywhere, then set `f[n-1][n-1] = 0` and `g[n-1][n-1] = 1`.
Fill the cells from bottom-right to top-left, and skip `X` cells and the `S` cell.
Over the reachable neighbors below, right, and diagonal, take the max score and add the counts that tie.
If the cell is reachable, add its digit to `f[i][j]`, with 0 for `E`. Keep `g` modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Each cell is reached from below, from the right, or diagonally. Keep the best score and the count of paths that reach that score.

monotonic-array.insight: One pass can test both directions: the array is monotonic when no adjacent pair goes down or no adjacent pair goes up.
steps: Set `inc` and `dec` to true.
For each adjacent pair, set `inc` to false if `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`.
Set `dec` to false if `nums[i] < nums[i + 1]`.
Return `inc or dec`.
hints: An array is monotonic when no adjacent pair goes down, or when no adjacent pair goes up.

concatenate-non-zero-digits-and-multiply.insight: Read the digits of `n` from the low end, build `x` from the non-zero digits in their order, sum them, and return the product.
steps: Set `x = 0`, `s = 0`, and the place value `p = 1`.
While `n > 0`, take the last digit `d = n % 10`, and set `n = n / 10`.
If `d > 0`, add `d * p` to `x`, add `d` to `s`, and multiply `p` by 10.
Return `x * s`.
hints: Read the digits from the low end, and put each non-zero digit at the next place value of `x`. Sum the same digits.

count-number-of-nice-subarrays.insight: Treat odd numbers as 1 and even numbers as 0, then count subarrays whose prefix sums differ by `k` with a hash map.
steps: Set `cnt[0] = 1` and the running odd count `t = 0`.
For each number, add 1 to `t` if the number is odd.
Add `cnt[t - k]` to the answer.
Then increment `cnt[t]`.
hints: Change each odd number to 1 and each even number to 0. Then a nice subarray has a sum of exactly `k`.

ipo.insight: Capital never falls, so sort projects by capital and, each round, push all affordable projects into a max-heap of profits and take the top.
steps: Sort the projects by `capital`.
Repeat up to `k` times.
Push the profit of each new project with capital at most `w` into a max-heap.
If the heap is empty, stop; else pop the max profit and add it to `w`.
Return `w`.
hints: Capital never goes down, so a project that is affordable now stays affordable. Each round, take the largest profit among the affordable projects.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-ii.insight: After a sort by value, a greedy jump to the farthest node within `maxDiff` is optimal, and binary lifting answers each query in logarithmic time.
steps: Sort the node indices by `nums`, and record the sorted position `pos` of each node.
With two pointers, set `nxt[i]` to the last sorted position within `maxDiff` of position `i`.
Build `up[k][i]`, the position after `2^k` jumps, from `up[k - 1]`.
For each of the `q` queries, let `a <= b` be the positions of `u` and `v`, and return 0 if `a == b`.
For `k` from high to low, if `up[k][a] < b`, set `a = up[k][a]` and add `2^k` to the jump count.
Return the jump count plus 1 if `nxt[a] >= b`, else return -1.
hints: In value order, each node reaches one contiguous block of nodes. A move to the far end of that block, toward the target, never leaves you worse off.

sum-of-square-numbers.insight: Two pointers from `0` and `floor(sqrt(c))` move toward each other, because each square grows with its pointer.
steps: Set `a = 0` and `b = floor(sqrt(c))`.
While `a <= b`, compute `s = a * a + b * b` with 64-bit integers.
Return true if `s == c`.
Increment `a` if `s < c`, else decrement `b`.
Return false after the loop.
hints: If `a * a + b * b < c`, then `a` also fails with every smaller `b`. If the sum is above `c`, `b` also fails with every larger `a`.

unique-middle-element.insight: Take the middle element at index `n / 2` and count its occurrences in one pass.
steps: Set `mid = nums[n / 2]`.
Count the elements that equal `mid`.
Return true if the count is 1.
hints: The middle element is `nums[n / 2]`, so count how many times that value appears.

shift-2d-grid.insight: A shift of `k` steps rotates the row-major flat array, so each cell moves to flat index `(i * n + j + k) % (m * n)`.
steps: Make a new `m` by `n` grid `ans`.
For each cell `(i, j)`, compute `t = (i * n + j + k) % (m * n)`.
Put `grid[i][j]` at `ans[t / n][t % n]`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Read the grid row by row as one flat list. A shift of `k` rotates that list by `k` positions.

second-minimum-time-to-reach-destination.insight: Total time grows with hop count alone, so find the strictly second-shortest hop count with a BFS that keeps two distances per node.
steps: Build adjacency lists for the `m` edges, and set `d1` and `d2` to infinity for each node.
Start BFS from node 1 with `d1[1] = 0`.
For each popped `(u, d)` and neighbor `v`, if `d + 1 < d1[v]`, set `d1[v] = d + 1` and push it.
Else, if `d1[v] < d + 1 < d2[v]`, set `d2[v] = d + 1` and push it.
Simulate `d2[n]` hops: before each hop, if `(t / change) % 2 == 1`, wait to the next multiple of `change`.
Add `time` to `t` for each hop, and return `t` after all hops.
hints: All edges take the same time, so the total time depends only on the hop count. Find the strictly second-smallest hop count to `n`.

count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.insight: Put the allowed letters in a 26-bit mask; a word is consistent when the bit of each of its letters is in that mask.
steps: Build `mask` with bit `c - 'a'` set for each letter `c` in `allowed`.
For each word, check that each letter has its bit in `mask`.
Count the words that pass; `L` is the total length of all words.
hints: Only 26 letters exist, so one integer with 26 bits can store the allowed set.

construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.insight: The last postorder value is the root, and its inorder index splits the remaining values into the left and right subtrees.
steps: Map each value to its index in `inorder`.
Write `build(lo, hi)` for an inorder range, and keep a pointer `p` at the end of `postorder`.
If `lo > hi`, return null.
Make the root from `postorder[p]`, decrement `p`, and find its inorder index `mid`.
Build the right subtree from `(mid + 1, hi)` first, then the left subtree from `(lo, mid - 1)`.
Return the root.
hints: The last postorder value is the root. Its position in `inorder` splits the left and right subtrees.

hand-of-straights.insight: The smallest remaining card must start a group, so greedily take the next `groupSize` consecutive values from it.
steps: If `len(hand) % groupSize != 0`, return false.
Count each card, and sort the distinct values.
For each value `x` in order with `cnt[x] > 0`, start `c = cnt[x]` groups at `x`.
For each `y` from `x` to `x + groupSize - 1`, return false if `cnt[y] < c`, else subtract `c`.
Return true after all values.
hints: The smallest remaining card must start a group. So that group needs the next `groupSize - 1` consecutive values too.

minimum-time-to-complete-trips.insight: Binary search on the answer works because the trip count by time `t`, the sum of `t / time[i]`, never decreases as `t` grows.
steps: Let `m = min(time)`. Set `lo = 1` and `hi = m * totalTrips`, because the fastest bus alone finishes by `hi`.
Use 64-bit integers for `lo`, `hi`, `mid`, and the trip sum.
While `lo < hi`, set `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` with integer division.
Add `mid / time[i]` with integer division for all buses to get the trip sum.
If the sum is at least `totalTrips`, set `hi = mid`. Else, set `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo` after the loop.
hints: The trip count by time `t` is the sum of `t / time[i]` rounded down, and it never decreases as `t` grows.

maximum-product-of-two-digits.insight: The maximum product always comes from the largest digit and the second largest digit, so track only these two values.
steps: Set `a = 0` and `b = 0` for the largest and second largest digits.
Remove the last digit `x` of `n` with `n % 10` and `n / 10` until `n` is zero.
If `x > a`, set `b = a` and then `a = x`.
Else, if `x > b`, set `b = x`.
Return `a * b`.
hints: Digits are never negative. What happens to the product when you replace one factor with a larger digit of `n`?

partition-labels.insight: A greedy scan with the last index of each letter closes a part as soon as the scan reaches the farthest last index seen.
steps: Record `last[c]`, the last index of each letter `c` in `s`.
Set the part start `j = 0` and the part end `end = 0`.
For each index `i`, set `end = max(end, last[s[i]])`.
If `i == end`, add `i - j + 1` to the result and set `j = i + 1`.
Return the result list.
hints: A part that holds a letter must reach the last index of that letter. What is the earliest index where a part can end?

vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.insight: Record a (column, row, value) tuple for each node with DFS, then one sort puts the nodes in the required output order.
steps: Run DFS from the root at row 0 and column 0.
For each node, record `(col, row, val)`. Send the left child to `col - 1` and the right child to `col + 1`, both at `row + 1`.
Sort the tuples by column, then row, then value.
Scan the sorted tuples and start a new list each time the column changes.
Add each value to the current list and return all lists.
hints: Collect the position and value of every node first. The visit order does not have to match the output order.

maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.insight: Binary search on the answer: if each child can get `v` candies, each child can also get any smaller amount.
steps: Let `M = max(candies)`. Set `lo = 0` and `hi = M`.
While `lo < hi`, set `mid = (lo + hi + 1) / 2` with integer division. This rounds up, so the search always moves.
Add `candies[i] / mid` with integer division for all piles to get the number of full portions. Use a 64-bit sum.
If the count is at least `k`, set `lo = mid`. Else, set `hi = mid - 1`.
Return `lo` after the loop. The value 0 is the answer when the total candies are less than `k`.
hints: If each child can get `v` candies, each child can also get fewer. For a fixed `v > 0`, pile `i` serves `candies[i] / v` children, rounded down.

step-by-step-directions-from-a-binary-tr.insight: The shortest path goes up to the lowest common ancestor and then down, so find both root paths and remove their common prefix.
steps: Use DFS to find the path of `L` and `R` moves from the root to `startValue`.
Use DFS to find the same type of path from the root to `destValue`.
Remove the longest common prefix of the two paths. This prefix leads to the lowest common ancestor.
Replace each remaining move in the start path with `U`.
Return the `U` moves followed by the remaining moves of the destination path.
hints: The shortest route goes up to the deepest node above both nodes, then goes down. How can the two paths from the root find that node?

count-valid-sequences.insight: Use complementary counting: subtract the all-odd compositions from all compositions of `n` into `k` positive parts.
steps: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo `10^9 + 7` up to `n`.
Count all ordered sequences with stars and bars as `C(n - 1, k - 1)`.
If `n + k` is odd, no all-odd sequence exists, so return the total.
Else, write each part as `2a + 1`. The `a` values sum to `(n - k) / 2`.
Subtract `C((n + k) / 2 - 1, k - 1)` from the total and return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: The product is even unless every part is odd. Count all sequences, then subtract the sequences where every part is odd.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.insight: Build the first half letter by letter, and use the count of multiset permutations, capped at `k`, to skip whole blocks of ranks.
steps: Count the letters of `s`. Halve each count to get the multiset for the first half, and keep the odd letter as the middle.
Count permutations as a product of binomials `C(R, c)`, capped at `k + 1`. Build each binomial term by term, and stop once it exceeds `k`, because it only grows.
If the full half count is less than `k`, return an empty string.
For each position, try letters from `a` to `z` that have a remaining count above 0. Remove one and count the permutations of the rest.
If that count is at least `k`, keep the letter. Else, subtract the count from `k` and put the letter back.
Mirror the half around the middle letter and return the palindrome.
hints: The first half fixes the palindrome. Choose the half one letter at a time, and count how many halves start with each candidate letter.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.insight: State machine DP: four variables hold the best profit after the first buy, first sell, second buy, and second sell.
steps: Set `buy1 = -prices[0]`, `sell1 = 0`, `buy2 = -prices[0]`, and `sell2 = 0`.
For each later price `p`, set `buy1 = max(buy1, -p)`.
Set `sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p)` and `buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p)`.
Set `sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p)`.
Return `sell2`. A buy and sell on the same day gives 0, so the order of updates is safe.
hints: On each day you are in one of four states: after the first buy, first sell, second buy, or second sell. Track the best profit for each state.

how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.insight: Counting sort with prefix sums gives, for each value, the number of smaller values, because values are at most `M = 100`.
steps: Make an array `cnt` of size 102 and count each value of `nums`.
Change `cnt` into prefix sums, so `cnt[v]` is the number of values less than `v`.
For each `nums[i]`, put `cnt[nums[i]]` in the answer.
Return the answer array.
hints: Values are at most 100. If you know how often each value occurs, the count below `v` is the total for all smaller values.

sort-array-by-parity.insight: Two pointers from both ends move in place, and each swap sends an odd value right and an even value left.
steps: Set `i = 0` and `j = n - 1`.
While `i < j`, if `nums[i]` is even, increase `i`.
Else, if `nums[j]` is odd, decrease `j`.
Else, swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`, then increase `i` and decrease `j`.
Return `nums`.
hints: An odd value near the left end and an even value near the right end are both in the wrong half, so swap them.

ugly-number.insight: Divide out all factors of 2, 3, and 5; the number is ugly only if 1 remains.
steps: If `n < 1`, return false, because ugly numbers are positive.
For each `x` in 2, 3, and 5, divide `n` by `x` while `n % x == 0`.
Return true if `n == 1`, else return false.
hints: Only positive values can be ugly. Remove every factor 2, 3, and 5 from `n`; what value remains if `n` has no other prime factor?

stone-game-iv.insight: Game theory DP: a pile is a win if some square move leaves the opponent at a pile that loses.
steps: Make a boolean array `win` of size `n + 1`. Set `win[0] = false` because the player to move loses.
For each `i` from 1 to `n`, try each square `j * j <= i`.
If `win[i - j * j]` is false, set `win[i] = true` and stop the loop.
Return `win[n]`.
hints: A pile size is a win if some square move leaves the opponent at a losing size. Size 0 is a loss for the player to move.

check-if-object-instance-of-class.insight: Walk up the prototype chain with `Object.getPrototypeOf` and compare each prototype with `classFunction.prototype`; this also works for primitives.
steps: If `obj` or `classFunction` is `null` or `undefined`, return false.
Set `proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`. This call boxes a primitive such as 5 into its wrapper object.
While `proto` is not `null`, compare `proto` with `classFunction.prototype`.
If they are equal, return true. Else, set `proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto)`.
Return false when the chain ends at `null`. The chain has `d` levels.
hints: An object has the methods of a class when `classFunction.prototype` occurs in its prototype chain. Primitives other than `null` and `undefined` also have a chain.

counting-bits.insight: Bit DP: the count for `i` equals the count for `i >> 1` plus the lowest bit of `i`.
steps: Make an array `ans` of size `n + 1` with `ans[0] = 0`.
For each `i` from 1 to `n`, set `ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`.
Return `ans`.
hints: A right shift of `i` by one bit drops only its lowest bit. How does the count for `i` relate to the count for `i >> 1`?

length-of-longest-subarray-with-at-most-.insight: A sliding window with a frequency map stays valid if no count exceeds `k`, and only the new value can break this rule.
steps: Keep a map `cnt` of value counts in the window and a left pointer `l = 0`.
For each right index `r`, increase `cnt[nums[r]]`.
While `cnt[nums[r]] > k`, decrease `cnt[nums[l]]` and increase `l`.
Update the answer with `r - l + 1`.
Return the answer.
hints: When a new value enters the range, only that value can go above `k`. Move the left end until its count is back to `k`.

count-elements-with-maximum-frequency.insight: Count the frequency of each value, then add the frequencies of all values that reach the maximum frequency.
steps: Count each value of `nums` in a map or an array of size 101.
Find `mx`, the largest count.
Add every count that equals `mx`.
Return the sum. It counts elements, not distinct values.
hints: The answer counts elements, not distinct values. Find the largest frequency, then add the frequencies of all values that reach it.

longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.insight: A segment tree stores the longest prefix run, suffix run, and inner run of each segment, so each point update merges in logarithmic time.
steps: Build a segment tree over `s`. Each node stores `pre`, `suf`, and `best` run lengths for its segment.
To merge two children, copy `pre` from the left child, `suf` from the right child, and the larger `best`.
If the left child's last letter equals the right child's first letter, compare `best` with `left.suf + right.pre`.
In that case, if the left child is one full run, add `right.pre` to `pre`.
In that case, if the right child is one full run, add `left.suf` to `suf`.
For each query, change the leaf letter, merge up to the root, and record the root `best`.
hints: For any segment, keep the run at its left edge, the run at its right edge, and the best run inside. Two segments combine from these values.

maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.insight: A sliding window with letter counts stays valid while each letter occurs at most twice.
steps: Keep a count array for 26 letters and a left pointer `l = 0`.
For each right index `r`, increase the count of `s[r]`.
While the count of `s[r]` is more than 2, decrease the count of `s[l]` and increase `l`.
Update the answer with `r - l + 1`.
Return the answer.
hints: When a new letter enters the range, only that letter can occur three times. Move the left end forward until it occurs twice.

remove-all-occurrences-of-a-substring.insight: Use a stack of characters with a KMP match length for each entry, so a removal restores the old match state in constant time.
steps: Build the KMP prefix function `lps` for `part`, with `m` as the length of `part`.
Keep a stack of characters and a parallel stack `match` of matched prefix lengths.
For each character `c`, let `j` be the top `match` value, or 0 if the stacks are empty.
While `j > 0` and `part[j] != c`, set `j = lps[j - 1]`. If `part[j] == c`, add 1 to `j`.
Push `c` and `j`. If `j` equals `m`, pop `m` entries from both stacks.
Join the character stack and return it.
hints: Build the result one character at a time, and store with each character how much of `part` ends there. A removal then restores the earlier match length.

find-the-largest-almost-missing-integer.insight: Case analysis on `k`: when `1 < k < n`, only the first and last elements can be in exactly one window of size `k`.
steps: If `k == n`, return the maximum of `nums`, because one window holds all values.
If `k == 1`, return the largest value that occurs exactly once, or -1.
Else, keep `nums[0]` only if it does not occur at another index.
Keep `nums[n - 1]` only if it does not occur at another index.
Return the larger kept value, or -1 if none is kept.
hints: When `1 < k < n`, every inner index is in at least two subarrays of size `k`. Only the first and last elements can be in one.

number-of-steps-to-reduce-a-number-to-ze.insight: Each 1 bit costs one subtraction and each bit after the highest bit costs one shift, so count bits or simulate.
steps: Set `steps = 0`.
While `num > 0`, subtract 1 if `num` is odd, else shift `num` right by one bit.
Increase `steps` after each operation.
Return `steps`.
hints: Each 1 bit costs one subtraction, and each bit below the highest bit costs one halving.

maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.insight: A fixed-size sliding window updates the vowel count in constant time when one letter enters and one letter leaves.
steps: Count the vowels in the first `k` letters. Set the answer to this count.
For each index `i` from `k` to `n - 1`, add 1 if `s[i]` is a vowel.
Subtract 1 if `s[i - k]` is a vowel.
Update the answer with the current count.
Return the answer.
hints: When the substring of length `k` moves one step, one letter enters and one letter leaves. Update the vowel count with only these two letters.

remove-linked-list-elements.insight: A dummy node before the head lets one pointer remove each node with value `val`, and the head too, with the same rule.
steps: Make a dummy node that points to `head`. Set `pre = dummy`.
While `pre.next` is not null, check `pre.next.val`.
If it equals `val`, set `pre.next = pre.next.next` and do not move `pre`.
Else, move `pre` to `pre.next`.
Return `dummy.next`.
hints: The head node can also have the value `val`. Put an extra node before the head so that every removal follows the same rule.

repeated-dna-sequences.insight: Slide a window of length 10 and count each substring in a hash map; a 2-bit rolling hash can make each step constant time.
steps: Make a map `cnt` from substring to count and an empty result list.
For each start `i` from 0 to `n - 10`, take `t = s[i..i+9]`.
Increase `cnt[t]`.
If `cnt[t]` becomes 2, add `t` to the result. This adds each repeat only one time.
Return the result.
hints: When `n >= 10`, there are only `n - 9` substrings of length 10. How can you tell that you saw one of them before?

number-of-dice-rolls-with-target-sum.insight: Use DP over dice and sums: the ways to reach sum `j` with `i` dice add up the ways for `i - 1` dice over each face.
steps: Let `f[i][j]` be the number of ways for `i` dice to sum to `j`. Keep only two rows, `prev` and `curr`.
Set `prev` to `target + 1` zeros, then set `prev[0] = 1` for zero dice.
For each die from 1 to `n`, set `curr` to `target + 1` zeros.
For each `j` up to `target`, set `curr[j]` to the sum of `prev[j - h]` for each face `h` up to `min(j, k)`.
Take each sum modulo `10^9 + 7`. After the die, set `prev = curr`.
Return `prev[target]`.
hints: The last die shows some face `h`. The other dice then make the sum `target - h` with one fewer die.

redundant-connection.insight: Union-find: the first edge whose two ends already share a component closes the only cycle, and it is the last cycle edge in input order.
steps: Make a union-find structure for nodes 1 to `n`, with path compression and union by size.
For each edge `[a, b]` in input order, find the roots of `a` and `b`.
If the roots are equal, return `[a, b]`.
Else, join the two components.
hints: Add the edges in input order and track which nodes are already connected. The first edge whose two ends are already connected closes the cycle.

sign-of-the-product-of-an-array.insight: The sign depends only on zeros and the count of negative values, so do not compute the product.
steps: Set `sign = 1`.
For each value `v`, return 0 if `v == 0`.
If `v < 0`, set `sign = -sign`.
Return `sign`.
hints: The sign depends only on a zero value and on the number of negative values. Do not compute the product.

time-needed-to-buy-tickets.insight: When person `k` finishes, each person ahead has bought at most `tickets[k]` tickets, and each person behind at most `tickets[k] - 1`.
steps: Set `total = 0`.
For each person `i` with `i <= k`, add `min(tickets[i], tickets[k])`.
For each person `i` with `i > k`, add `min(tickets[i], tickets[k] - 1)`.
Return `total`.
hints: When person `k` buys the last ticket, how many tickets has each person ahead of `k` bought, and each person behind `k`?

trips-and-users.insight: Join `Users` two times to remove trips with a banned client or driver, then GROUP BY day and average a cancel flag. Let `n` be the row count of `Trips`.
steps: Join `Trips` to `Users` on `client_id` and keep rows where the client has `banned = 'No'`.
Join `Users` again on `driver_id` and keep rows where the driver has `banned = 'No'`.
Keep rows with `request_at` between '2013-10-01' and '2013-10-03'.
GROUP BY `request_at` and compute `AVG(status != 'completed')`.
Round the average to two decimals and name the columns `Day` and `Cancellation Rate`.
hints: Each trip row has two user ids, so match the `Users` table two times, once for the client and once for the driver. Then group the rows by day.

alien-dictionary.insight: Each adjacent word pair gives one order edge at its first different letter; a topological sort of these edges gives the alphabet.
steps: Add every letter in `words` to the graph with in-degree 0. Let `C` be the total letter count.
For each adjacent pair, find the first index where the letters differ. If that edge is new, add it and increase the in-degree of the second letter by 1.
If no letters differ and the first word is longer, return an empty string, because the order is invalid.
Run Kahn's algorithm: put all letters with in-degree 0 in a queue.
Pop a letter, add it to the result, and decrease the in-degree of its neighbors. Push neighbors that reach 0.
If the result has fewer letters than the graph, a cycle exists, so return an empty string. Else, return the result.
hints: Two adjacent words give one order rule at their first different letter. The alphabet is an order of letters that obeys every rule.

smallest-stable-index-i.insight: Precompute suffix minimums, then scan from the left with a prefix maximum to test each index in constant time.
steps: Build `sufMin[i]`, the minimum of `nums[i..n-1]`, with one pass from the right.
Set `preMax` to the smallest possible value.
For each index `i` from left to right, set `preMax = max(preMax, nums[i])`.
If `preMax - sufMin[i] <= k`, return `i`.
Return -1 if no index is stable.
hints: For each index `i`, you need the largest value up to `i` and the smallest value from `i` to the end. Compute the smallest values from the right first.

best-sightseeing-pair.insight: Split the score into `values[i] + i` and `values[j] - j`, then keep the best left part while you scan `j`.
steps: Set `best = values[0] + 0` and `ans` to the smallest possible value.
For each `j` from 1 to `n - 1`, update `ans` with `best + values[j] - j`.
Then update `best` with `values[j] + j`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Split the score into `values[i] + i` and `values[j] - j`. For each `j`, which earlier `i` gives the best first part?

max-points-on-a-line.insight: Fix each point as an anchor and group the other points by reduced slope in a hash map; use GCD so slopes stay exact integers.
steps: For each anchor point `i`, make an empty map from slope to count.
For each later point `j`, compute `dx` and `dy` from point `i` to point `j`. Let `M` be the coordinate range.
Divide `dx` and `dy` by `gcd(dx, dy)`. If `dx < 0`, or `dx == 0` and `dy < 0`, negate both.
Increase the count of the pair `(dx, dy)` and update the answer with the count plus 1.
Return the answer, which is at least 1 for one point.
hints: Fix one point. Other points share a line with it when they have the same slope from it, so store each slope as a reduced integer pair.

count-commas-in-range.insight: Because `n` is at most `10^5`, each number from 1000 to `n` has exactly one comma and smaller numbers have none.
steps: Numbers from 1 to 999 have no comma.
Each number from 1000 to `n` has one comma, because no number reaches seven digits.
Return `max(0, n - 999)`.
hints: Because `n` is at most `10^5`, no number has two commas. Which numbers have exactly one comma?

excel-sheet-column-number.insight: The title is a base-26 number with digits from 1 to 26, so fold the letters from left to right.
steps: Set `ans = 0`.
For each letter `c` from left to right, set `ans = ans * 26 + (c - 'A' + 1)`.
Return `ans`.
hints: The title is a base-26 number where the digits go from 1 to 26 instead of 0 to 25.

path-sum-ii.insight: Backtracking DFS keeps one shared path list, copies it at each leaf with the target sum, and removes the node on return.
steps: Start with an empty result and a shared empty `path`. Call DFS on `root` with `targetSum`, then return the result.
In DFS, return at once if the node is null.
Else, append the node value to `path` and subtract it from the remaining sum.
If the node is a leaf and the remaining sum is 0, add a copy of `path` to the result.
Recurse into the left and right children.
Remove the last value from `path` before you return.
hints: Paths that go into different children share the path to their parent. How can one list hold the current path without mixing the branches?

zero-array-transformation-ii.insight: Binary search on the number of queries `k`, because more queries never hurt, and check each `k` with a difference array.
steps: To check `k`, make `d` as `n + 1` zeros. Add `val` at `d[l]` and subtract `val` at `d[r + 1]` for the first `k` queries.
Scan `i` from 0 to `n - 1` with a running prefix sum of `d`, starting at 0. If any `nums[i]` is greater than that sum, the check fails.
Binary search `k` from 0 to `m`, where `m` is the number of queries.
If the check for `m` fails, return -1.
Else, return the smallest `k` that passes.
hints: If the first `k` queries make a zero array, more queries also do. For a fixed `k`, compare each `nums[i]` with the total `val` that covers index `i`.

defanging-an-ip-address.insight: Build a new string and replace each period with the three characters `[.]`.
steps: Make an empty string builder.
For each character, append `[.]` if it is a period, else append the character.
Return the built string.
hints: Build a new string in one pass, and write `[.]` in place of each period.

find-the-pivot-integer.insight: Both sides equal when `x * x = n * (n + 1) / 2`, so the pivot is the integer square root of the total sum.
steps: Compute `total = n * (n + 1) / 2`.
Compute `x` as the integer square root of `total`.
Return `x` if `x * x == total`, else return -1.
hints: Both sides include `x`. Write each side with the formula for the sum of consecutive integers, and simplify the equation.

to-lower-case.insight: In ASCII, an uppercase letter and its lowercase letter differ only in bit 5, so OR the code with 32.
steps: For each character `c`, check if it is between `A` and `Z`.
If it is, replace it with the character for `c | 32`.
Else, keep `c` as it is.
Return the new string.
hints: In ASCII, an uppercase letter and its lowercase letter differ by 32, which is one bit of the character code.

maximum-number-of-non-overlapping-substr.insight: Build the smallest valid interval that starts at each letter's first index, then pick intervals greedily by earliest right end.
steps: Record `first[c]` and `last[c]` for each letter `c`.
For each letter `c`, set `l = first[c]` and `r = last[c]`. Scan `i` from `l` to `r`.
If `first[s[i]] < l`, drop this interval. Else, set `r = max(r, last[s[i]])`.
Sort the valid intervals by right end. Valid intervals are nested or disjoint, never partly overlapping.
Take each interval whose left end is after the last taken right end.
Return the substrings of the taken intervals.
hints: A letter inside a candidate substring can push its right end farther. If that letter also occurs before the left end, the candidate is not valid.

baseball-game.insight: A stack holds the valid scores, so each operation reads or removes only the top one or two scores.
steps: Make an empty stack.
For `+`, push the sum of the top two scores. For `D`, push two times the top score.
For `C`, pop the top score.
For a number, push it.
Return the sum of all scores in the stack.
hints: Each operation reads or removes only the most recent one or two valid scores.

smallest-index-with-digit-sum-equal-to-i.insight: Scan the indices from 0 and return the first index where the digit sum of `nums[i]` equals `i`.
steps: For each index `i` from 0, compute the digit sum of `nums[i]` with `% 10` and `/ 10`.
If the digit sum equals `i`, return `i`.
Return -1 after the scan.
hints: Check the indices in increasing order, and compute each digit sum with `% 10` and `/ 10`.

brace-expansion-ii.insight: Recursion: expand the innermost brace group first, because the first `}` always closes a group that has no nested braces.
steps: Find the first `}` in the string. If none exists, add the string to a result set and return.
Find the nearest `{` to the left of that `}`.
Split the text between them on commas into options.
For each option, recurse on the prefix, plus the option, plus the suffix.
Sort the result set and return it as a list. Let `W` be the number of words that the recursion makes, with repeats.
hints: The first `}` in the string closes a group with no braces inside it. What happens when you replace that group with each of its options?

maximum-subarray-sum-with-one-deletion.insight: Kadane DP with two states: the best sum that ends here with no deletion, and with exactly one deletion.
steps: Set `keep = arr[0]`, `del = -infinity`, and `ans = arr[0]`.
For each later value `x`, set `del = max(del + x, keep)`. The second term deletes `x`.
Then set `keep = max(keep + x, x)`.
Update `ans` with `max(keep, del)`.
Return `ans`. The `keep` state keeps the subarray non-empty after a deletion.
hints: For each end index, track two best sums: one with no deletion and one with exactly one deletion. The deletion removes the current value or an earlier value.

find-x-value-of-array-i.insight: The kept part is any non-empty subarray, so count subarrays by product remainder with DP over `k` remainders.
steps: Set `f` and `result` to arrays of `k` zeros. `f[r]` counts subarrays that end at the previous index with product remainder `r`.
For each `x` in `nums`, make a new array `g` of `k` zeros.
For each `r`, add `f[r]` to `g[(r * x) % k]`. Then add 1 to `g[x % k]` for the single element.
Add each `g[r]` to `result[r]`, then set `f = g`.
Return `result`.
hints: Removing a prefix and a suffix leaves any non-empty subarray. Track how many subarrays that end at each index have each product remainder modulo `k`.

maximum-nesting-depth-of-two-valid-paren.insight: Greedy by depth parity: give alternate nesting layers to the two groups, so each group gets about half of the depth.
steps: Keep a balance `x`, the number of open `(` before the current index.
For `(`, set `ans[i] = x % 2` and then increase `x`.
For `)`, decrease `x` first and then set `ans[i] = x % 2`.
A matched pair gets the same parity, so both groups stay valid.
Return `ans`. The larger group depth is `ceil(d / 2)`, where `d` is the depth of `seq`.
hints: Only nested pairs add depth; pairs side by side do not. Which pairs must go to different groups to cut the depth in half?

replace-elements-with-greatest-element-o.insight: Scan from right to left and keep the running maximum of the values to the right.
steps: Set `mx = -1`.
For each index `i` from `n - 1` down to 0, save `x = arr[i]`.
Set `arr[i] = mx`, then set `mx = max(mx, x)`.
Return `arr`.
hints: Scan from the right end and keep the largest value seen so far.

print-binary-tree.insight: Compute the tree height `h` first to size the matrix, then use DFS to place each child at an offset of `2^(h - r - 1)`.
steps: Compute the height `h` with DFS, where a single node has height 0.
Make a matrix of `h + 1` rows and `2^(h + 1) - 1` columns, filled with empty strings.
Place the root at row 0 and column `(cols - 1) / 2`.
For a node at `(r, c)`, place the left child at column `c - 2^(h - r - 1)` in row `r + 1`.
Place the right child at column `c + 2^(h - r - 1)` in row `r + 1`, and return the matrix.
hints: Carry the row and column of each node when you visit its children. Find the tree height before you make the matrix.

minimum-insertions-to-balance-a-parenthe.insight: Greedy scan: count open `(` that wait for `))`, and add an insertion each time a needed character is missing.
steps: Set `open = 0` and `ans = 0`.
For `(`, increase `open`.
For `)`, if the next character is also `)`, skip it. Else, add 1 to `ans` for a missing `)`.
Then, if `open > 0`, decrease `open`. Else, add 1 to `ans` for a missing `(`.
After the scan, add `2 * open` to `ans` and return it.
hints: Each `(` waits for a pair `))`. Scan once, and count a missing character each time a `)` has no partner `)` or no open `(`.

maximum-alternating-sum-of-squares.insight: Signs do not matter for squares, so sort the squares and give the largest values to the plus positions.
steps: Replace each value with its square and sort in ascending order.
Let `m = n / 2` with integer division. The array has `n - m` plus positions.
Subtract the first `m` squares from the score.
Add the remaining `n - m` squares to the score.
Return the score. Use 64-bit integers.
hints: Squares remove the signs of the values. Give the largest squares to the plus positions, and there are `n - n / 2` of them.

longest-string-chain.insight: Sort words by length and use DP in a hash map: each word extends the best chain of any word made by one deletion.
steps: Put `words` into buckets by length, and process the buckets in ascending order.
Keep a map `dp` from word to the longest chain that ends at that word.
For each word `w`, delete each position in turn to make a candidate predecessor.
Set `dp[w]` to 1 plus the largest `dp` value of a candidate in the map, or 1 if none.
Return the maximum value in `dp`. `L` is the maximum word length.
hints: A predecessor of a word is that word with one letter removed. Process the words from short to long, and try every one-letter deletion.

longest-arithmetic-subsequence-of-given-.insight: DP in a hash map keyed by value: the best chain that ends at `x` extends the chain that ends at `x - difference`.
steps: Make an empty map `f` from value to chain length.
For each `x` in `arr` from left to right, set `f[x] = f[x - difference] + 1`. Use 0 if the key is absent.
Track the maximum value of `f[x]`.
Return the maximum.
hints: The best chain that ends at value `x` extends the best earlier chain that ends at value `x - difference`.

evaluate-division.insight: Weighted union-find stores each variable as a ratio to its root. Let `E`, `Q`, and `V` be the counts of equations, queries, and variables.
steps: For each variable `x` in `equations`, set `parent[x] = x` and `w[x] = 1.0`. `w[x]` is the value of `x` divided by `parent[x]`.
In `find`, compress the path and multiply the weights along it, so `w[x]` becomes `x / root`.
For each equation `a / b = v`, find roots `ra` and `rb`. If they differ, set `parent[ra] = rb` and `w[ra] = w[b] * v / w[a]`.
For a query `c / d`, return -1.0 if a variable is unknown. Else, call `find` on both and return -1.0 if the roots differ.
Else, return `w[c] / w[d]`, because both weights are now ratios to the same root.
hints: Express each variable as a multiple of one representative variable in its connected group. Then `c / d` is a ratio of two known multiples.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.insight: An in-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, so stop at the `k`-th visited node.
steps: Use an explicit stack. Push nodes while you move left from the current node. `h` is the tree height.
Pop a node and decrease `k`.
If `k` becomes 0, return the value of the node.
Else, move to the right child and repeat.
For frequent updates, store subtree sizes in each node to find the answer in `O(h)`.
hints: In a BST, all values in the left subtree of a node are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. Which visit order gives increasing values?

find-k-closest-elements.insight: Binary search for the left end of the window of size `k`, and compare the values `arr[mid]` and `arr[mid + k]` at its two edges.
steps: Set `lo = 0` and `hi = n - k`.
While `lo < hi`, set `mid = (lo + hi) / 2`.
If `x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x`, set `lo = mid + 1`. Else, set `hi = mid`.
The tie case keeps the left value, because the smaller value wins a tie.
Return `arr[lo..lo + k - 1]`.
hints: The answer is `k` contiguous values. For a start `i`, compare `x - arr[i]` with `arr[i + k] - x` to decide whether a later start is better.

asteroid-collision.insight: A stack holds the survivors, and a collision occurs only when a negative asteroid meets a positive asteroid on top of the stack.
steps: For each asteroid `x`, push `x` if `x > 0`.
Else, while the stack is not empty and its top is positive and smaller than `-x`, pop it.
If the stack is not empty and its top equals `-x`, pop it and drop `x`.
Else, if the stack is empty or the top is negative, push `x`.
Return the stack.
hints: A collision occurs only when a left-moving asteroid meets the most recent surviving right-moving asteroid. Keep the survivors in order.

reorganize-string.insight: Greedy fill: if no letter occurs more than `(n + 1) / 2` times, place the letters on even indices first, then odd indices.
steps: Count each letter. If the maximum count is more than `(n + 1) / 2`, return an empty string.
Order the letters so that the most frequent letter comes first.
Set `i = 0` and place each copy of each letter at index `i`, then add 2 to `i`.
When `i` reaches `n` or more, set `i = 1`.
Return the filled string.
hints: Copies of the most frequent letter need other letters between them. Which positions keep its copies apart, and when are there too few?

count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.insight: DP: the largest all-ones square that ends at a cell is one more than the minimum of its top, left, and top-left neighbors.
steps: Let `f[i][j]` be the side of the largest all-ones square with bottom-right corner at `(i, j)`.
If `matrix[i][j] == 0`, set `f[i][j] = 0`.
Else, on the first row or column, set `f[i][j] = 1`.
Else, set `f[i][j]` to the minimum of `f[i-1][j]`, `f[i][j-1]`, and `f[i-1][j-1]`, plus 1.
Add each `f[i][j]` to the answer, because a cell with side `s` ends `s` squares.
hints: If the largest all-ones square that ends at a cell has side `s`, that cell ends `s` squares. Its top, left, and top-left neighbors limit `s`.

combination-sum-iv.insight: DP over the sum, with the sum in the outer loop and each number in the inner loop, counts ordered sequences instead of sets.
steps: Make `f` of size `target + 1`, filled with 0. Set `f[0] = 1`.
For each sum `i` from 1 to `target`, loop over each `x` in `nums`.
If `x <= i`, add `f[i - x]` to `f[i]`. Skip values above `2^31 - 1`, because they cannot reach `target`.
Return `f[target]`. Put the sum loop outside, so that each order counts.
hints: Order matters, so look at the last number of the sequence. The ways to reach `i` add the ways to reach `i - x` for each `x`.

intersection-of-two-linked-lists.insight: Two pointers that each walk both lists in turn travel the same total length, so they meet at the intersection or at null.
steps: Set `a = headA` and `b = headB`.
While `a != b`, move `a` to `a.next`, or to `headB` when `a` is null.
In the same loop, move `b` to `b.next`, or to `headA` when `b` is null.
Return `a`. It is null when the lists do not intersect.
hints: A walk of list A then list B has the same length as a walk of list B then list A. Where do two such walks meet?

number-of-closed-islands.insight: Flood fill each land region with DFS, and count the region only if no cell of it is on the grid border.
steps: For each land cell with value 0, start a DFS and count it as a new region.
In the DFS, mark each visited cell as water so that you do not visit it again.
Return false from the DFS if any cell of the region is on the border.
Visit all four neighbors even after a false result, so that the full region gets marked.
Add 1 to the answer only when the DFS returns true.
hints: A land region is closed only if none of its cells touch the grid border. Visit each whole region and check this condition.

recover-binary-search-tree.insight: An in-order traversal of a BST is sorted, so the two swapped nodes show up as one or two drops in that order.
steps: Set `prev`, `first`, and `second` to null. Do an in-order traversal, where `prev` is the last visited node.
At each `node`, if `prev` is not null and `prev.val > node.val`, set `second = node`. Also set `first = prev` if `first` is null.
Set `prev = node` after this check.
After the traversal, swap the values of `first` and `second`.
The recursion uses `O(h)` space, where `h` is the tree height. Use Morris traversal for `O(1)` extra space.
hints: The in-order values of a BST increase. After two nodes swap values, this order shows one or two places where a value drops.

largest-divisible-subset.insight: After a sort, divisibility is transitive along a chain, so use LIS-style DP where each value extends a chain that ends at a divisor.
steps: Sort `nums` in ascending order.
Set every `f[i] = 1` and `prev[i] = -1`. `f[i]` is the longest chain that ends at `nums[i]`, and `prev[i]` is the index before it.
For each `j < i` with `nums[i] % nums[j] == 0`, set `f[i] = f[j] + 1` and `prev[i] = j` if this is larger.
Find the index `k` with the largest `f[k]`.
Start at `k`. Add `nums[k]` to the subset and set `k = prev[k]` until `k == -1`. Return the subset.
hints: After you order the values from small to large, a set is valid when each value divides the next one. Find the longest such chain.

find-and-replace-in-string.insight: Mark each valid match on the original indices first, then build the result in one left-to-right pass so that indices do not shift.
steps: Make an array `op` of size `n`, filled with -1.
For each operation `i`, if `sources[i]` occurs in `s` at `indices[i]`, set `op[indices[i]] = i`.
Scan `s` with index `j`. If `op[j]` is not -1, append `targets[op[j]]` and skip the length of `sources[op[j]]`.
Else, append `s[j]` and move to `j + 1`.
Return the built string. `L` is the total length of all input strings.
hints: A replacement changes the output length, but every later match still refers to a position in the original string.

design-linked-list.insight: A singly linked list with a dummy head and a size counter makes every insert and delete the same walk. Let `n` be the list length.
steps: Store a dummy head node and a count `size`.
For `get(index)`, return -1 if `index` is out of range. Else, walk `index + 1` steps from the dummy and return the value.
For `addAtIndex(index, val)`, do nothing if `index > size`. Else, walk `index` steps from the dummy and link a new node after it.
Implement `addAtHead` as `addAtIndex(0, val)` and `addAtTail` as `addAtIndex(size, val)`.
For `deleteAtIndex(index)`, check the range, walk `index` steps, and unlink the next node. Update `size` on each change.
hints: Keep a dummy node before the head and a size counter. Then every insert and delete walks to the node before the index.

integer-break.insight: Math greedy: parts of size 3 give the largest product, but a remainder of 1 must change one 3 into a 4.
steps: If `n <= 3`, return `n - 1`, because at least two parts are necessary.
Else, return `3^(n / 3) * 2`.
hints: For `n > 4`, parts of size 3 give the largest product, and a part of size 1 adds nothing. What do you do when `n % 3 == 1`?

final-value-of-variable-after-performing.insight: The middle character of each operation is `+` for an increment and `-` for a decrement, so add 1 or subtract 1.
steps: Set `x = 0`.
For each operation `op`, add 1 if `op[1] == '+'`, else subtract 1.
Return `x`.
hints: The middle character of every operation gives the direction: `+` or `-`.

build-an-array-with-stack-operations.insight: Simulate the stream: a number not in `target` needs Push and Pop, and a number in `target` needs only Push.
steps: Set `cur = 1`, the next number from the stream.
For each `x` in `target`, while `cur < x`, add Push and Pop, then increase `cur`.
Add Push for `x` and increase `cur`.
Stop after the last value of `target`, and do not read more numbers.
Return the list of operations.
hints: The stream gives the numbers in order, so a number not in `target` still enters the stack. It cannot stay there.

strictly-palindromic-number.insight: Brainteaser: in base `n - 2`, every `n > 4` is written as `12`, which is not a palindrome, so the answer is always false.
steps: For `n = 4`, base 2 gives `100`, which is not a palindrome.
For `n > 4`, base `n - 2` gives `12`, which is not a palindrome.
Return false for all inputs.
hints: Write `n` in base `n - 2`. What are its digits when `n > 4`?

subarrays-with-k-different-integers.insight: Exactly `k` distinct equals at most `k` minus at most `k - 1`, and a sliding window counts the at-most case.
steps: Write `atMost(t)`, which counts subarrays with at most `t` distinct values.
In `atMost`, keep a count map and a left pointer `l`. For each right index `r`, add `nums[r]`.
While the map has more than `t` keys, remove `nums[l]` and increase `l`. Delete keys that reach 0.
Add `r - l + 1` to the total for each `r`.
Return `atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1)`.
hints: Exactly `k` distinct values equals at most `k` distinct values minus at most `k - 1` distinct values. The at-most count is easier to find.

maximum-level-sum-of-a-binary-tree.insight: Use BFS level by level, sum each level, and update the answer only on a strictly larger sum to keep the smallest level.
steps: Put the root in a queue. Set `level = 0` and `best` to the smallest possible value.
While the queue is not empty, increase `level` and pop all nodes of the current level.
Add their values to a sum and push their children.
If the sum is greater than `best`, set `best` to the sum and `ans = level`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Process the tree one level at a time and sum each level. Change the answer only on a strictly larger sum to keep the smallest level.

divide-array-in-sets-of-k-consecutive-nu.insight: Greedy from the smallest value: the smallest remaining number must start a group, so it takes the next `k - 1` numbers too.
steps: If `n % k != 0`, return false.
Count each value in a map, and sort the values.
For each value `x` in ascending order with `cnt[x] > 0`, take `c = cnt[x]`.
For each `y` from `x` to `x + k - 1`, return false if `cnt[y] < c`. Else, subtract `c` from `cnt[y]`.
Return true after the loop.
hints: The smallest remaining number must start a group. So it also uses one copy of each of the next `k - 1` numbers.

design-parking-system.insight: Keep one counter of free slots for each car type, so each request is a constant-time check and decrement.
steps: Store `cnt = [0, big, medium, small]` so that `carType` is the index.
In `addCar`, return false if `cnt[carType] == 0`.
Else, decrease `cnt[carType]` and return true.
hints: Each car type uses only its own slots, so keep one counter of free slots for each type.

pascals-triangle-ii.insight: Update one row in place from right to left, so each new value uses the old values on its left.
steps: Make an array `f` of size `rowIndex + 1`, filled with 1.
For each row `i` from 2 to `rowIndex`, loop `j` from `i - 1` down to 1.
Set `f[j] = f[j] + f[j - 1]`.
Return `f`. The right-to-left order keeps the old row values that you still need.
hints: Each new value is the sum of the two old values above it. If you update one array from right to left, the old values you need stay there.

score-of-a-string.insight: Sum the absolute ASCII differences of each adjacent pair in one scan.
steps: Set `score = 0`.
For each `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, add `abs(s[i] - s[i - 1])` to `score`.
Return `score`.
hints: Each adjacent pair adds `abs(s[i] - s[i - 1])`, so one scan over the string gives the score.

valid-mountain-array.insight: Two pointers climb from both ends while the values strictly rise; a valid mountain makes them stop at the same inner peak.
steps: If `n < 3`, return false.
Move `i` right from 0 while `i + 1 < n` and `arr[i] < arr[i + 1]`.
Move `j` left from `n - 1` while `j > 0` and `arr[j - 1] > arr[j]`.
Return true only if `i == j`, `i > 0`, and `j < n - 1`. The peak cannot be an endpoint.
hints: Climb from the left while the values rise, and climb from the right while the values rise. A valid mountain makes both climbs stop at the same inner index.

base-7.insight: Convert by repeated division by 7, and handle zero and the sign as special cases.
steps: If `num == 0`, return "0".
Remember the sign and set `num` to its absolute value.
While `num > 0`, append `num % 7` and set `num = num / 7`.
Reverse the digits, add `-` if the input was negative, and return the string.
hints: Repeated division by 7 gives the digits from last to first. Handle zero and the negative sign as special cases.

binary-tree-preorder-traversal.insight: An explicit stack does preorder without recursion: pop a node, record it, then push the right child before the left child.
steps: If `root` is null, return an empty list.
Push `root` on a stack.
While the stack is not empty, pop a node and append its value.
Push the right child, then the left child, if they exist. The left child then comes out first.
Return the list of values.
hints: Preorder visits a node before its children. Without function calls, keep the pending nodes and add the right child before the left child.

shortest-unsorted-continuous-subarray.insight: Two scans give the bounds: the last index below the left-to-right running maximum, and the first index above the right-to-left running minimum.
steps: Set `right = -1` and `left = 0`, so a sorted array gives length 0.
Set `mx = nums[0]` and scan from left to right. If `nums[i] < mx`, set `right = i`. Then set `mx = max(mx, nums[i])`.
Set `mn = nums[n - 1]` and scan from right to left. If `nums[i] > mn`, set `left = i`. Then set `mn = min(mn, nums[i])`.
Return `right - left + 1`.
hints: A value smaller than some earlier value must be inside the subarray, and so must a value larger than some later value.

sum-of-distances-in-tree.insight: Tree DP with rerooting: when the root moves to a child, its subtree nodes get one step closer and all others one step farther.
steps: Build an adjacency list for the tree.
Run a first DFS from node 0 to get `size[v]`, the subtree size of each node.
In the same DFS, add each node depth to get `ans[0]`.
Run a second DFS from node 0. For each child `c` of `v`, set `ans[c] = ans[v] - size[c] + (n - size[c])`.
Return `ans`.
hints: Move the reference node from `v` to its child `c`. Nodes in the subtree of `c` get one step closer, and all other nodes get one step farther.

hamming-distance.insight: The XOR of `x` and `y` has a 1 bit exactly where the bits differ, so count the 1 bits of `x ^ y`.
steps: Set `z = x ^ y` and `count = 0`.
While `z > 0`, set `z = z & (z - 1)` to clear the lowest 1 bit, and add 1 to the count.
Return the count.
hints: The XOR of `x` and `y` has a 1 bit exactly where their bits differ. Count those 1 bits.

odd-even-jump.insight: Find each index's odd and even jump target with sorted order and a monotonic stack, then fill two reachability DP arrays from the right.
steps: Sort indices by `(arr[i], i)` and scan them in that order with a stack of indices.
Pop each stack index less than the current index, and set its `higher` target to the current index. Then push the current index.
Repeat with indices sorted by `(-arr[i], i)` to get each `lower` target.
Set `odd[n-1] = even[n-1] = true`. For `i` from `n - 2` down, set `odd[i] = even[higher[i]]`.
Also set `even[i] = odd[lower[i]]`. A missing target gives false.
Return the count of indices with `odd[i]` true, because the first jump is odd.
hints: Find the odd jump target and the even jump target of each index first. From the right, an odd jump from `i` reaches the end if an even jump from its target reaches the end.

minimum-distance-to-type-a-word-using-tw.insight: One finger always rests on the last typed letter, so the DP state needs only the position of the other finger.
steps: Let `dp[j]` be the minimum cost when one finger is on the previous letter and the other is on `j`.
Use `j = 26` for an unplaced finger, with move cost 0. Set `dp[26] = 0` and all others to infinity.
For each next letter `b` after letter `a`, move the finger on `a`: set `new[j] = dp[j] + dist(a, b)` for every `j`.
Then move the other finger: for each `j`, set `new[a] = min(new[a], dp[j] + dist(j, b))`. Then set `dp = new`.
Use `dist(p, q) = |p / 6 - q / 6| + |p % 6 - q % 6|` with integer division. Return the minimum of the final `dp`.
hints: After each letter, one finger always rests on that letter. So the state needs only the position of the other finger.

inverse-coin-change.insight: Rebuild the coins in increasing order with unbounded knapsack counts: amount `i` is a coin exactly when the current count is one short.
steps: Make `f` of size `n + 1`, filled with 0, and set `f[0] = 1`. It counts ways with the coins found so far.
For each amount `i` from 1 to `n`, compare `f[i]` with `numWays[i]`, which is at index `i - 1` in the input.
